articles.title: The Myth of ‘Stable Russia’: Why Washington Must Stop Fearing Russia’s Collapse
articles.body:
Daily reality for millions of Ukrainians is facing strikes by Russian kamikaze drones and ballistic missiles. Yet, amid the destruction, we are forced to confront a deeply painful paradox: the weapons raining down on our cities are heavily powered by American microelectronics.
For years, Western – and particularly Washington – policymakers have been paralyzed by a phantom fear: “What happens if Russia collapses?”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This anxiety over a fragmented, nuclear-armed state has led to a slow, drip-feed approach to arming Ukraine. But while the West worries about preserving a stable Russia, it is blind to the fact that the so-called “Russian Bear” has devolved into a “hollow imperial machine,” propped up entirely by Western corporate negligence.
The 2026 paradox
Russia is incapable of manufacturing even basic circuit boards for its jet-powered drones and missiles. All these “Shaheds,” “Lancets,” and “Iskanders” fly using microchips smuggled through Central Asia. This is not a matter of old, pre-war stockpiles.
According to official data from Ukraine’s Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, recent examinations of downed “Shahed-238” drones and “Iskander-M” missiles revealed hundreds of foreign components, prominently including parts from US giants like Texas Instruments, Amphenol, and ON Semiconductor.
Kallas Rebukes Lavrov Over ‘Lies’ and Falsehoods at G20
Shockingly, some of these microchips were manufactured as recently as 2026.
This proves that the smuggling networks are active right now. While these Western corporations may not sell directly to Russia, their products are systematically bypassing export controls, flooding through front companies in intermediary countries. How can the West fear Russian military might when that very might is entirely dependent on bypassed US export controls?
The collapse is already happening
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s regime is a house of cards. The West must stop fearing its collapse and look at the reality on the ground.
Logistics are burning: The unwritten pact between people and regime of stability in Russia is dead. Massive fires at critical logistics hubs and data-centers, like the giant Wildberries, Ozon and Yandex warehouses, are no coincidence. The regime hides military dual-use goods inside civilian supply chains, and as a result, the civilian network is crumbling.
Economic and infrastructural suicide: Top Russian economists openly predict severe shortages. To sustain the military meat grinder—which consumes over 1,000 Russian lives daily – the regime is draining its economy of labor.
Furthermore, domestic infrastructure is rotting away: as federal budgets are aggressively funneled into the military-industrial complex, regional utility systems and public housing infrastructure (JKH) are facing unprecedented systemic failures and physical decay, leaving ordinary citizens to freeze or suffer chronic grid collapses.
The North Korea state is impossible: Some believe Putin will turn Russia into an isolated, manageable totalitarian camp. But you cannot lock down the largest landmass on Earth with people who have already tasted freedom and global integration. As Moscow tightens the screws to feed its war machine, regional elites will inevitably push back to save their populations from the Kremlin’s grinder.
Ultimately, the regions will choose development and democracy over imperial ruin – things the federal center, controlled by Moscow’s mafia-like “Ozero” cooperative and security-criminal structures of the Federal Security Service (FSB), has always denied them.
Military collapse: Beneath the Kremlin’s aggressive rhetoric and nuclear threats lies a hollowed-out system. Russia is no longer the military superpower it claims to be. Its defense-industrial complex, built on the legacy of the USSR (including Ukrainian factories and engineers) and now entirely dependent on stolen Western technology and components smuggled through gray markets, is facing a systemic collapse.
When a regime that claims to rival NATO is reduced to begging for artillery shells from North Korea and kamikaze drones from Iran, it is a clear signal: the sanctions are working, and the Ukrainian resistance is bleeding the empire dry. The recent catastrophic failures of Russia’s prized strategic weapons, such as the Sarmat missile program, only highlight this irreversible degradation.
The call to Washington
As lawmakers in the US Senate and officials in the FBI and Department of Commerce debate “escalation,” American technology continues to flow into Russian weapons. The hesitation in Washington does not prevent Russia’s collapse; it merely prolongs the agony and costs countless Ukrainian lives.
It is time for the West to abandon the illusion of a stable Russia. The FBI and the Department of Commerce must aggressively dismantle these gray-market supply chains.
You cannot defeat an enemy if your own technology is unknowingly – or indifferently – supplying its arsenal. Stop holding back long-range capabilities, cut off the smuggled lifelines, and help Ukraine finish the job. The hollow imperial machine is already burning; it is time to let it fall:first to the side of the road of history, and then into a deep ditch.
The resulting bottom line
It would seem that the only real thing Russia is currently capable of is acts of terror and the genocide of Ukrainians – as well as of its own multi-ethnic population.
It is time to drop the fear of Russia’s transformation and give Ukraine the full means to dismantle this aggressive machine once and for all. Stop holding back and playing it safe. Arm Ukraine decisively, so we can finally end the war that Putin is too terrified to stop.

articles.title: How Merz’s five-day Asia trip ended up being mostly about Europe
articles.body:
How Merz’s five-day Asia trip ended up being mostly about Europe
Security concerns are following the German Chancellor to Singapore, Japan and Korea. And his proposal for a new trade alliance is already facing hurdles.
KOREAN DEMILITARIZED ZONE — Friedrich Merz ended his five-day trip to Asia on Friday reflecting on Europe's past.
After visiting the blue barracks where the armistice that ended the Korean War was signed in 1953, in the Joint Security Area where North and South Korean troops stand face-to-face, the German chancellor addressed the obvious parallels between his country's history and Korea's present.
"Thoughts are running through my mind about how grateful we may be that in Germany we haven't had to experience this for 36 years," Merz said.
Advertisement
The remarks concluded a tour of Singapore, Japan and South Korea, where the chancellor was challenged by Asian capitals over security and trade cooperation — and often reminded of how the region's turmoil are intertwined with Europe's precarious moment.
'Collective security'
One only has to look across the border. Shortly before Merz arrived in the demilitarized zone, North Korea fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan. The chancellor's greatest security concerns at home — Russia’s war against Ukraine and Moscow’s threat to Europe — are increasingly becoming problems in the Asia-Pacific region as well.
The fact that Pyongyang is able to launch so many ballistic missiles, testing and expanding its long-range strike capabilities, is directly linked to its cooperation with Russia. North Korea has been sending soldiers to the Russian front in Ukraine for two years and in return benefited from combat experience and technology transfers.
North Korean state television on Thursday showed leader Kim Jong Un with new military drones, including a potential stealth drone, underscoring the great strides the country is also making in drone development. These are serious security issues that other countries in the region, including Japan, cannot ignore.
Besides provocations from Pyongyang, there is China, which is not only becoming increasingly dominant in trade but also casting its eye toward Taiwan, making far-reaching territorial claims in the South China Sea and putting strong pressure on critics such as Japan. And there is Russia, which is forging close military ties with Beijing and carrying out joint bomber flights with the Chinese air force near the Japanese border.
“Russia’s war against Ukraine is ever-present here in the region,” Merz told reporters following his visit to the border. “There is no longer such a thing as unilateral security in the world, only collective security,” he added, underscoring his call to “work closely” with Japan, South Korea and Singapore “on security policy issues” and in the defense industry.
Advertisement
Middle power struggle
This German offer has generated considerable interest. Given Berlin’s position as Ukraine’s largest supporter, German defense companies are highly active in the war-torn country and cooperate with local manufacturers, giving them access to rapid technological developments. This makes them attractive to Asian partners who fear falling behind North Korea and China as they benefit from their cooperation with Russia.
The fact that the chancellor traveled with a large business delegation — the kind previously seen only on visits to China — underscores this focus. Among the companies were several defense firms, including aircraft manufacturer Airbus, air defense manufacturer Diehl Defense and drone specialist Quantum-Systems. Japan welcomed the cooperation, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaking of a “premium partnership” with Germany.
Yet Merz's trip was about more than defense deals. The chancellor used his visits to warn against violations of international law by Russia but also increasingly by China and the United States. “We are on the threshold of a new era,” he said in Tokyo. “We are witnessing how the major powers are pursuing a new policy and how international rules are eroding.”
Friedrich Merz arriving in Japan on Oct. 28, 2026. | Hans Von Der Burchard
His words echoed a similar warning issued by German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier during a parallel trip to Beijing. “An order that was never perfect, but at least served as the foundation for international cooperation, is eroding. Lawlessness looms. I see this as a great danger for all of us,” said Steinmeier.
To counter this trend, Merz built on Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's proposal that “middle powers” should team up to better defend themselves in the face of unreliable major powers and toothless international organizations.
In speeches in Tokyo and Seoul, Merz proposed a “global political alliance for rules-based trade.” Medium-sized powers such as the EU, Asian nations, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the South American Mercosur trade bloc should “coordinate” and “act together” if others challenged international rules “or if economic pressure were to be exerted,” said the chancellor.
Advertisement
It's a thinly veiled reference to Chinese threats to restrict access to rare earth metals and the tariff threats made by U.S. President Donald Trump. Merz also said the alliance could strengthen the World Trade Organization and seek to unblock the nomination of judges to the organization's appellate body.
“Considerable concern” over Franco-German car deal
During his trip, however, Merz experienced firsthand just how difficult it is to put such an ambitious proposal into practice when special interests complicate an alliance of small and medium-sized powers.
This became most evident when the Asian countries issued a sharp protest over planned “Made in Europe” rules for the car industry. Under a proposal agreed by Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, Brussels would restrict subsidies for cars to vehicles produced inside the EU, Switzerland and the U.K., putting foreign manufacturers at a disadvantage.
In polite but direct terms, South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung told reporters he had “asked Merz for support so that Korea would be treated like the EU member states.” A similar complaint was voiced in Japan.
“That was, in fact, a topic that surprised me a bit, given the intensity with which it was presented,” Merz told reporters before returning to Germany on Friday evening. He admitted that the Franco-German proposal had “sparked considerable concern in the region — in Singapore, Japan, and Korea — that we may be facing a new wave of protectionism in Europe, that we are closing ourselves off from other countries.”
Merz vowed to take those complaints “very seriously” and raise them at the next EU leaders' summit. Yet they are a sharp reminder of how much industry-specific details can hamper the implementation of his proposed broader alliance.
Advertisement
The chancellor's trip also revealed challenges when it comes to security cooperation: A request for Japan to supply Patriot anti-aircraft missiles to Ukraine fell flat. And it remains unclear whether Tokyo continues to contribute several billions to a new Ukraine loan next year, as Brussels hopes.
A Japanese diplomat, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, posed a different question to the German delegation: “How exactly will you help us if China attacks Taiwan?”

articles.title: Trump speaks with Netanyahu shortly after discussing military operations with senior commanders
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump addressed overnight on Sunday the possibility of an additional military strike in Iran, claiming the United States is capable of hitting what remains of the Iranian nuclear program "in just ten minutes."
"There are 'one or two sites' left that need to be dealt with, including Pickaxe Mountain. We can do it in ten minutes. We have a plan for it, and we can execute it very quickly," the president said.
Referring to negotiations with Iran, Trump later said, "They want to reach an agreement, and we will see what happens. Things are moving along fine, but they are not really reliable. They reach an agreement and then back out. They want to reach an agreement, and we will see if they actually sign it."
Hours earlier, Trump spoke by phone with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as the United States prepares to resume strikes on Iran, according to a report in the Wall Street Journal.
The call took place after Trump discussed options for resuming military operations with senior military commanders, including a meeting with CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine.
US, Israel posture for strikes, but war unlikely to occur before midterm elections
According to previous reports, the Pentagon reinforced air defense systems, ammunition, and military equipment in the Middle East in recent weeks, while simultaneously repositioning forces from bases that could be vulnerable to an Iranian retaliatory attack.
The timing is particularly sensitive politically. Trump is in the final stretch of the campaign for the congressional midterm elections, which will take place this Tuesday, November 3.
The war with Iran and rising fuel prices in the United States weigh heavily on Republicans, and the president seeks to bolster support for his party in the final days of the campaign.
As such, the United States has reportedly been pushing back the timeline for war with Iran, with the latter itself reportedly deliberately prolonging negotiations ahead of the US midterm elections.
Defense officials assess that despite preparations by CENTCOM and Israel for a strike on Iran, the White House will not order an operation against the Islamic regime before the elections take place unless it detects preparations for a surprise attack.
Israel's defense establishment has remained ambiguous regarding preparations for a possible escalation with Iran, as the White House attempted to offer the Iranian regime another opportunity to return to negotiations, according to Israeli defense assessments.
Defense officials assess that the Iranians, who are facing an economic crisis that is worsening from week to week, will not sign an agreement requiring them to completely abandon their nuclear program, and certainly will not agree to stop producing ballistic missiles that now also threaten Europe.
US Air Force aircrafts arrive at IAF bases
Last week, ten US Air Force (USAF) transport aircraft arrived at IAF bases in southern Israel as part of a larger Middle East air convoy transferring military equipment across the region, KAN News reported.
The aircraft, which came from Texas' Fort Bliss base, are likely stocked with air defense systems intended to protect regional assets amid reported US warnings earlier this week of a potential "short, focused war with Iran," according to KAN.
Other aircraft in the air convoy landed in Jordan, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia, with the KAN report coming after an earlier report that the US had transferred an additional Patriot system to the region pending a potential escalation with Iran.
An Israeli source told KAN that the US and Israel are closely coordinating on Iran, with reports that an additional US naval aircraft carrier will join American forces in the region, alongside an additional Marine unit.\
Two weeks ago, dozens of Israel Air Force fighter jets flew "as far as the Iranian border" before turning around and returning to Israel in a practice sortie, according to an Axios report citing US and Israeli officials.
Tehran: Ready for negotiations, but also for war
Alongside diplomatic signals, Iran recently escalated its threats toward the United States and Israel.
According to an announcement published in Tehran, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered military commanders to prepare for an immediate and powerful response, without geographical limits, in the event of an additional attack.
Iranian Chief of Staff General Ali Abdollahi warned that his country has expanded its list of potential targets and that another American attack would be met with a broad response. According to him, Iran will be the one to determine the end date of any new war.
Conversely, the US administration continues to stress that it prefers a diplomatic agreement over a strike. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said today that if Trump wanted to act militarily, he would have done so weeks or months ago, though he clarified that the United States possesses all necessary capabilities for a successful operation.
At this stage, talks with Iran and military preparations are proceeding in parallel. The report of the phone call between Trump and Netanyahu underscores coordination between Washington and Jerusalem, though it remains unclear whether diplomatic contacts will yield an agreement or if the American president will choose to resume strikes following the elections.

articles.title: Ukraine: Russian attacks leave tens of thousands without power
articles.body:
Ukraine: Russian attacks leave tens of thousands without power
Published October 31, 2026last updated November 1, 2026
What you need to know
- Russian strikes leave tens of thousands across Ukraine without power
- Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire limited to Kherson region set to expire
- Oleshky civilians arrive in Ukrainian territory from Belarus
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says preparations for talks with US and Russia underway after meeting with Turkey's Recep Tayyip Erdogan
Here is a roundup of events from Russia's war in Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday, October 31 and November 1:
Preparations for trilateral talks underway, Zelenskyy says after Erdogan meeting
Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with his Turkish counterpart Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Istanbul on Saturday evening for talks that the Ukrainian president said included preparations for a three-way summit between Ukraine, Russia and the United States.
He said the meeting would be held in the first half of November.
"President Erdogan and I discussed the prospects for this format and other possibilities, including ways to involve Turkey and all of Europe, as well as the possibility of holding meetings here in Turkey," Zelenskyy said.
"At every level, Russia must be sent signals that there is no alternative to peace and that support for Ukraine will not diminish."
Previous rounds of talks between Ukraine and Russia brokered by Turkey failed to yield a lasting peace agreement.
Describing the meetings as "important and substantive," Zelenskyy said he and Erdogan had also discussed security issues concerning shipping through the Black Sea.
"This includes food security, and today President Erdogan and I agreed to work on a Black Sea grain corridor to ensure that the corridor exists and operates effectively," the Ukrainian leader told a press conference.
Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire for Kherson set to expire
A ceasefire limited to the Kherson region in eastern Ukraine that was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump was set to expire on Sunday evening, after neither Russia nor Ukraine announced an extension.
The rare truce, which began on Tuesday, is the longest since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The ceasefire allowed for a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
While neither side reported violations of the ceasefire, Russian strikes continued overnight, with fresh power outages reported across Ukraine on Sunday, its energy ministry and president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian strikes on the Russian-occupied region of Luhansk killed at least four people since Sunday evening, Russian-backed local authorities said.
Russian strikes leave vast numbers of Ukrainian homes without power
Hundreds of thousands of households lost electricity after overnight Russian strikes hit energy infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.
In a post on X, the Ukrainian president said energy infrastructure in four regions — Dnipro, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, and Khmelnytskyi — had been struck.
"Substations, transformers, and power lines that supply electricity to our people's homes were targeted. Repair crews are working everywhere. As of now, hundreds of thousands of families remain without power," Zelenskyy said Sunday.
He added that "massive Russian attacks on Ukraine's other critical infrastructure are also continuing unabated."
"The intensity of the strikes is very high," he said, accusing Russia of seeking to exploit Ukraine's shortage of interceptors used to shoot down ballistic missiles.
Zelenskyy repeated his call to the US, Europe and Ukraine's other partners to do more to deliver missiles and other weaponry to better defend against the Russian attacks.
"These deliveries cannot take years. Russia is destroying infrastructure and killing our people right now, and it is betting on ballistic missiles this winter. Accordingly, decisions on air defense must also be implemented now," the Ukrainian president said.
Kremlin wants initial Ukraine talks without Europe
Russia wants the opening rounds of renewed peace negotiations to involve only Moscow, Kyiv and Washington, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.
Asked whether European countries should participate, Ushakov pointed to Russia's existing contacts with the United States.
"We have working contacts with the Americans," Interfax quoted him as saying. It was therefore "logical" for at least the first rounds to take place in a trilateral format, he added.
Russia reports major damage after drone attack near refinery
A drone attack caused "significant damage" to an industrial facility east of Moscow, a Russian governor said, following Ukrainian reports of a strike on a major oil refinery.
Nizhny Novgorod Governor Gleb Nikitin reported a "massive drone attack" overnight, saying more than 100 drones were destroyed. Preliminary information indicated no casualties, he added.
Nikitin did not identify the damaged facility. Ukrainian media reported that the target was the Kstovo oil refinery, describing it as one of Russia's largest.
The reports could not be independently verified.
Authorities said they were taking steps to keep fuel available at gas stations.
Russia said Ukraine had resumed attacks on its refineries after a pause. US President Donald Trump had pressured Kyiv to stop such strikes, blaming them for rising diesel prices.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil and gas facilities in response to Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
Welcome back to our live coverage
Welcome back to our coverage. Follow the latest developments throughout the day.
We're pausing the blog for today
Thank you for joining today. We'll be back with the latest developments on Sunday.
IN PHOTOS: Evacuees reunite with family after fleeing Oleshky
Ukraine spent months demanding that Russia allow people to evacuate out of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, after food delivery supplies stopped earlier this year.
Hundreds of people made their way out on Saturday.
Wadephul says Europe and US are 'on the same side' on Russia
At a news conference after the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, DW correspondent Benjamin Alvarez Gruber asked German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul whether Sergey Lavrov's presence and the possibility of Russian President Vladimir Putin attending the G20 summit in Doral, Florida, in December signaled a normalization of relations with Russia.
Wadephul said the US and European countries were "on the same side."
"Speaking to the Russian Foreign Minister is not a concession we're making to Russia, but it is normal to speak," he said, adding that foreign ministers must be prepared to engage even with adversaries.
"You don't have to negotiate with partners, but you have to negotiate with somebody who has a different position and who's somehow also an adversary to freedom and to security in Europe. So it is necessary that we speak, and for that reason I think it was useful," Wadephul added.
The G20 foreign ministers skipped their traditional family photo at a meeting in Atlanta on Friday, amid objections from several European countries, Australia and Canada to appearing alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
Wadephul said: "We are not in a position that it was necessary or useful or a good idea to have a family photo because in the very situation we are in, Russia does not really show an interest to share our values and to share our interests."
The US State Department removed the photo from the agenda to prevent it from becoming a distraction or a spectacle.
Zelenskyy in Istanbul for talks on Black Sea shipping
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in Istanbul for talks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, with Black Sea shipping among the issues on the agenda.
"We're working to strengthen the protection of our people, our bilateral partnership with Türkiye, and real diplomatic prospects," Zelenskyy wrote on X, using the alternative spelling for Turkey.
The Ukrainian president also plans to meet Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, the Istanbul-based Orthodox Christian leader.
US warns Russia of a 'mass casualty' plot to attack Moscow
The US embassy in Russia warned there was "a credible threat of a mass casualty event" at a historical site in southern Moscow.
"The US government is coordinating with appropriate Russian authorities on a response," the US embassy in Moscow said in a post on X.
The alleged plot would target the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve, a sprawling complex of palaces and gardens built under the orders of Empress Catherine the Great in the late 18th century.
Russia's federal law enforcement agency, the FSB, said it received the warning and was doing "appropriate work" in response to it, according to Russian news agencies.
Ukraine says it hit Russian rocket fuel factory
Ukraine's military said it struck a factory producing solid rocket fuel in Russia's Rostov region, setting a warehouse ablaze and damaging four production workshops.
The attack on the Kamensky plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky involved drones and Neptune missiles, according to the Ukrainian account.
The military said the plant supplies fuel for ammunition used by Russia's Uragan, Smerch and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as other missiles and air-launched weapons.
Ukraine also reported strikes on four Russian military supply depots in occupied parts of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Luhansk regions.
The claims have not been independently verified.
Ukraine welcomes civilians from Oleshky after complex evacuation effort
The first evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky have reached Ukrainian-controlled territory amid a localized ceasefire.
Oleshky, near the front line in the southern Kherson region, has been occupied by Russia since 2022. In recent weeks, the town has faced a severe humanitarian crisis.
Both sides have recently agreed to a localized ceasefire to extract the estimated 2,000 civilians still in Oleshky, down from its pre-invasion population of 24,000.
Moscow and Kyiv credited the US first lady, Melania Trump, with brokering the truce.
Residents were given a choice to go to Russia or travel via Belarus to the part of Ukraine controlled by Kyiv.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the initiative required "an enormous amount of work."
He said evacuees included a 1-year-old baby and a 94-year-old resident of Oleshky. The evacuees brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon, according to Lubinets.
He expressed hope that the Oleshky arrangement can be replicated elsewhere.
The truce started on Tuesday and is due to end on Sunday night.
Welcome to our coverage
Welcome to DW's coverage of the latest developments in the Russian war on Ukraine.
You join us as Ukraine welcomes evacuees from Oleshky, a town in the Kherson region that has been occupied by Russia since 2022.
Meanwhile, Kyiv claimed it hit the Kamensky plant in the Rostov region deep inside Russia. The factory produces solid fuel for rockets and missiles.
Stay tuned for the latest news and analysis from the ongoing war.

articles.title: Zelensky Says Hits on Rostov Plant, S-400 Post, Pantsir Cost Russia $70M
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces have struck the “Kamensky” missile-production chemical enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region alongside high-value Russian air defense assets, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Nov. 1.
He added that the attack destroyed a Pantsir-S2 surface-to-air missile, an anti-aircraft artillery complex, and an S-400 Triumf command-and-staff vehicle with an aggregate value of approximately $70 million.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Writing on Telegram, Zelensky characterized the precision strikes as an application of Kyiv’s sovereign long-range sanctions directly against the Kremlin’s defense-industrial base and air defense shield.
“Our long-range sanctions – in the Rostov region,” Zelensky stated. “The Kamensky plant was hit – an enterprise of the Russian military-industrial complex involved in the production of missiles.”
The president confirmed that Ukrainian forces simultaneously neutralized high-tier air defense platforms protecting the military-industrial area.
“The Ukrainian military struck a Pantsir-S2 complex and a command-and-staff vehicle of the S-400 Triumf system,” Zelensky stated.
“The total value of the struck air defense assets is about $70 million.”
Zelensky extended official commendations to the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and partner branches of the Defense Forces of Ukraine for planning and executing the precision operation.
Russia Launched 36 Ballistic Missiles, 1,940 Drones in the Last Week
“We are justly defending ourselves against Russian aggression and doing everything to reduce Russia’s capabilities to continue it,” the president emphasized.
Strategic missile propellant manufacturing at Kamensky
The targeting of the Kamensky plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, located roughly 20 kilometers east of the Ukrainian border in Rostov region, constitutes a direct blow to the Russian Federation’s production of solid rocket motors and guided munitions.
The enterprise operates as a primary supplier for the Russian defense industry, specializing in the chemical synthesis of solid rocket propellants, propulsive charges, and specialized nitrocellulose compounds.
The output of the Kamensky facility supplies propellant motors for multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), including 220mm Uragan, 300mm Smerch, and modernized 300mm Tornado-S systems, as well as specialized rocket propellants integrated into tactical guided missiles and aircraft-delivered strike weapons.
The presidential confirmation follows earlier operational assessments released by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, which reported that overnight into Saturday, Oct. 31, a coordinated strike involving strike drones and Ukrainian Navy Neptune coastal cruise missiles in a land-attack role ignited a warehouse storing finished solid rocket propellant and inflicted structural damage on four production workshops across the facility.
Broadened campaign against defense supply chains
Concurrent with the Rostov operation, Ukrainian precision units executed synchronized strikes against four Russian military logistics depots across occupied Ukrainian territories, hitting supply bases near Khartsyzk and Dokuchaievsk in Donetsk region, Novovasylivka in Zaporizhzhia region, and Novoaidar in Luhansk region.
The operation also coincides with resumed long-range interdictions against Russian downstream oil refining and chemical processing centers.
Overnight into Sunday, Nov. 1, Ukrainian strike drones penetrated Nizhny Novgorod region, striking the 17-million-ton Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez refinery and the adjacent Novogorkovskaya combined heat and power plant in Kstovo, triggering large-scale blazes across Russia’s second-largest automotive gasoline production center.

articles.title: India is running out of time on fifth-generation fighter
articles.body:
India is running out of time on fifth-generation fighter
Despite India’s increased defense spending, robust government support for domestic arms and military technology manufacturers, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s personal focus on the development of the military-industrial complex, experts warn that the Indian Air Force faces a critical squadron decline that may influence its ability to counter potential adversaries.
This paradox stems from India’s procurement policies, which do not prioritize the acquisition of advanced aircraft for the air force. Apparently, segments of India’s business elite and military leadership, possibly influenced by Western companies, are lobbying for contracts that offer questionable benefits to the country’s armed forces.
While India’s geopolitical and military rivals (China and Pakistan) invest in cutting-edge technology – such as the fifth-generation J-20 and J-35 multi-role fighters – India continues to acquire fourth-generation aircraft like the Rafale and Tejas fighters. However, such aircraft cannot address modern combat challenges or threats effectively.
The situation looks even more dire considering that the Rafale and Tejas fighters are not superior to the Su-30MKI, the primary fighter in service with the Indian Air Force, and may even fall short when it comes to certain tactical specifications. The Su-30MKI boasts significant advantages in speed, maneuverability, payload capacity, and operational range.
This raises a crucial question: why are substantial financial resources from the Indian budget allocated for the purchase of expensive aircraft (Rafale fighters cost about €160 million each) directly from the French private firm Dassault Aviation, when the state-owned Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) offers the option to procure Su-30MKI aircraft assembled under license from Russia at a considerably lower cost?
Real threats
Clearly, the rivalry between Pakistan (and China, which stands behind it) and India is not going to fade anytime soon. In fact, competition will likely intensify in the foreseeable future. A critical factor in preventing the most dangerous scenarios lies in maintaining a balance of military capabilities and defense potential between the opposing sides. So, what does the power balance look like today?
Islamabad and Beijing are heavily investing in fifth-generation multirole fighters. By 2030, Pakistan is expected to field no fewer than 40 J-35AE fighters, while the Chinese Air Force could deploy up to 500 J-20s and J-35 fighters. Additionally, the Chinese Navy may have over 50 carrier-based J-35s. In total, this amounts to about 600 fifth-generation fighters – each one of them superior to any fourth-generation aircraft.
Armed with highly effective long-range air-to-air weapons, Pakistan and China’s stealthy fifth-generation fighters will be able to launch missile attacks without being detected by Indian Air Force radar systems. Under such circumstances, India’s military aviation could face a devastating defeat, leading to humiliation and a prolonged recovery process. This is inevitable, since fifth-generation fighters surpass fourth-generation aircraft.
The strategy of overwhelming the enemy with sheer numbers and concentrating an extensive air force over specific combat zones, is fundamentally flawed: no number of Rafale or Tejas fighters can match the combat capabilities of J-20 and J-35 aircraft.
The air forces of Pakistan and China possess cutting-edge technologies like stealth capabilities, advanced radar systems capable of covertly tracking opponents, and long-range missiles that significantly outdistance those in the arsenals of Rafale and Tejas fighters.
However, if the Indian Air Force were to acquire Su-57E fighters, equipped with stealth technology, the modern N-036 Byelka radar, long-range RVV-BD missiles, and other state-of-the-art munitions, India’s ability to confront its neighbors in the above-mentioned scenarios would change dramatically.
Why Russia?
For over 70 years, Soviet and Russian aviation technology has been in service with the Indian military, demonstrating remarkable efficiency and reliability. Russia has proven to be a dependable partner in military-technical cooperation.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has praised the quality and effectiveness of Russian weapons, particularly highlighting their successful deployment during Operation Sindoor in May 2025. Moscow is eager to continue the mutually beneficial collaboration with New Delhi in the defense sector. This includes maintaining the joint Su-30MKI program and potentially organizing licensed assembly of the fifth-generation Su-57E fighter at facilities operated by India’s HAL.
The ongoing modernization of the Pakistani Air Force and the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Air Force with advanced aircraft has prompted India to take decisive actions to restore parity and the balance of power. Given the current circumstances, a swift acquisition of 50 Su-57E fighters from Russia under a fast-track mechanism, along with plans for licensed production of an additional 450 units in India, seems like the most prudent course of action. This could involve the latest two-seat variant, the Su-57D. Over the next few decades, such a project would effectively address the challenges and threats that India faces.
More than just a prototype
The Su-57 fighter jet has already entered service with the Russian Air Force and has participated in combat operations.
India contributed to the development of the fighter that served as the basis for the Su-57. In 2010, the Indian Ministry of Defense initiated the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) program to create an indigenous fifth-generation fighter. However, after more than 15 years, this program has yet to reach the flight testing stage. Serial production is not likely to commence before 2035.
Alexander Mikheev, head of Rosoboronexport, and Vadim Badekha, head of the United Aircraft Corporation (UAC), confirmed that the Su-57 aircraft – specifically its export version, the Su-57E – is already being delivered abroad. The Su-57E is available for friendly countries collaborating with Russia on defense projects. If India approaches Moscow regarding the supply of this combat aircraft, Russia would likely respond in a positive manner.
Moreover, advanced Russian technologies transferred to India under a licensing agreement will assist Indian specialists in refining and successfully implementing several national projects, including the AMCA.
Unlike American F-35s – which have struggled to maintain supersonic speeds in sustained cruise mode – the Su-57 meets all the criteria expected of a fifth-generation fighter.
For New Delhi, the Su-57 offers multiple advantages, especially since it was designed at the same bureau that developed the Su-30MKI – the Indian Air Force’s primary combat aircraft as of 2026. This continuity provides valuable benefits in terms of operational procedures, maintenance, repair, and logistical support, leveraging existing airfield, storage, and training infrastructures.
Indigenous programs
Prime Minister Narendra Modi highly supports India’s national defense industry initiatives. He made history as the first prime minister of India to fly in the cockpit of a supersonic fighter jet.
Professional pilots who have flown the Tejas aircraft praise its performance, noting it surpasses the MiG-21, which the Tejas was designed to replace under the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) program that began in 1983. However, the mission was not fulfilled; the project has faced significant delays, and by the time the Tejas was deployed in 2015, the vast majority of the 874 MiG-21s acquired by the Indian Air Force between 1963 and 1987 had already been retired due to wear and tear. Instead of 20 squadrons of MiG aircraft, by 2026, the Indian Air Force had just two Tejas squadrons consisting of 30 single-seat and six two-seat models. Field tests are being conducted to identify and rectify issues on aircraft from the initial production batch.
The 18th Squadron, formed in 2020, has already lost two Tejas planes in accidents – one in March 2024 and another in November 2025. The latter incident involved a fatal failure during a demonstration flight at an airshow in Dubai. The initial variant (Mark I) will no longer be produced, as it proved unreliable and technically inadequate.
Like many Indian projects, Tejas is plagued by delays which result in technological obsolescence by the time of production. Consequently, the substantial financial investments in such programs fail to deliver the expected returns or strengthen India’s defense capabilities.
Indian manufacturers also developed a naval version of the Tejas. Testing began in 2020 aboard the INS Vikramaditya aircraft carrier (built by Russia under Project 11430) and continued three years later on the indigenously constructed INS Vikrant. The compact design of the Tejas offers advantages for hangar storage; however, with a standard combat load, it can only operate within a few hundred miles. During combat operations, the carrier would need to approach the target closer, increasing the risk of retaliatory strikes from the enemy.
After conducting evaluations, the Indian Navy concluded that such an aircraft was not suitable for carrier operations. The official reason for rejecting the LCA-Navy was its low thrust-to-weight ratio, which prevented full utilization of the aircraft’s potential when taking off from an aircraft carrier. In response to requests from Indian industry, further tests were conducted on an upgraded version, but its performance still fell short of naval requirements.
Coming to terms with the LCA-Navy’s inability to meet expectations, Indian aerospace engineers proposed a completely new aircraft – the Twin Engine Deck Based Fighter (TEDBF), which bears a striking resemblance to the French Rafale-M. This move signifies a concession by the creators and advocates of the Tejas, acknowledging their defeat in the competition for carrier aviation. Work on the TEDBF began in 2020. The prototype’s first flight is scheduled for 2032 and serial production is anticipated in 2038.
Meanwhile, last year, the People’s Liberation Army Navy received its third aircraft carrier, the Fujian, equipped with fifth-generation J-35 fighters. Construction has also begun on the fourth Type 004 aircraft carrier. It will likely have a displacement of around 100,000 tons and accommodate an air wing of 100 aircraft, including the J-35.
Dependence on the US
In coordination with the main contractor, Indian industry continues Tejas Mark IA testing, which started in spring 2022. Without waiting for these trials to conclude, the Indian Air Force has placed two successive orders totaling 141 single-seat and 41 two-seat aircraft, scheduled for delivery between 2027 and 2032. Production will take place at two facilities in Bangalore and Nasik.
Following this, production of the Tejas Mark II is expected to commence. The first test flight has faced multiple delays and is now expected no earlier than 2028. While no firm order has been placed for this new model, the Air Force leadership hopes to eventually have 18 squadrons of Tejas aircraft, including 10 Mark II variant squadrons.
The idea to direct resources into producing fourth-generation fighters for the next decade seems imprudent, given that China has mastered mass production of fifth-generation aircraft and is set to begin transitioning to sixth-generation models in the coming years. Deliveries of Chinese J-35 fifth-generation fighters to Pakistan are underway, while existing JF-17s are being upgraded with systems and munitions developed for the J-35.
However, a far more pressing issue is the potential deepening dependence on the United States. Throughout the practical implementation of the LCA program, the technical specifications of the aircraft have been repeatedly adjusted, primarily by replacing certain Indian components with foreign ones, which gradually increases the foreign share in the cost of mass-produced products. Among the imported items, the most expensive was the US engine, which had to replace the GTX-35VS Kaveri engine which faced challenges in meeting technical criteria.
Negotiations for a licensed production agreement for the F414 engine have been challenging, largely because Washington is reluctant to share advanced General Electric technologies developed with Pentagon funding. The US is only willing to share some of the technology, omitting the most sensitive components.
The reluctance to fully share F414 engine technology can be explained by one factor: Washington seeks to maintain leverage over New Delhi by controlling the pace of the licensed production of engines for India’s frontline air force.
The second most costly imported component is the onboard radar system. Development of an indigenous MMR radar was halted due to unsatisfactory test results, leading to a preference for foreign alternatives. The prototype aircraft utilized the Ericsson-Ferranti PS-05 radar, originally designed for the Swedish JAS-39 Gripen. Delays in the LCA program rendered the PS-05 obsolete, resulting in its discontinuation. It has since been replaced by the EL/M-2032, which now equips Mark I variants.
It’s worth noting that Elta’s product is also outdated; it was developed in the 1980s for the Israeli Lavi fighter jet (canceled in 1987). The obsolescence is particularly evident in its use of mechanical beam scanning, while the Russian N-011M radar on the Su-30MKI, which was introduced into the Indian Air Force in 2002, boasts more advanced electronic scanning technology.
Recently, Elta proposed the EL/M-2052 with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar configuration. The manufacturer promises to refine it by the time Mark IA aircraft (formed in 2015) are delivered to the air force, projected for late this year or early next year. Various publications have diligently presented Israeli radars as a “temporary solution” for the Tejas program, but as seen with General Electric engines, “temporary” solutions often end up being used much longer than expected.
Strategic decision-making
The practical implementation of the LCA program has resulted in yet another fourth-generation supersonic fighter jet emerging on the global stage. However, the Tejas does not surpass its foreign counterparts. Technically, the Tejas Mark I barely matches the Chinese FC-1, which was adopted by the Pakistan Air Force as the JF-17 in 2007. At best, the Tejas Mark II might reach the level of the JF-17 Block III (with AESA, operational since 2023) and the J-10CE, which Pakistani pilots effectively utilized to fend off an Indian airstrike in May 2025.
With the Indian Air Force already operating a substantial fleet of over 300 Su-30MKIs and Rafale aircraft, which are far better suited for the interception of aerial threats and air superiority missions, the Tejas Mark I may only serve effectively in ground attack operations and pilot training. Fortunately, being a lightweight, single-engine aircraft means it has low fuel consumption. Nevertheless, its limited thrust-to-weight ratio, outdated radar, reduced payload capacity, and narrow selection of munitions (lacking long-range air-to-air missiles), along with the absence of critical stealth technologies naturally confine the aircraft to its own niche. The Su-57E is in a different class altogether.
Consequently, the Tejas cannot be viewed as a viable alternative to the Su-57E. Continuing the LCA program in its current form hampers the decision-making process, since the program competes for budget resources. Moreover, there’s another contender for state funding – the AMCA, with its first flight planned for 2034 and serial production slated for 2036.
In selecting a fifth-generation fighter program, decision-makers in India will need to consider numerous factors and criteria that can sometimes be conflicting and contradictory. Among these is the inherent bias towards domestic projects (i.e. AMCA, LCA, etc.), even if they may not be technically or technologically superior compared to the best foreign alternatives.
The desire to produce everything domestically is understandable, but there are many compelling arguments in favor of purchasing the best foreign technologies or producing them under license. The advanced Su-57E, a premier frontline fighter, is one of such example. For India, Russia remains a reliable partner as decades of effective military-technical collaboration have proven.

articles.title: Deep Strikes in October: Missile Production, Oil Refineries and Russian Aircraft
articles.body:
In October, Ukraine’s Defense Forces focused their deep strikes not only on Russian oil refineries, as they traditionally do, but also on military airfields and facilities involved in ballistic missile production.
Russia’s tactical aviation losses were particularly significant: 3 attacks on airfields resulted in the destruction of at least 8 combat aircraft and damage to 2 more.
This overview is based on October data from Militarnyi Strike, a deep-strike map maintained by Militarnyi’s GEOINT team. It records verified, geolocated attacks on Russian territory and deep inside Ukraine’s temporarily occupied territories.
Oil and gas industry facilities accounted for the largest category in the October dataset, with 20 recorded strikes, or about one-third of the total. Defense industry facilities were hit 9 times, while the chemical industry was targeted 6 times.
A further 10 attacks targeted military facilities, 9 hit infrastructure, 4 targeted logistics facilities, and 2 struck electricity infrastructure.
The Samara region and St. Petersburg recorded the most strikes, with 6 each. The Rostov and Voronezh regions were hit 4 times each. The strikes also covered Bashkortostan, Perm Krai, the Komi Republic, and industrial areas of Western Siberia.
The median distance from the front line to targets attacked in Russia in October was 551.5 km. The most distant targets were 2,508 km from the line of contact. The closest was an oil depot in the Belgorod region, which was struck on October 9, just 45 km from the front line.
The most distant targets included the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant and the Omsk Rubber Plant (Omsky Kauchuk). The map estimates that both are approximately 2,500 km from the front line. On the same day, an Ozon logistics center in Omsk was also hit.
The oil and gas category includes refineries, pumping stations, storage facilities, and transshipment sites. October targets included the Ryazan, Novokuibyshevsk, and Ukhta refineries, as well as Bashneft-Novoil.
The Samara oil pumping station, which has Europe’s largest tank farm, was struck at least four times. Four trunk pipelines converge at the facility: Almetyevsk-Kuibyshev, Kaltasy-Kuibyshev, Nizhnevartovsk-Kurgan-Kuibyshev, and Guryev-Kuibyshev.
The blending station combines oil flows to achieve specified quality characteristics. Crude oil with different sulfur content is mixed in the required proportions to maintain the properties of Urals crude for refining and export.
Another category included data centers belonging to Yandex, Sberbank, VKontakte, and Russia’s Federal Tax Service.
These facilities are located in the Vladimir, Kaluga, Ryazan, Saratov, Nizhny Novgorod, and Leningrad regions.
According to industrial media outlets, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian data centers likely knocked out all three of Yandex’s supercomputers.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces paid considerable attention to facilities manufacturing propellant charges, power sources, and microelectronics for ballistic missiles.
Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara has described the threat of ballistic missile strikes as critical, saying that existing and potential supplies of interceptor missiles are insufficient to fully counter it. Therefore, alongside efforts to secure new interceptor missiles, Ukraine is pursuing an asymmetric response by striking Russian launchers and facilities involved in the missile production supply chain.
On October 3, the Defense Forces attacked the Voskhod enterprise (Voskhod-KLRZ), also known as the Kaluga Radio Tube Plant, in Kaluga. It manufactures RUD20 microchips for 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles, as well as electronic components for the onboard computer and inertial navigation system of 9M727 Iskander-K cruise missiles. The plant also supplies electronics for Kh-101 missiles.
On October 23, the Defense Forces struck the Proton plant in Oryol with cruise missiles, likely Storm Shadow missiles. The plant manufactures 249LP5 switching inverters for 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles, diode modules for S-71 Kover air-launched cruise missiles, and electronic components for the Pantsir-S1 system.
On October 25, Storm Shadow cruise missiles struck the Energia plant in Yelets, Lipetsk region. The facility manufactures 9B283 thermal batteries for 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles and HIT 59I6 power sources for RM-48U strike missiles launched from S-400 systems.
Energia also produces 9B280-1 power cells for 9M727 Iskander-K cruise missiles, batteries for glide bombs equipped with UMPK kits, and UMPB D-30SN munitions. The plant supplies certain types of power sources to manufacturers of Zircon and Kinzhal missiles and the Pantsir air defense system.
On the same day, Ukrainian drones attacked the AVISMA plant in Berezniki, Perm Krai. It produces 96% of Russia’s titanium sponge, which other companies within the parent corporation, VSMPO-AVISMA, process into titanium products. Russian manufacturers of military aircraft and various types of missiles widely use the corporation’s titanium products.
On October 31, the Defense Forces struck the Kamensky Chemical Plant in the Rostov region with Neptune missiles and drones. The facility manufactures propellant charges for 9Kh820 rocket motors used in 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles, as well as charges and igniters for 9Kh837 booster motors used in 9M727 Iskander-K cruise missiles. The plant also supplies propellant to manufacturers of Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket system munitions.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian units attacked a broader network of suppliers of special fuels for cruise missiles, polymers, acids, and other materials used to produce munitions and military equipment.
On October 9, strike drones attacked the Redkino Experimental Plant in the Tver region. The chemical facility manufactures components for the Decilin-M special fuel used in Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as additives for diesel fuel and aviation kerosene.
On October 23, Ukrainian drones attacked the Azot plant in Berezniki, Perm Krai. The facility supplies concentrated nitric acid and melange, a mixture of acids used for nitration, to explosives and chemical plants. These facilities use the raw materials to manufacture explosives and propellant charges.
On October 24, the Defense Forces attacked Tolyattikauchuk in the Samara region. The plant manufactures synthetic rubber, monomers, and high-octane gasoline additives. Manufacturers of solid rocket propellant and rubber products use its polymer output as a raw material.
Special grades of synthetic rubber perform two functions in composite solid propellants: they bind the components into a single charge and serve as fuel that burns during the chemical reaction.
On the same day, Ukrainian drones struck the Omsky Kauchuk plant in Omsk. The facility, part of the Titan Group, manufactures synthetic rubber, phenol, acetone, and the MTBE fuel additive. A major fire broke out at the site following the strikes.
On October 26, Ukrainian drones attacked Voronezhsintezkauchuk. The plant manufactures synthetic rubber and thermoplastic elastomers. Manufacturers of tires and rubber products use these materials, among other things, to make components for military equipment.
On October 28, deep-strike drones attacked the Azot plant in Novomoskovsk, Tula region. Between 2022 and 2024, the facility supplied nearly 5,000 metric tons of nitric acid to the Sverdlov Plant in Dzerzhinsk. That plant manufactures RDX and HMX for military munitions.
On October 29, Ukrainian drones attacked the Bashkir Soda Company facility in Sterlitamak. The facility manufactures terephthaloyl chloride, a raw material for high-strength aramid fibers. Manufacturers of protective equipment use these fibers to make body armor, helmets, and other military gear.
October saw a significant increase in publicly reported successful uses of Neptune cruise missiles, continuing a trend that began in early 2026.
In April, May, and June, one successful use was reported in each month. Two cases were reported in August and September, while October saw three successful attacks: on the Borisoglebsk and Marinovka airfields and on the Kamensky Chemical Plant, which manufactures rocket propellant.
On October 15, the Ukrainian Navy struck the Borisoglebsk airfield in the Voronezh region. The military initially reported hits on 6 Su-34 aircraft. Satellite imagery confirmed the destruction of at least 4 bombers, while two more aircraft were damaged.
On October 29, the Ukrainian Navy attacked Marinovka airfield in the Volgograd region with Neptune missiles. Satellite imagery confirmed the destruction of 2 Su-34 aircraft. The blast and subsequent fire also damaged a nearby aircraft hangar. In total, the 2 missile strikes destroyed 6 bombers and damaged 2 more.
During the night of October 31, the Defense Forces struck the Kamensky Chemical Plant in the Rostov region with Neptune missiles and strike drones. The attack damaged at least 4 production workshops and caused a fire at a warehouse storing finished products at the facility, which manufactures solid rocket propellant.
On October 4, SSU drones destroyed a Su-35 and a Su-34 at Khanskaya airbase in Adygea. Satellite imagery confirmed the loss of both aircraft. Ukrainian drones also struck an ammunition depot at the airfield.
At Borisoglebsk, Marinovka, and Khanskaya airbases, the Defense Forces destroyed at least 7 Su-34s and 1 Su-35, and damaged 2 Su-34s.
In addition, Russian military aviation suffered significant non-combat losses. On October 21, a Su-30SM fighter crashed in the Kaliningrad region during a training flight. The aircraft went down in Chernyakhovsky District, between the settlements of Timofeyevka and Zeleny Bor. Both pilots ejected but sustained injuries.
On the same day, Russia lost another Su-30SM during a training flight. Colonel Oleg Yerofeyev and Lieutenant Colonel Vladimir Kochetov, members of the Russian Knights aerobatic team, were killed. On October 29, the team confirmed their deaths. The circumstances of the crash remain unknown.
On October 29, a Su-57 fighter caught fire at Akhtubinsk airbase in the Astrakhan region. The aircraft is believed to have caught fire following an abnormal incident during engine startup. Satellite imagery showed the aftermath of the fire at the aircraft parking area.
On October 1, Russia lost a Mi-8 military transport helicopter in the Voronezh region. The helicopter was likely shot down by a Russian Su-35 during an attempt to repel a drone attack: the fighter’s crew mistakenly identified it as a Ukrainian drone. All three Mi-8 crew members were killed.
On October 30, the 3rd Assault Brigade released footage showing the destruction of another Mi-8 near Tarasivka in the occupied Luhansk region. Members of the brigade’s SKYFOM platoon, part of its unmanned systems battalion, struck the helicopter twice with HORNET drones after it had landed. The aircraft burned down.
Overall, Russia was confirmed to have irretrievably lost 11 aircraft and 2 Mi-8 helicopters in October alone. Another two Su-34s sustained damage of unknown severity.

articles.title: Zelensky Eyes Missile Loans Against 500 US Patriot Deal
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky plans to negotiate with individual international partners to secure an emergency temporary transfer of 10 to 30 air defense missiles from their stockpiles, with Kyiv guaranteeing repayment from a newly approved US purchase package of 500 interceptors.
Speaking to Ukrainian media during a press briefing in Istanbul on Saturday, Oct. 31, the head of state outlined a queue-swapping mechanism designed to bridge an acute munitions deficit ahead of winter, as deliveries under the American procurement program face multi-year production delays.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Several times during this war, during various dialogues, we executed an operation where you swap queues,” Zelensky explained.
“I will try to do this with certain partners, where against that 500-missile package we could take 10, 20, 30 missiles somewhere, sign appropriate guarantees and contracts stipulating that we will later return them from that American package – with some interest, or perhaps without interest.”
Zelensky noted that such bilateral borrowing arrangements would allow Ukrainian air defense batteries to receive interceptors directly from partner arsenals long before factory-fresh munitions roll off American assembly lines.
Multi-year US delays
The president explained that deliveries under the US proposal are deferred by several years due to industrial manufacturing cycles and Washington’s reluctance to draw down directly from its own strategic military reserves.
Zelensky Arrives in Turkey for Talks With Erdogan on Black Sea Safety
Zelensky emphasized that the sluggish delivery pace cannot provide adequate protection for Ukrainian civilians as Russian standoff bombardments escalate, noting that significant volumes of Western air defense packages have simultaneously been directed toward the Middle East.
“We are grateful to the United States of America. This is a very good proposal. Naturally, money must be gathered for this proposal. I am confident that we will find the financing, thanks above all to our European partners,” Zelensky stated.
The president added that Ukraine will continue aggressively pursuing surface-to-air interceptors through bilateral agreements with European and other allied nations, underscoring that relying solely on American deliveries is insufficient to safeguard national airspace.
Post-2030 timeline
Zelensky’s comments follow the Trump administration’s formal authorization on Friday, Oct. 30, of a possible Foreign Military Sale to Ukraine encompassing 500 Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE) interceptor missiles, spare parts, and support equipment at an estimated cost of $2.1 billion.
However, diplomatic sources cited by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty correspondent Alex Raufoglu revealed that the contracted munitions represent newly manufactured hardware rather than drawdowns from existing American military inventories, with deliveries not expected until after 2030.
“As sources inform me, these are new missiles, with deliveries not expected until after 2030,” Raufoglu reported. “This does virtually nothing to resolve the acute deficit of interceptors in Ukraine ahead of winter.”
Raufoglu noted that bilateral discussions have not yet secured an agreement for joint coproduction of the interceptors within Ukraine, with the Pentagon still engaged in an extended review regarding whether to grant Kyiv domestic manufacturing licenses.
Zelensky initially voiced frustration with the extended timetable late Friday, pointing out that deliveries would only begin in several years and appealing to American and European partners to identify immediate solutions for the impending winter heating season.
Pre-winter infrastructure defense and monthly interceptor needs
The drive to secure immediate missile loans comes amid an intensifying Russian air campaign against Ukraine’s civil life-support networks.
Ukrainian government figures indicate that during the final two weeks of October alone, Russian tactical and strategic forces executed more than 30 coordinated strikes against critical electricity generation and transmission infrastructure.
Zelensky previously stated that Kyiv requires an emergency winter allocation of 100 PAC-3 interceptors per month to establish a reliable defensive shield against Russian ballistic barrages.
Over the preceding 90 days, Ukraine received only 24 Patriot interceptors from the US, despite facing salvos that included more than 20 ballistic missiles fired in a single day on Oct. 22.
The head of state stressed that securing 10 to 30 missiles in the near term from partner inventories would provide critical localized reinforcement for batteries shielding high-density urban areas and regional power grids from catastrophic winter blackouts while multi-year procurement contracts proceed through standard defense-industrial channels.

articles.title: Zelensky confirms attack on Russian rocket fuel factory, missile launcher system
articles.body:
Ukraine successfully attacked Russia's Kamensky Plant, a missile production facility in Rostov Oblast, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Nov. 1.
The General Staff reported an attack on the factory the previous day, using a combination of drones and Neptune cruise missiles.
"Our long-range strikes have targeted the Rostov region. The Kamensky Plant – a Russian defense industry facility involved in missile production – has been struck," Zelensky wrote on social media.
The Kamensky facility has been sanctioned by the EU, the U.K., and the U.S., for its role in Russia's war against Ukraine. Located some 15 kilometers from the border with Ukraine, the plant produces solid rocket propellant for a range of Russian rockets, missiles, and aircraft weapons.
"A ‘Pantsir-S2’ system and a command and control vehicle belonging to the S-400 ‘Triumph’ system were also struck," Zelensky said, causing an estimated $70 million in damage.
The attack comes as Russia continues to pummel Ukrainian cities, civilians, and energy infrastructure, ahead of what is expected to be Ukraine's most difficult winter yet.
Ukraine lacks sufficient air defenses to counter Russia's attacks, and even though allies approve the transfer of interceptor missiles, Zelensky has said the amounts delivered have been too little, and beset with delays.
The attack against the Kamensky Plant comes as Ukraine has intensified its long-range strikes inside Russia and across Russian-occupied territories since the summer, hitting targets such as oil refineries, military-industrial plants, and airfields, aimed at degrading Russia's military-industrial capacity.
Carrying out attacks against facilities producing the ingredients of Russian missiles and drones, and launch systems such as the S-400, are other means by which Ukraine can protect its cities from future attacks.
"We are rightfully defending ourselves against Russian aggression and doing everything we can to limit Russia’s ability to continue it," Zelensky said.

articles.title: Iran and US explore diplomacy amid rising threats of war
articles.body:
Iran and US explore diplomacy amid rising threats of war
Tehran says it could reopen Hormuz in a shorter period if conditions are met, as Trump says the US still has several Iranian targets to ‘take care of’.
Iran’s Foreign Minister speaks to Al Jazeera about US proposals
Tehran, Iran – Ongoing contacts through mediators have provided a potential diplomatic opening between Iran and the United States, even as both sides express readiness for renewed military escalation.
After two days of Qatari-mediated talks, Iranian authorities have signalled that a deal remains possible provided that their demands are tangibly implemented. At the same time, they have doubled down on a willingness to expand attacks or even launch preemptive strikes if they deem war is inevitable.
“We are prepared for all scenarios,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday. “We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms. Our forces are at the highest level of readiness.”
His comments came as US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the talks were going “fine” but added that Iranian authorities were not “reliable”.
The Republican leader, who ordered attacks alongside Israel against Iran on February 28, has repeatedly raised prospects of once more hitting the country’s civilian infrastructure. In recent weeks, he has suggested that an attack could potentially take place after the November 3 midterm elections in the US.
“We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” Trump told reporters at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago Club in Florida about further bombing Iran’s nuclear facilities.
Sequencing and timeline
The mediated talks in Tehran on Friday, and then in Qatar on Saturday, appear to have produced a new tangible result by shortening the period after which Iran’s proposal to partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz can be enforced.
Tehran had previously offered seven days, but that has now come down to two, Araghchi said in his interview with Al Jazeera.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, said there are “indications” of US interest in a negotiated settlement, citing the continuing Qatar-mediated talks and US Vice President JD Vance’s recent outreach.
“However, Iran is seeking a series of concessions while the United States insists on progress on Iran’s nuclear programme before concessions are made,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Therefore the central difficulty is sequencing and leverage. Each side wants the other to act first.”
Araghchi’s two-day offer indicates some flexibility over sequencing that could also allow both sides to claim an initial diplomatic achievement without immediately resolving their fundamental disagreements, according to Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group.
“However, the military statements show the limits of this opening. Iran appears increasingly determined to prevent a repetition of previous scenarios in which negotiations or temporary ceasefires were followed by renewed military conflict,” he wrote on social media. “From Tehran’s perspective, the objective is to make another attack so costly and unpredictable that Washington would have to reconsider the option altogether.”
As the talks were ongoing on Saturday, the office of Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he had a meeting earlier with top military commanders to demand “maximum deterrence” through preparedness for an immediate response “without geographical restriction” to any threat.
Targets would include “tangible and intangible” US and Israeli assets, Khamenei said. Iranian authorities have previously said if Iran’s civilian infrastructure is attacked again, seabed cables and infrastructure across the region could also become targets.
After Khamenei’s statement, commanders of the general staff of the armed forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the traditional army separately expressed readiness to launch missile, drone and other attacks in case of an escalation of conflict.
State media on Sunday also aired footage of missiles and drones being taken out of massive underground storage sites and deployed during the eight months of war so far.
The authorities also signalled that they expect more potential attacks from the US and Israel, including against Iran’s power grid.
Gholamreza Jalali, commander of the National Organization for Passive Defense, said during a speech on Sunday that they have identified 14 sectors most dependent on electricity that would need support if the war restarts, without naming any.
“Adopting preventive measures in the area of passive defence for the electricity grid is a fundamental principle that all authorities must follow up in their capacities,” he said, adding that officials were considering “network islanding” practices to create different segments that would not all be simultaneously affected by potential bombing.
‘Positive change in tone’
In and around the Strait of Hormuz, vessels continue to be attacked if they refuse to coordinate with the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, the entity set up by Iranian authorities to enforce control and sovereignty in the critical waterway.
At least four tankers were identified as being hit on Friday and Saturday, although not all attacks are reported by vessels and monitors. According to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a vessel carrying liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) was struck by three Iranian projectiles on Saturday about 40 nautical miles (74km) south of Iran’s Lavan Island, deep into the Gulf.
Transit in the strait and surrounding waterways will not return to normal unless the US takes steps towards Iran’s conditions, security chief Mohsen Rezaei told state television during an interview on Saturday night.
For the sequencing to work, he said Tehran wants the US to lift its naval blockade that has halted oil exports and the majority of Iran’s trade, which used to be facilitated through its southern ports. The US must also issue waivers for oil sanctions, unfreeze Iran’s assets abroad, stop fighting on all regional fronts, including Lebanon, and recognise a bilateral Iran-Oman arrangement for Hormuz.
Rezaei said he has yet to respond to a letter addressed to him by Vance, although he said the missive indicated a “change in tone” that he described as “positive”.
Mostafa Najafi, a Tehran-based political analyst said to be linked with Rezaei, said if the conditions are not met, the letter is likely to go unanswered and negotiations – including on Iran’s nuclear programme – will not enter a higher level.
“It is unclear how willing Washington is to accept these demands. It is clear that not recognising rights emphasised by Iran will lead to the failure of the negotiations,” he wrote on X.
The US has also doubled down on the effectiveness of its Operation Economic Outcast involving the blockade, sanctions and pressure on overland trade and aviation.
A report by the US Treasury to inform Trump’s decision-making, which was publicised by news outlet Axios, said no new oil had been loaded onto tankers at Iran’s terminals since August 25. It also showed overseas crude deliveries were down, while Iran’s year-on-year inflation neared 90 percent in September and the national currency continued to dwindle.
The report said Iran’s economy was “crippled” by the combined measures, but did not argue that it was close to collapsing.

articles.title: U.S. F-16s Resume Combat Air Patrols from Eareckson Air Station, Over 1,500 km from Mainland Alaska
articles.body:
U.S. Air Force F-16 fighter jets carried out a North American defense mission from Eareckson Air Station, located on Shemya Island in the Bering Sea, more than 1,500 km from mainland Alaska.
The North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) said this in a statement.
The aircraft conducted air defense operations from the remote airbase during a deployment from October 18 to 26. On October 25, the fighter jets launched on a North American defense mission, which also involved aircraft from two other bases in Alaska and one Canadian airbase.
After deploying to Eareckson Air Station, the F-16s began carrying out missions as part of Operation NOBLEDEFENDER. The mission was subsequently continued under Operation NOBLE EAGLE, supporting efforts to protect sovereignty in the northern region.
The mission evolved into a coordinated U.S.-Canadian operation involving two F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter jets, F-35 Lightning II aircraft from Eielson Air Force Base, an E-3 Sentry airborne early warning and control aircraft from Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, and Royal Canadian Air Force CF-18 Hornet fighter jets from Cold Lake Air Base in Alberta.
Several KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft and one CC-150 Polaris provided aerial refueling, while an HC-130 Combat King II provided search-and-rescue support and personnel recovery.
Eareckson Air Station is located about 2,600 km from Eielson Air Force Base and 4,200 km from Cold Lake Air Base, highlighting the vast distances over which NORAD coordinated the participating forces.
F-16s deployed to Eareckson Air Station provided coverage over the southern part of the zone, while F-35s and additional F-16s from Eielson operated in the northwest, and Canadian CF-18s covered the northern approaches.
“The joint operation demonstrated NORAD’s ability to rapidly assemble, deploy, and coordinate a combat-ready air force to defend North America,” the command stated.
According to TWZ, regular fighter patrols at Eareckson Air Station ceased in the early 1990s. As a result, the October 2026 deployment marked a significant milestone, representing a return to combat air patrol operations at one of the westernmost U.S. military installations.
The island is also home to the AN/FPS-108 Cobra Dane radar station, located directly opposite Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula and the Kura missile test range.
The powerful phased-array radar plays a critical role in detecting ballistic missiles and tracking their trajectories.
