articles.title: North Korea tests cluster-bomb warhead for ballistic missiles
articles.body:
- North Korea tested a “Standard Type 2” cluster-bomb warhead for tactical ballistic missiles on Oct. 31, claiming it can destroy 12 to 13 hectares.
- The Missile Administration said units will be able to use four types of cluster warheads by the end of the year.
North Korea tested a cluster-bomb warhead for its tactical ballistic missiles on Oct. 31 and said it will let its military units choose from four types of cluster warheads by the end of the year, state news agency KCNA reported on Nov. 1.
The Missile Administration, which runs North Korea’s missile development, said the test assessed the warhead’s combat readiness and destructive power. Its Ballistic Missile System Institute and Warhead Institute said they confirmed that the “Standard Type 2” cluster warhead can destroy a target area of 12 to 13 hectares, about 30 to 32 acres. Kim Jong Sik, a member of the ruling Workers’ Party’s Central Military Commission and first vice director of a Central Committee department, oversaw the test. Leader Kim Jong Un was not reported to have attended.
KCNA did not name the missile or give its range, altitude or launch site. The missile was fired at an uninhabited island target in the West Sea, also known as the Yellow Sea, South Korea’s JKN reported, and analysts said it appears to be the first time North Korea has fired a cluster-armed missile from a wheeled mobile launcher.
“We classify the cluster-bomb warheads into four categories according to special and standard purposes. Within this year we will enable units to select and use all those types according to operational aims and specific features of targets,” said the general director of the DPRK Missile Administration.
A cluster warhead opens in the air and scatters dozens or hundreds of small bomblets over a wide area, making it effective against troops, vehicles, artillery positions and airfields rather than a single hardened target. Neither North Korea nor South Korea has joined the international convention banning cluster munitions.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff did not announce the launch on the day it happened, a break from its usual practice of reporting North Korean ballistic missile launches in real time. The military said on Nov. 1 that it had tracked related activity before the launch in close information sharing with the United States and maintained a readiness posture. Because the missile flew a short range at low altitude, the military wanted to complete its analysis before confirming it was a ballistic missile, Financial News reported.
North Korea has tested cluster warheads on its tactical missiles before. In April, it tested a Hwasong-11A short-range ballistic missile with a cluster warhead alongside other new weapons, and later that month Kim Jong Un watched the launch of Hwasong-11 Ra missiles fitted with cluster bomb and fragmentation mine warheads, which state media also claimed could devastate an area of about 13 hectares.
The test came two days after North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area during a firepower demonstration tied to a drone exhibition, where Kim called for “absolute superiority” in drone technology. The Missile Administration described the Oct. 31 launch as part of regular research work to improve the power of its weapon systems.

articles.title: Trump ‘checks in’ with Netanyahu amid fears of renewed hostilities – WSJ
articles.body:
Trump ‘checks in’ with Netanyahu amid fears of renewed hostilities – WSJ
US President Donald Trump spoke by phone with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday morning, checking in amid preparations for possible strikes on Iran, the Wall Street Journal has reported, citing people familiar with the call.
According to the WSJ, Trump had earlier held another meeting with senior military commanders at the White House to discuss options for resuming major combat operations. Over the past few weeks, multiple media outlets have reported that the US could resume strikes on Iran after the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to bomb Iran, warning of “another little Epic Fury” if Tehran fails to meet his peace terms. US officials have reportedly warned Arab allies hosting American military bases to prepare for a short but intense operation.
Asked at a Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago in Florida on Saturday night whether he expected to “go back to war with Iran” in the coming weeks, Trump replied: “Let’s say I did – would I tell you? I can’t tell you this.”
The Pentagon has reportedly presented Trump with potential targets ranging from Iranian nuclear facilities and underground military sites to Kharg Island, a major oil export hub in the Persian Gulf. The US has also been sending additional missile interceptors to the region and relocating troops from vulnerable bases.
According to a Jerusalem Post report published on Saturday, the US and Israel have already drawn up plans for renewed military action, but Trump is unlikely to order strikes before Tuesday’s vote unless intelligence indicates preparations for a surprise attack.
A resumption of hostilities would come at a sensitive time for Netanyahu, whose right-wing bloc failed to secure a parliamentary majority in last week’s election. He will remain in office as coalition negotiations continue.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump had not decided whether to launch new strikes against Iran but preferred a diplomatic solution. His remarks came as Iranian negotiators met Qatari mediators in Doha following more than 12 hours of discussions in Tehran on Friday. A source familiar with the talks told Reuters that diplomacy was being coordinated through regular contacts with Washington.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran had reviewed a letter from US Vice President J.D. Vance aimed at reopening negotiations, describing the initiative as a “positive step.”
Meanwhile, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered the armed forces to prepare for “an immediate and effective response, without geographical restriction” if the country is attacked again, according to a statement released by his office on Saturday.

articles.title: Russia Launched 36 Ballistic Missiles, 1,940 Drones in the Last Week
articles.body:
Russian forces launched 1,940 strike drones, more than 1,580 guided aerial bombs (KABs), and 44 missiles of various types – including 36 ballistic missiles – against Ukraine over the past week, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Writing on Telegram and reported by state news agency Ukrinform, the president emphasized that Moscow is deliberately exploiting an acute shortage of ballistic missile interceptors to maximize destruction against Ukraine’s civilian life-support systems ahead of winter.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“During this week, Russia launched 1,940 strike drones, more than 1,580 KABs, and 44 missiles of various types, of which 36 were ballistics, against Ukraine,” Zelensky stated.
“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are trying to take maximum advantage of our deficit of ballistic interceptors.”
Zelensky highlighted that Russian military doctrine for the approaching winter season is anchored fundamentally by high-speed ballistic salvos, which give air defense units only minutes to react and can only be engaged by specialized Western surface-to-air systems such as the Patriot PAC-3 and SAMP/T.
Overnight power grid attacks across four regions
The president reported that overnight into Sunday alone, Russian forces struck critical electrical energy facilities across four administrative regions: Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, and Khmelnytskyi.
Russian munitions struck high-voltage substations, power transformers, and primary transmission lines directly supplying electricity to residential neighborhoods and municipal heating circuits.
Sybiha: Oleshky Success Proves War Can Be Stopped Everywhere
Emergency engineering detachments, utility specialists, and mobile repair crews deployed across the four regions to isolate damaged segments and restore voltage. However, Zelensky noted that hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian families remain without electricity as temperatures drop.
The overnight barrage compounds infrastructure damage sustained over recent days. On Oct. 30, Russian strikes damaged combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and Shostka alongside four substations in Dnipropetrovsk region, severing power to roughly 280,000 households across central and eastern Ukraine.
“Russia continues to destroy infrastructure and kill Ukrainians, making ballistic missiles its primary bet this winter,” Zelensky emphasized. “Therefore, decisions regarding the reinforcement of air defense must be implemented right now.”
Appeals for Patriot missiles
Addressing the urgent requirement for anti-ballistic munitions, Zelensky underscored that Kyiv is engaging international partners daily to secure immediate supplies of Patriot interceptor missiles from active inventories rather than waiting for long-term manufacturing contracts.
“Every day we communicate about our need for missiles for Patriots with America, Europe, and other partners who can help,” Zelensky stated.
“And this month there were new decisions from the US and European countries regarding new packages for Ukraine. But these deliveries cannot wait for years.”
The warning follows the Trump administration’s formal authorization on Friday, Oct. 30, of a possible $2.1 billion Foreign Military Sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 MSE missiles to Ukraine.
However, diplomatic sources cited by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty revealed that the approved interceptors represent new production with delivery timelines extending past 2030, offering no near-term relief ahead of winter.
In response to the multi-year production backlog, Zelensky announced in Istanbul on Saturday that Kyiv plans to negotiate emergency loans of 10 to 30 air defense missiles from European partners’ existing arsenals.
Under the proposed queue-swapping mechanism, Ukraine would guarantee reimbursement to partner nations from the 500-missile American procurement contract once factory production rolls off assembly lines.
Kyiv has requested a winter allocation providing 100 PAC-3 interceptors per month to establish a reliable defensive perimeter over power generation stations, water pumping nodes, and municipal district heating networks.
“Thank you to everyone who supports the protection of the Ukrainian sky,” the president concluded, urging Western governments to accelerate physical munition handovers to avert widespread civilian catastrophe.

articles.title: Mediators continue US-Iran negotiations amid war rhetoric: What we know
articles.body:
Mediators continue US-Iran negotiations amid war rhetoric: What we know
Trump says latest talks ‘going fine’; while Iranian leaders say they favour diplomacy but are ready for maximum response if the US resumes war.
Iranian officials have been speaking with Qatari mediators about a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, in the latest effort to find a diplomatic path out of the US-Israel war on Iran that has caused a serious global energy crisis.
But even amid signs of diplomatic progress, officials from both sides say they are ready for renewed military escalation.
President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly suggested the United States could attack Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, said the latest negotiations were “going fine”, but added that the US still had several Iranian targets to “take care of”.
Meanwhile, Araghchi has also said Iran’s military was more prepared than ever for renewed war, while the country’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, threatened Iran would use “new weaponry” in response to any future attack.
Here’s what we know about the latest diplomatic efforts and the sharp rhetoric from both sides, and what it could mean for what lies ahead:
What is the status of talks?
Araghchi said on Saturday that an Iranian delegation, including one of his aides, travelled to Doha to meet Qatari mediators. Earlier, Qatari officials also travelled to Tehran for consultations.
The latest discussions in Doha centred on a plan that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a global energy chokepoint, within two days and restart peace talks with the US, provided Washington meets a set of demands from Tehran, Araghchi told Al Jazeera.
Those demands include the lifting of recently imposed US sanctions, the reinstatement of oil waivers granted in June, a reduction in the US military presence in the region, recognition of new shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz designated by Iran and Oman, and an end to the conflict on all fronts, including Israel’s attacks on Lebanon, said Araghchi.
Qatari and Pakistani mediators were “continuing consultations regarding our conditions”, said the top Iranian diplomat.
Pakistan has been mediating between the US and Iran, with its army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, visiting Tehran several times as part of the diplomatic efforts to end the war. Doha and Islamabad played key roles in the signing of the June memorandum of understanding (MoU) that collapsed in August.
Iran’s Rezaei said the US had “indicated its readiness” to accept its conditions, although Washington has not confirmed this.
On the US side, Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed Qatar-led talks were ongoing, but said he was not aware of a timeframe for them.
“There are multiple talks. Talks have actually never stopped,” said Rubio. “If there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it.”
Why has Iran noted a change in the US’s ‘tone’?
The renewed diplomatic activity comes after US Vice President JD Vance sent a letter earlier this week to Rezaei, reportedly seeking to gauge the prospects of restarting negotiations and averting another round of military escalation.
Rezaei confirmed on Saturday that he had read the letter, whose tone he said had “completely changed” compared with earlier correspondence from Trump.
Araghchi also said he had studied Vance’s letter, which he described positively.
“The American side’s attempt to open the door to dialogue and understanding more broadly is a positive step,” Araghchi told Al Jazeera.
However, he warned, “If Washington’s goal in sending this letter is to stir up discord, it would be yet another mistake to add to its previous ones.”
What has Iran said about prospects for peace and war?
Iranian officials have said they are open to new peace talks if the US meets their conditions, but also ready to act more aggressively in any new military confrontation.
“I know that our armed forces are more prepared for war than any time before, and we are ready for any scenario,” Araghchi told Al Jazeera.
In the event of any new military threat from the US or Israel, Iran’s response would be “immediate” and “without geographical limitations”, according to a statement by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
Khamenei ordered commanders to update Iran’s target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy”.
Rezaei told Al Jazeera that Iran would use “new weaponry” in its response to any future attacks. He also said Iran’s government was weighing a change to its “nuclear doctrine”, which currently includes a ban on nuclear weapons.
Iran’s nuclear programme has been a major point of contention in the conflict with the US, and Trump has repeatedly said Iran must never be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon. Tehran insists its nuclear programme is for civilian purposes.
What is the latest from Trump?
The US president has sent mixed signals about the status of peace talks. On Saturday, he said negotiations were “going fine” but added that they were “not very reliable”.
He also said the US military still needed to “take care of” several Iranian sites, singling out a suspected underground nuclear complex known as Pickaxe Mountain.
Trump added that the US could achieve its military objectives “very quickly” and was not in a hurry.
Previously, he threatened to renew attacks that would “finish off” Iran, while the US has reportedly warned its Gulf allies to prepare for a short, high-intensity round of conflict after the midterm elections.
Rubio said Trump had not yet decided on whether to carry out new strikes, but warned the US “can achieve military objectives if we seek to”.
How could Israel play into the calculation?
Israel, which joined the US in initiating the war against Iran in February, is preparing for another round of potential conflict right after the US midterm elections, according to a senior Israeli official cited by Israel’s Ynet News site.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said Israel has a “historic, one-time opportunity … to remove the Iranian threat once and for all”. While Netanyahu’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority in recent legislative elections, the 77-year-old leader remains in office as caretaker until a new government is formed.
Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu’s threats complicate Iran’s calculus because Tehran fears “even a nuclear agreement with Washington may not end the threat of another Israeli attack”.
Brigadier-General Yadollah Javani, the deputy for political affairs of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said Iranian forces are operating on the assumption that the US or Israel could strike at any moment.
What explains the parallel diplomatic efforts and war rhetoric?
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst with the Crisis Group, said Tehran is pursuing diplomacy while also “attempting to redefine” the military implications of another potential conflict.
“For now, diplomacy and military preparations are proceeding simultaneously,” he wrote in a post on X. “The emerging Iranian position seems to be that an agreement remains possible, but another war would be fought under different rules and on a much wider battlefield.”
He added, “Whether Washington takes these warnings as credible deterrence or further escalatory threats could significantly influence what happens next.”
Krieg said the November 3 elections give Iran an incentive to delay concessions to deny Trump a diplomatic victory. But that calculus could change afterwards when he has fewer domestic political restraints on military action.
“We could therefore reach a situation where Iran becomes more willing to compromise precisely when Washington becomes more willing to strike,” said Krieg.

articles.title: Drones Strike Lukoil Refinery and Power Plant in Kstovo
articles.body:
Ukrainian long-range strike drones attacked the “Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez” oil refinery and the adjacent Novogorkovskaya combined heat and power plant in the city of Kstovo in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region overnight into Sunday, Nov. 1, triggering multiple large fires across the strategic industrial complex.
Residents in Kstovo began circulating footage of major blazes lighting up the skyline around 4:00 a.m. local time, reporting repeated loud detonations and low-flying drone engine sounds over the municipal industrial zone.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Open-source intelligence monitors, including Ukrainian OSINT channel Exilenova+, reported that incoming unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) penetrated dense local air defenses, causing simultaneous large fires in several operational sections of the facility.
Monitoring group Crimean Wind corroborated the strikes, confirming that blazes engulfed sections of the refinery.
The enterprise, operated by Russian oil major Lukoil, functions as one of the largest petroleum refining facilities in Russia, boasting an annual design crude throughput capacity of approximately 17 million metric tons – equivalent to roughly 340,000 barrels per day.
Nationally, the Kstovo facility ranks fourth among Russian refineries by total processing volume and stands as the country’s second-largest producer of commercial motor gasoline.
The installation manufactures high-octane automotive gasoline, diesel fuel, jet propulsion kerosene, bitumen, and specialized petroleum fractions utilized directly by Russian military logistics and heavy mechanized equipment.
Stubb Refutes Putin Slavic History Lecture, Backs Kyiv
Concurrent strike on Novogorkovskaya CHP
In addition to direct hits on the refinery, Exilenova+ reported an aerial strike on the neighboring Novogorkovskaya combined heat and power plant (CHP).
Situated directly within the Kstovo industrial belt, the Novogorkovskaya CHP serves as the primary regional energy backbone supplying high-pressure steam and electricity to surrounding heavy petrochemical complexes, including the Lukoil refinery.
Deepening asymmetric campaign against Russian refining nodes
Overnight Oct. 30-31, Ukrainian long-range strike drones struck the northern industrial hub of Ufa in the Republic of Bashkortostan, located 1,400 kilometers east of Ukraine.
Open-source intelligence analysis confirmed that the Ufa strike ignited the critical L-35 catalytic reforming unit at the Bashneft-Novoil refinery and damaged facilities at the adjacent Bashneft-UNPZ plant, disrupting high-octane gasoline output across the 23.5-million-ton Ufa refining cluster.
That raid followed an attack 24 hours earlier, overnight into Friday, Oct. 30, against Rosneft’s 8.8-million-ton Novokuybyshevsk Oil Refinery in Samara region, which produces specialized aviation fuel for the Russian Aerospace Forces, struck alongside an enterprise supplying military combat food rations.
Combined strikes on defense-industrial and propellant supply chains
The sequential targeting of major refineries coincides with synchronized precision interdiction against Russian military-industrial supply chains and tactical logistics.
Overnight Oct. 30-31, the Ukrainian Navy and unmanned aerial units launched a combined strike utilizing domestically manufactured Neptune cruise missiles in a land-attack role and long-range drones against the “Kamensky” chemical plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov region.
The strike ignited a warehouse storing finished solid rocket propellant and damaged four production workshops at an enterprise producing propulsive charges for 220mm Uragan, 300mm Smerch, and 300mm Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as tactical guided missiles.
Concurrently, Ukrainian precision strikes destroyed four Russian material-technical logistics supply depots across occupied Ukrainian territories near Khartsyzk, Dokuchaievsk, Novovasylivka, and Novoaidar.
These operations build upon earlier deep-rear strikes against critical single-source defense suppliers, including the Avisma titanium and magnesium complex in Perm region, the Omsky Kauchuk rocket propellant and polymer plant in Siberia, the Tolyattikauchuk synthetic rubber facility in Samara, and the Energiya defense accumulator plant in Yelets.

articles.title: Three Russian refineries hit since Friday handle roughly 10% of Russia’s refining and over 10% of its diesel
articles.body:
Drones set fire to Lukoil’s refinery in Kstovo, one of Russia’s largest, overnight on 1 November, Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported. The raid came days after a US newspaper reported a pause in Ukraine’s refinery strikes, though Zelenskyy said units never had an order to stop. Over the same weekend, Ukraine’s military reported striking a rocket-fuel plant in southern Russia, and drones also hit a refinery in Ufa.
Russia’s war runs on fuel and oil money, and refineries have been Ukraine’s main long-range target. Ukraine says its drones hit 12 Russian refineries in September alone. Strikes then went quiet after Washington declared an energy ceasefire in mid-October. US President Donald Trump later called Ukraine’s renewed refinery strikes “a disgrace.” Every new refinery fire revives a campaign Washington has pressed Kyiv to drop.
Fire burned past dawn at Lukoil’s Kstovo plant
Exilenova+ began posting footage of explosions over Kstovo shortly after 04:00 Kyiv time. The fire kept growing past dawn, sending up a huge plume of smoke. The channel suggested the blaze centered on the AVT-6 and AVT-5 crude units and a tar visbreaker, or on unit 35/11-600. Satellite images would give a clearer picture, it added.
Nizhny Novgorod Governor Gleb Nikitin claimed drone strikes caused “significant damage” to an “industrial enterprise” in Kstovo district, Russian Telegram channel Astra reported. He did not name the facility. The regional government later urged drivers to fill up “as needed, without creating a rush,” Astra added. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed it downed 235 drones over 17 Russian regions overnight, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast among them. Ukraine’s General Staff had not commented on Kstovo by midday.
Kstovo was the third Russian refinery attacked in three days, after Novokuibyshevsk and Ufa, Russian Telegram channel Agentstvo calculated. Together, the three plants process about 24 million tons of crude a year, roughly 10% of Russia’s refining, and make more than 10% of its diesel. Nikitin also claimed air defenses destroyed more than 100 drones over the region overnight and in the morning. Regional authorities said they were taking measures to keep gas stations supplied, Agentstvo Novosti noted.
The Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez plant can process 15 million to 17 million tons of crude a year, depending on the estimate. It supplies about 30% of Moscow Oblast’s gasoline. The plant sits about 780 km from Ukraine’s border. Ukraine has hit it repeatedly: in November 2025, in April, and in May, when a strike halted its main crude unit.
Explosions rock Russia’s Kstovo as drone strikes target the oil industry hub overnight (MAP)
Days after a reported pause
On 29 October, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported that Ukraine had paused refinery strikes under US pressure until after the 3 November midterms. Hours later, drones hit the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in Samara Oblast. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on 30 October that “every Russian strike on our cities and communities always gets our fully justified response.” Ukraine’s deep-strike units will also be expanded, he added. On 27 October, he told reporters that units had been “a little more careful” but “do not have an order” to stop, WSJ reported.
Neptune missiles and drones hit a rocket-fuel plant
Ukrainian forces struck the Kamensky Combine in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov Oblast, overnight on 31 October, Ukraine’s General Staff reported. Strike drones and the Navy’s Neptune coastal missiles hit the plant together. The strike set a finished-goods warehouse on fire and damaged four workshops. The combine makes solid rocket fuel for Russia’s Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple rocket launchers, Ukraine’s General Staff said.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed it intercepted four of Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles and two Neptunes that night. Ukraine’s General Staff also reported hitting four Russian supply depots in occupied Ukraine. They sit near Khartsyzk and Dokuchaievsk in Donetsk Oblast, Novovasylivka in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, and Novoaidar in Luhansk Oblast.
A refinery fire in Ufa
On the morning of 31 October, drones hit the Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Ufa, Bashkortostan, Astra’s OSINT analyst found from eyewitness photos. Local residents said two plants came under attack. By the afternoon, the fires had been contained, Ukrainian Telegram channel Supernova+ said. Ukraine’s drones struck Bashneft’s Ufa refineries in June, and a fire in the city’s refinery zone was last reported on 21 September, Astra noted.
Lipetsk, Rostov, and the road to Crimea
Early on 1 November, agents of Atesh, a Crimean Tatar-Ukrainian partisan movement, reported explosions near the Lipetsk Tractor Plant during a mass drone raid. Atesh says the plant is Russia’s only maker of tracked chassis for air defense systems. Russian officials have not confirmed any damage.
Overnight on 1 November, locals reported attacks in Taganrog and six districts of Rostov Oblast, the Ukrainian Telegram channel of Petro Andriushchenko’s Center for the Study of Occupation said. Local sources also reported drone attacks on Pochep in Bryansk Oblast. Two Belgorod Oblast villages came under attack on the evening of 31 October. The results remain unknown.
Ukraine’s strikes on Russian logistics are also thinning traffic to occupied Crimea, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said on 31 October. Anatoly Tsurkin, head of the Russian-installed freight carriers’ association in Crimea, claimed daily truck traffic from Rostov Oblast fell from 2,000–3,000 to 600–800. He claimed the M-14 highway, which occupation officials call the R-280, is the only road trucks can use. Drone strikes have also scared off drivers, he claimed.

articles.title: Moscow Reports Drone Attack On Nizhny Novgorod As Russian Strikes Cut Power In Ukraine
articles.body:
Moscow and Kyiv traded strikes on November 1, with dozens of drones reportedly destroyed over Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region and energy infrastructure hit in four Ukrainian regions, leaving hundreds of thousands without power.
The governor of Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, Gleb Nikitin, said that an "industrial enterprise" in the Kstovo district had been struck by a "massive drone attack" overnight, causing "significant damage."
He added that more than 100 drones were destroyed in the attack, with no casualties reported so far.
Ukrainian media reports suggested the strike had hit the LukOil refinery in Kstovo as well as the combined heat and power plant in Novogorkovskaya. RFE/RL could not independently verify the information.
The development came less than 24 hours after the Ukrainian military said it targeted the Russian state-owned Kombinat Kamensky chemical and defense enterprise in Russia's Rostov region with drones and Neptune coastal missile systems.
Bordering Ukraine, the region is a strategically important industrial and logistics hub in southwestern Russia. Last month, Reuters reported that Russia had nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones there in just six weeks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that the October 31 attack on the Rostov region had caused tens of millions of dollars' worth of damage, as Kyiv seeks to curb Moscow's war efforts with what it calls "long-range sanctions," referring to its strikes inside Russia.
With the Kremlin showing no interest in compromising to end the war while continuing to pound Ukraine with devastating strikes, the country's military has increasingly responded by targeting energy and military sites deep inside Russia.
On November 1, Zelenskyy said Russia attacked energy infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, leaving hundreds of thousands without power as cold weather sets in accross the Eastern Europe.
"Just this night, our energy sector in four regions was under Russian attacks: Dnipro, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytsky. These are substations, transformers, and power lines that provide electricity to our people's homes," he wrote on Telegram.
"Repair crews are working everywhere. As of now, hundreds of thousands of families remain without electricity," Zelenskyy said, adding that this week along Russia has launched 1,940 strike drones, over 1,580 glide bombs, and 44 missiles of various types over Ukraine, 36 of which are ballistic.
"The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic interceptors," he added.
The Ukrainian military said Russian forces attacked the country with 433 drones just on November 1 and that the drones were fired from Oryol and Shatalovo in Russia, as well as the Russian-occupied region of Donetsk.
Last Day Of Oleshky Cease-Fire
The evacuation of residents from the Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been completed as Moscow and Kyiv continued a localized cease-fire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump on November 1.
Trapped in the largely ruined city, which was surrounded by land mines and cut off from the outside world, Oleshky residents had endured extreme conditions for months, with little to no access to food, drinking water, medicine, or electricity.
On October 30, dozens of buses carrying civilians left the war-torn area for the first time in more than four years without incident, with people choosing whether to travel to Ukrainian- or Russian-controlled territory.
Zelenskyy, thanking the United States and Melania Trump for their mediation, said residents who wished to travel to Ukraine had crossed into the country on October 31.
"Until we got on the buses, we were still afraid," Oleshky evacuee Liubov told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service. "We were so worried and nervous. Before that, we couldn't sleep at night, wondering how this would go."
While the humanitarian efforts in Oleshky have set a rare precedent for cooperation between Ukrainian and Russian civilian representatives, the Kremlin said the temporary cease-fire there should not be extrapolated to the broader peace settlement process in Ukraine.
Moscow has repeatedly said it was not seeking a partial easing of the conflict, urging a complete resolution that would include its hard-line demands, including full control over Ukrainian territories that Russian forces have been unable to seize on the battlefield.
Zelenskyy, in turn, has been for years calling for a leaders' meeting in response, saying that issues surrounding control of Ukrainian territories have to be discussed at the highest level.
As Russian and Ukrainian officials are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi in mid-November amid US-mediated negotiations to end the war, a senior Russian official said that Russian President Vladimir Putin would respond if Zelenskyy wished to speak to him by phone.
"I think he will, of course. Putin has never refused to talk," Putin aide Yuri Ushakov was quoted as telling Russian media on November 1.
Putin has previously sought to cast doubt on Zelenskyy's legitimacy and has repeatedly said the presidents could only meet when a comprehensive peace deal has been agreed, though he has also suggested he and Zelenskyy could meet in Moscow.
The Kremlin knows that the prospect of a meeting in the capital of the country that is attacking Ukraine is unacceptable to Kyiv. Zelenskyy has expressed readiness to meet with Putin in a third country.

articles.title: Israel completes 'preparations' for Iran confrontation as US weighs options — report
articles.body:
Israel has completed preparations for a renewed military attack on Iran, whilst US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper has presented President Donald Trump with military options for resuming attacks, the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported.
“The Israeli military has finalised defensive and offensive readiness for a potential return to combat, though any decision to launch an offensive remains with Trump as diplomatic contacts continue.”
Citing unnamed political sources, the daily reported that Israel is approaching another round of fighting, but its leadership cannot unilaterally initiate the campaign, which hinges on whether Washington pursues an agreement with Tehran or orders coordinated strikes.
Preparations have advanced beyond planning.
The Israeli air force has carried out multiple long-range drills involving dozens of fighter jets and mid-air refuelling tankers across Syrian and Iraqi airspace towards Iranian frontiers to rehearse potential strike corridors.
Strategic dilemmas
Cooper tabled strike plans during a White House briefing attended by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine, though no order to resume combat has been given.
In recent days, 10 US military transport aircraft have landed at Israeli airbases delivering equipment, coinciding with broader American force reinforcements.
Sources noted a fundamental strategic dilemma: the lack of clearly defined US operational objectives.
Striking Iranian nuclear facilities, missile infrastructure, and military assets would not guarantee government collapse or policy shifts, though Washington could leverage threats to extract concessionary terms.
Regional escalation remains a critical hazard, with officials warning Hezbollah could enter the fray, stretching Israeli air defences and interceptor stockpiles.
Concurrently, indirect contacts mediated by Qatar continue, exploring prospective terms regarding Iran's nuclear programme, the Strait of Hormuz, and economic incentives, with Russia and China as potential guarantors.
Hostilities originally erupted on February 28, following joint US-Israeli strikes, before an April truce broke down into renewed exchanges in July amid stalled diplomacy.

articles.title: Rubio Casts Doubts On Quick Deal To End War In Ukraine, Defends Russian Contacts
articles.body:
ATLANTA, Georgia -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was unsure whether a negotiated end to the war in Ukraine was possible, while European officials told RFE/RL the top US diplomat also privately expressed doubts that Russian President Vladimir Putin would attend December's Miami G20 summit.
The European officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Rubio also privately shared his doubts with Western counterparts of a peace deal in the coming months during the two days of G20 foreign ministers' talks in Atlanta, which wrapped up on October 31.
Rubio's public remarks at his closing news conference were notably cautious. Asked by RFE/RL whether he believed a negotiated settlement was achievable given Moscow's unchanged position, he said Washington was still trying to establish whether an agreement could be reached.
"I don't know if negotiated peace is achievable in Ukraine. That's what we're trying to find out," Rubio said. "I don't think anyone here is claiming that we're on the verge of a negotiated settlement."
He said President Donald Trump's envoys, including Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, were devoting much of their time to the Ukraine and Iran portfolios. "But I'm not here to tell you we're on the verge of one," Rubio said, adding that he hoped an agreement could eventually be reached.
He also clarified that Ukraine negotiations were not discussed at the Atlanta G20 gathering itself.
Putin's Miami Invitation
Rubio was equally careful when asked whether Putin would attend the December summit, which Trump plans to host at his Doral resort in Florida.
"I don't even know if President Putin is going to come to Miami. They haven't announced that and they haven't confirmed that," he said.
The three European officials told RFE/RL that Rubio had privately expressed doubts the Russian leader would accept the invitation.
They also said the secretary of state defended the administration's decision to invite Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov to Atlanta and extend an invitation to Putin, arguing that diplomatic engagement was necessary to achieve a settlement.
"How can you have a negotiated settlement between Russia and Ukraine if you don't have the ability to talk to both Russia and Ukraine?" Rubio later asked when pressed by reporters.
He said Trump did not regard meeting or talking with a foreign leader as legitimizing that leader's actions or agreeing with everything they stood for.
Rubio also cited Russia's nuclear arsenal as a reason for maintaining communication between Washington and Moscow, regardless of the state of bilateral relations.
"It is always important that the United States and Russia have communications at some level because of the danger of escalation in the future," he said.
Describing his own interaction with Lavrov in Atlanta, Rubio said the two had not held a formal meeting. They spoke briefly about the possibility of their countries' leaders interacting at the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering, but made no firm commitments concerning the G20 summit.
The Western officials said Rubio's private assessment also covered Ukraine's potential NATO membership, which he reportedly described as unrealistic in the short term and unacceptable to Putin.
Rubio reportedly warned that Russia's acquisition of the entire Donbas region would not satisfy the Kremlin's territorial ambitions. It "will not end Russian appetite," he told the Europeans, according to the officials.
The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the reported private remarks.
Black Sea Opening
While Rubio offered little public optimism about a comprehensive peace agreement, he identified a more limited diplomatic objective that Washington hopes could produce results: a cease-fire covering the Black Sea.
European officials pressed Moscow during the Atlanta talks to halt attacks affecting shipping in the strategic waterway, which is vital for Ukrainian agricultural exports.
Rubio warned that disruptions to grain and energy shipments were creating serious consequences for vulnerable countries, particularly those dependent on food imports. "This is threatening the world for food security and some energy security as well," he said.
The issue was also raised by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during talks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Istanbul on October 31. Zelenskyy thanked Ankara for supporting Ukraine's sovereignty and efforts to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea.
Europeans Challenge Lavrov
The Atlanta gathering exposed deep divisions between Moscow and European governments, with Lavrov's presence prompting several delegations to refuse participation in the traditional G20 family photograph. The photograph was ultimately canceled.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accused Lavrov of presenting false narratives about the war during the discussions.
Kallas told reporters that Russia did not appear ready for peace negotiations, pointing to the continued intensity of attacks on Ukraine.
Lavrov, meanwhile, criticized what he called Europe's "arrogant boycott" and praised the Trump administration's willingness to engage with Moscow.
Rubio said the US remained committed to exploring a diplomatic solution, describing the war as devastating for both countries.
He pointed to Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and rising civilian casualties, while also citing the heavy Russian military losses. He estimated that around 20,000 Russians were being killed each month.
"It's a very deadly and destructive war," Rubio said, warning that every additional month of fighting would make the eventual reconstruction of Ukraine more difficult.
He described Washington's central objective as determining whether it could use its contacts with both sides to facilitate an end to the conflict.
The two-day ministerial ended without a joint communique, as disagreements over Ukraine, the Middle East, trade, and maritime security prevented the world's largest economies from reaching consensus.

articles.title: Greece receives second FDI frigate HS Nearchos
articles.body:
- Naval Group delivered HS Nearchos, Greece’s second FDI frigate, at Lorient on Oct. 30, ten months after the first ship, HS Kimon.
- The third Greek frigate is due by the end of 2026, and a fourth, ordered in November 2025, is scheduled for 2028.
Naval Group handed over HS Nearchos, the second of Greece’s new French-built defense and intervention frigates, to the Hellenic Navy at its shipyard in Lorient, France, on Oct. 30, ten months after Greece received the first ship of the class.
Greek Defense Minister Nikos Dendias and French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin attended the ceremony. The third Greek frigate, HS Formion, is due by the end of 2026, which would give the Hellenic Navy three of the ships within a year, the company said. Naval Group did not say when Nearchos will sail for Greece or enter operational service.
“Only ten months after the delivery of HS Kimon, it is an honour to deliver the second FDI frigate for the Hellenic Navy, HS Nearchos, in the presence of Catherine Vautrin and Nikos Dendias, whom I would like to thank for their renewed trust,” said Pierre Éric Pommellet, chairman and CEO of Naval Group.
The FDI, short for Frégate de Défense et d’Intervention, is a French design of about 4,500 tons and 122 m (400 feet) built for air defense, anti-ship and anti-submarine warfare. Greece’s version, known as the FDI HN or Kimon class, carries a heavier weapons fit than the French Navy’s ships, with Thales Sea Fire radar and up to 32 Aster 30 long-range air defense missiles. Greece is also buying Schiebel CAMCOPTER S-100 drones to fly from Kimon, Nearchos and Formion for surveillance and anti-submarine work.
The first ship, HS Kimon, was delivered on Dec. 18, 2025, and arrived in Greece in January. In March, Greece sent it to Cyprus to help defend the island against Iranian attacks, alongside a Hydra-class frigate and F-16 fighters, its first operational mission. At the time, Kimon was the only Greek warship able to provide long-range air defense, Naval News reported.
Greece agreed in September 2021 to buy three of the frigates, with an option for a fourth, in a package worth about €3 billion including weapons, and the program started in 2022. It exercised the option in November 2025, ordering a fourth ship, HS Themistokles, along with maintenance and upgrades for the whole fleet. That ship is due in 2028.
More than 75 Greek companies are involved in Naval Group’s frigate and submarine programs for Greece, supplying parts ranging from electronic maps to pre-outfitted hull blocks and complex mechanical and electronic systems, the company said. Naval Group has committed to 25% local content on the fourth frigate. It has also won the initial in-service support contract for the Greek FDIs, which it will carry out with its Greek subsidiary, Naval Group Hellas, and local partners.
The Greek ships are part of a larger order book. Thirteen FDIs have now been ordered for three NATO navies, five for France, four for Greece and four for Sweden, and Naval Group says its Lorient yard can now deliver two of the frigates a year.

articles.title: Trump says US could strike Iran’s remaining nuclear sites in ’10 minutes’
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump on Saturday said that Washington could strike Iran’s remaining suspected nuclear facilities in “10 minutes,” signaling the possibility of further military action despite ongoing diplomatic negotiations, Anadolu reports.
Speaking to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, Trump claimed that US military operations had severely weakened Iran’s armed forces and nuclear infrastructure, leaving only a few sites to be targeted.
“We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes. So, we have that plan,” Trump said.
“You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly,” he added, referring to a suspected Iranian nuclear facility.
Trump made the remarks when asked whether there was a timeline for ongoing Qatari-mediated negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
He said the US was not in a hurry to reach an agreement, claiming that American military operations had destroyed much of Iran’s navy, air force, air defenses, military equipment and nuclear infrastructure.
Asked whether Washington could resume military operations against Iran as soon as this week, Trump declined to provide a direct answer.
“Why would you ask such a stupid question?” he said, before adding: “I can’t tell you.”
– Trump says Iran will ‘never have a nuclear weapon’
Trump reiterated Washington’s opposition to Iran acquiring nuclear weapons. “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. They want to make a deal; we’ll find out about that,” he said.
Asked about the progress of negotiations, Trump expressed skepticism about Tehran’s reliability despite describing the talks as progressing.
“They’re going fine, but they’re not very reliable. I will tell you, they make a deal and then they back out. They want to make a deal. We’ll see if they make a deal,” he said.
His remarks came after Iranian negotiators met Qatari mediators in Doha on Saturday, following talks in Tehran on Friday aimed at finding a diplomatic solution to the conflict.
Tensions in the Middle East have remained high since the US and Israel launched attacks against Iran on Feb. 28, triggering Iranian retaliation across the region.

articles.title: Ukraine Liberated 96 Sq Km in October, Inflicted Record Losses
articles.body:
The Defense Forces of Ukraine liberated 96.2 square kilometers of sovereign territory in October – surpassing Russian territorial advances by 10.4 square kilometers – while inflicting an unprecedented 54,400 casualties on the Russian military, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Writing on Telegram, the head of state presented a monthly assessment establishing that Ukrainian forces recaptured more land than Russian occupying units seized over the same 31-day period, while extracting the highest monthly casualty toll recorded since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“In October, our Defense Forces of Ukraine inflicted record losses on the enemy and regained more territory than the Russian occupiers were able to capture,” Zelensky stated.
According to data presented by the president, Russian forces suffered 54,400 military personnel killed and severely wounded during the month. The monthly attrition rate also produced a single-day casualty record on Oct. 21, when Russian forces sustained 2,250 casualties within a single 24-hour cycle.
“It is important that we continue to take back what is ours,” Zelensky emphasized.
“During October, the Defense Forces liberated 96.2 square kilometers of Ukrainian land, which is 10.4 square kilometers more than the occupiers managed to capture during this time.”
Zelensky Says Hits on Rostov Plant, S-400 Post, Pantsir Cost Russia $70M
The president extended formal commendations to all Ukrainian soldiers, combat brigades, and specialized service branches contributing to the counter-offensive maneuvers and frontline containment operations.
“Russia is losing. We are holding positions, liberating territory, and ensuring that every day of the war costs the aggressor as dearly as possible,” Zelensky underscored, adding that to halt these severe losses, Moscow need only choose an immediate ceasefire and genuine diplomacy.
Asymmetric impact of Unmanned Systems Forces
A decisive component of Ukraine’s battlefield efficiency in October stemmed from the operational scale of the Unmanned Systems Forces (USF).
Earlier on Sunday, USF Commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi reported that drone detachments under his command accounted for 16,796 Russian military casualties in October – nearly 31 percent of the total 54,400 personnel losses confirmed by the president.
Over the course of the month, USF units struck 64,807 adversary targets across 255,605 combat missions, neutralizing a Russian serviceman every 159 seconds on average.
Roughly 69.5 percent of drone-inflicted Russian casualties occurred along the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk, Oleksandrivka, and Huliaipole operational axes, where loitering munitions, thermal-equipped bomber drones, and first-person view (FPV) strike craft disrupted enemy staging areas and armored columns before assault teams reached forward contact lines.
Attrition metrics
The record monthly losses in personnel and equipment compound cumulative assessments tracking the exhaustion of Russia’s conventional force generation.
A statistical study by The Economist calculated that total Russian casualties since February 2022 range between 1.4 million and 2.1 million killed and wounded, with battlefield fatalities reaching between 374,000 and 770,000.
The publication noted that the sharp escalation in fatal casualties over recent months reflects the increasing reliance of Russian field commands on frontal infantry charges to compensate for armor shortfalls.
The mounting losses have severely strained Russian domestic labor reserves, prompting Moscow to deploy thousands of North Korean troops in frontline combat while utilizing illicit overseas networks to bring North Korean forced laborers into Russian defense factories on fraudulent student visas, according to recent human rights investigations by Global Rights Compliance.
Concurrently, Ukrainian forces have coupled frontline resistance with precision interdiction against Russian military-industrial supply chains and energy hubs.
Over the final days of October, Ukrainian precision strikes destroyed an S-400 Triumf command post and a Pantsir-S2 complex valued at $70 million alongside the Kamensky solid rocket fuel plant in Rostov region, while long-range drones struck major oil processing refineries in Kstovo, Ufa, and Novokuybyshevsk.

articles.body:
Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as drones damage Russian facility
- Russian strikes cut power to hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians in four regions, while Ukraine said it hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, linked to missile production.
- Nizhny Novgorod governor Gleb Nikitin said a Ukrainian drone attack caused “significant damage” to an industrial site, and fuel officials warned against “panic buying”.
- Both sides kept up long-range attacks despite a local ceasefire near Oleshky. Russia said it downed 235 drones, while Ukraine said it shot down 371 of 433 Russian drones.

KYIV – Russian strikes left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power on Nov 1, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, while the Russian authorities reported major damage to an industrial site following Ukrainian drone attacks on Nizhny Novgorod region.
Even as a six-day local ceasefire held on its final day around the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky, there was no let-up in fighting elsewhere along the front line and both sides kept up long-range air attacks.
Zelensky said Russia had hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, cutting electricity to hundreds of thousands of households.
“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” he said on Telegram.
He said Ukraine, meanwhile, had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacture of Russian missiles.
Moscow did not comment on the reported attack in Rostov. In Nizhny Novgorod region, however, Governor Gleb Nikitin said a large-scale overnight Ukrainian drone attack caused “significant damage” to an industrial facility.
He did not identify the site that was hit. The region is home to the NORSI oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest.
Overall, Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had downed 235 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight. Ukraine’s air force said it had shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched by Russia since the evening of Oct 31.
In its morning update, the air force said dozens of Russian drones were still in the air as at the morning of Nov 1. Six separate drone alerts had been issued in Kyiv since midnight.
Fuel supplies
Nizhny Novgorod’s regional government also did not identify the facility that was struck, but it said it was taking steps to ensure gas stations were supplied with fuel, urging motorists to “buy fuel only as needed and avoid panic buying”, Interfax reported.
The warning suggests the damaged facility was linked to the region’s oil-refining or fuel-supply infrastructure. Kyiv did not immediately claim responsibility for the Nizhny Novgorod attack.
On Oct 30, Russia said Ukraine had resumed strikes on its oil refineries and accused Kyiv of ignoring a request from US President Donald Trump to stop such attacks, which Trump has blamed for raising the cost of diesel before US midterm elections next week.
Ukraine says it supports a full ceasefire on energy targets, including its own battered power grid, but that Moscow is unwilling to agree to this.
In an interview with state TV channel Vesti on Nov 1, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the energy sector, did not mention the Nizhny Novgorod strike, but said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were adding to global fuel market imbalances and affecting prices. articles.title: Iran’s supreme leader warns of 'geographically unrestricted response' if US attacks again
articles.body:
Iranian officials have nevertheless noted positive steps in mediated negotiations with the US, which is gearing up for key midterm elections next week.
Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a warning to the world that “any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
It comes as urgent diplomatic efforts continue to avoid a new all-out Iran war, which would have devastating consequences for the Middle East and beyond.
Khamenei met with Iran’s top military commanders on Saturday, presenting them with directives to prepare for potential new US-Israeli military action, according to the official IRNA news agency.
It follows warnings from the US that its forces could conduct a short but intensive military campaign against Iran after the US midterm elections next week.
The threat of a "geographically unrestricted response" means Iran could look to target Europe as well as the South Caucasus in response to a renewed attack.
State media said that Khamenei - who hasn’t been seen publicly since the Iran war began with US and Israeli strikes in late February - also called for an updated list of potential US and Israeli targets, to include “all kinds of physical and non-physical assets."
Khamenei also said that Iran would decide the duration of any new war.
"Should Iran’s enemies resume military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine when and under what conditions those attacks will end," he said.
Iranian state media reported that in a meeting on Saturday, the commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Major General Ahmad Vahidi, together with the Iranian army commander and his chief of staff, briefed the supreme leader on Iran’s military readiness and told him that Iran’s weapons production has increased “seven-fold”.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a Washington-based think tank, estimated that Khamenei’s threats were “likely part of an Iranian effort to deter the United States and Israel from striking Iran.”
While Tehran continues its threats and defiant rhetoric, its foreign minister and its security chief have signalled positive steps in their mediated negotiations with the US via Qatar.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi announced on Saturday evening that Tehran could agree to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in just two days, instead of the previous timeline of seven days.
He said that Iranian diplomats were in Qatar for talks after a Qatari delegation mediated discussions in Tehran over the last few days.
Araghchi last month proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz within a week if the US agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions. That was rejected.
In an interview with Qatar-based broadcaster Al Jazeera, Araghchi said that Iran was not planning to meet with US officials but called recent US efforts toward “broader dialogue” a positive step.
Araghchi said a decision on whether negotiations would be direct or indirect would be made “once Washington agrees to Iran’s conditions.”
It comes as the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, said he had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance’s proposing negotiations.
Commenting on the letter, Rezaei said “the tone has completely changed” and called it a “very good sign.” Araghchi also called Washington’s attempt to open dialogue a “positive step.”
Rezaei singled out an important change to one of Iran’s conditions: Ships in a reopened Strait of Hormuz would travel on a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman. And “everyone passing through this waterway will do so under Iranian management.”
He said that Iran was now awaiting the latest US response. Separately, Rezaei warned on X that any attack would bring “devastating blows on the aggressor using new weapons.”
Rezaei, who state media this past week said had met with Iran’s supreme leader, also said that there has been no decision to change Iran’s nuclear doctrine, but he noted that some Iranians have questioned whether that should be rethought if Iran is attacked again.

articles.title: North Korea tests cluster warhead for tactical ballistic missile
articles.body:
North Korea conducted a test of a cluster warhead for a tactical ballistic missile to assess its combat applicability and destructive power, state media reported on Sunday.
The Missile Administration carried out the test on Saturday, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
The test was overseen by General Kim Jong-sik, a member of the Central Military Commission of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea and first deputy director of a department of the party's Central Committee.
North Korea's Ballistic Missile Systems Research Institute and Warhead Research Institute said the test confirmed that the country's "Type-2 standard cluster warhead" could devastate a target area of about 12 to 13 hectares (29 to 32 acres) at what they described as an "ultra-high density."
The head of the Missile Administration said North Korea classifies its cluster warheads into four categories, including special-purpose and standard types.
He said Pyongyang plans to make all four types available to military units by the end of this year, allowing them to select warheads according to operational objectives and the characteristics of targets.
The Missile Administration described the test as part of regular scientific research aimed at increasing the destructive power of its weapons systems.

Russia has reportedly lost approximately 13 military aircraft in just five weeks, including Su-34 fighter-bombers, Su-30SM fighters, a Tu-95MS strategic bomber, and a Su-57 stealth fighter, following Ukrainian strikes on Russian airbases and a series of aviation accidents.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on October 31, Ukrainian open-source monitoring project Oko Gora recorded 11 Russian combat aircraft and one helicopter lost in October, with two additional Su-34 bombers damaged. Including a Tu-95MS that crashed on September 29, the reported losses reached approximately 13 aircraft since late September.
The Su-34 fighter-bomber accounted for the largest share of reported losses. Russian forces regularly use these aircraft to launch guided glide bombs against Ukrainian military positions and cities.
On October 4, Ukrainian Security Service (SBU) drones reportedly struck a Su-34 and a Su-35 fighter at Khanskaya airbase in Russia’s Republic of Adygea, approximately 500 kilometers (310 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Another attack followed on October 14–15, when Ukrainian Neptune cruise missiles targeted Borisoglebsk airbase in Russia’s Voronezh region. Satellite imagery reportedly confirmed four Su-34 bombers destroyed and two others severely damaged.
On October 29, Ukrainian forces reportedly struck Marinovka airbase in the Volgograd region with Neptune missiles, destroying another two Su-34 aircraft. In total, seven Su-34 bombers were reportedly destroyed during October, while two more sustained damage.
According to Ukrainian military intelligence, Russia had approximately 140 Su-34 aircraft in service as of October 22. Russian manufacturers delivered 22 new aircraft of this type between October 2025 and October 2026, meaning the seven reported losses in October alone amounted to nearly one-third of the previous year’s deliveries.
However, Ukrainian strikes were not the only cause of Russia’s aviation losses. As Defence Blog reported, a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed during takeoff near Ukrainka airbase in Russia’s Amur region on September 29, killing six of its seven crew members. The aircraft, which Russia uses to launch Kh-101 cruise missiles against Ukraine, is no longer in production.
On October 21, a Su-30SM fighter crashed during a training flight in Russia’s Kaliningrad region. Russian authorities said both crew members ejected. A second Su-30SM was reportedly lost the same day, although Moscow has not officially confirmed that incident.
One of the most significant reported losses involved Russia’s fifth-generation Su-57 stealth fighter. On October 29, a Su-57 reportedly caught fire during engine startup at Akhtubinsk airbase in the Astrakhan region, one of Russia’s principal military aviation testing facilities.
Satellite imagery published by Ukrainian open-source researchers showed a burn mark at the airfield, although Russian authorities have not confirmed the aircraft’s destruction.
The reported losses occurred across a wide geographical area, from Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave on the Baltic Sea to its Far Eastern regions.
For context, the open-source intelligence project Oryx has visually documented 205 Russian military aircraft destroyed or damaged since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, according to figures cited by Defence Blog. The Su-34 accounted for 48 of those documented cases.
The losses also extended to Russian helicopters. On October 30, Ukraine’s Third Assault Brigade reported destroying a Russian Mi-8 transport helicopter in the Luhansk region using two Hornet attack drones after the aircraft landed.

articles.title: Ukraine Drone Force Hits Target Every 41 Seconds in Record Month
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) struck an adversary target every 41 seconds on average and neutralized a Russian soldier every 159 seconds throughout October, marking a historic monthly record in casualties inflicted on Russian military personnel by drone detachments, USF Commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi announced.
Presenting a comprehensive monthly operational assessment on social media, Brovdi reported that USF formations engaged and struck 64,807 adversary targets over the course of October. Russian personnel losses directly attributable to USF strikes reached 16,796 soldiers killed or wounded.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The casualty tally represents the highest monthly toll achieved by the drone service branch since the launch of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. The October figure marks a 52.6 percent increase compared to August and a 24.7 percent increase over September.
According to operational data compiled by the USF command, drone operators neutralized an average of 542 Russian servicemen per day. The peak single-day casualty figure occurred on Oct. 24, when USF units recorded 701 Russian personnel neutralized within a single 24-hour cycle.
Over the month, USF units executed 255,605 individual combat missions. The operational total encompassed approximately 151,500 direct-strike sorties alongside roughly 104,000 aerial reconnaissance, target-designation, and surveillance flights.
Melania Trump Hails Oleshky Rescue as Hope for Peace
Tactical concentration along eastern and southern sectors
Brovdi emphasized that USF operational activities were heavily concentrated along critical combat vectors in eastern and southern Ukraine, where Russian assault formations attempted to sustain high-tempo offensive pressure.
Approximately 69.5 percent of all Russian personnel losses inflicted by the USF occurred across three focal axes: the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk, Oleksandrivka, and Huliaipole operational sectors.
The Pokrovsk and Dobropillia sectors in Donetsk region have remained focal points of intense ground fighting, with Russian assault groupings attempting to bypass defensive bastions through saturated infantry attacks and mechanized pushes.
Heavy multi-rotor bomber drones and first-person view (FPV) strike drones operated by the USF played a pivotal role in interdicting Russian motorized columns and logistics staging areas before forward infantry reached defensive trenches.
Brovdi stressed that the published metrics reflect solely the combat actions executed by the Unmanned Systems Forces grouping and do not incorporate casualty figures or equipment losses inflicted by other branches of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the National Guard, or specialized security agencies.
Asymmetric battlefield impact
Brovdi, who has commanded the USF since June 2025 after rising to prominence as leader of the “Madyar’s Birds” tactical aerial reconnaissance unit, notedthat the drone force constitutes approximately 2.5 percent of Ukraine’s total armed forces personnel but accounts for roughly one-third of all adversary casualties across the theater.
“A small modern Ukrainian army is winning over the old Soviet system that was in Ukraine,” Brovdi told the publication, describing the branch’s shift toward institutionalizing high-speed digital coordination, autonomous targeting algorithms, and decentralized drone platoons.
In September, Brovdi disclosed that 79 members of his original unit had been killed since 2022, asserting that his forces had achieved an attrition ratio of 656 Russian soldiers killed or wounded for every fallen member of that foundational detachment, while stressing that even higher efficiency is necessary to offset Moscow’s demographic advantages.
Because of the severe attritional damage inflicted by his formations, Russian authorities have aggressively targeted Brovdi personally.
Moscow offered a $20 million bounty for actionable intelligence regarding his whereabouts, seeking to locate him through cross-border criminal syndicates, while a Russian military court sentenced him in absentia to life imprisonment on state-directed terrorism charges in March.
Strategic interdiction of the maritime shadow fleet
Beyond tactical front-line interdiction, the Unmanned Systems Forces have played a central role in strategic operations targeting Russian economic lifelines and logistics nodes across regional maritime waters.
In late September, the USF revealed the operational results of “Operation MoLoChKa” – a Ukrainian backronym translating to “Moscow Will Lie Across Crimea” – an 11-week campaign targeting Russia’s maritime “shadow fleet” in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
The shadow fleet consists of aging, non-Western flagged commercial crude oil and petroleum tankers used by Moscow to circumvent G7 price caps and export restrictions.
During the multi-week maritime interdiction campaign that began on July 6, USF maritime and aerial drone units struck 300 Russian shadow fleet tankers, including 134 vessels operating in the Sea of Azov and 166 tankers transiting the Black Sea.
The initial surge phase resulted in 159 tankers being struck within the operation’s first 12 days.
