articles.title: Are the US midterms going to see a blue wave of Democrats winning seats – or a blue flood?
articles.body:
He spoke admiringly of a senator’s posterior. He baselessly accused a Muslim candidate of being a terrorist. He boasted about his renovations of the White House. He quipped that his own supporters couldn’t afford a hamburger at his Mar-a-Lago club. Every now and then, he spoke about the cost of living, and other everyday concerns of voters.
Donald Trump has held dozens of campaign rallies before next week’s US midterm elections. The 80-year-old remains convinced that he can prove the doubters wrong again and help Republicans retain control of the US Congress. But it was five words he uttered at this summer’s Republican convention in Dallas that could seal his party’s fate: “Pretend I’m on the ticket.”
That plea was music to the ears of Democrats. It helped ensure that the midterms will deliver a national verdict on Trump’s second term in the White House. And opinion polls suggest that the judgment will be damning, piercing his aura of invincibility, reshaping the final two years of his presidency and setting the stage for a fierce battle to succeed him.
“Donald Trump nationalised these races, and now they’ll lose seats because of it,” said Michael Steele, a former chair of the Republican National Committee. “He made himself the referendum. Individual candidates wanted to run their individual races but he told them: ‘Put me on the ballot.’ He has political instincts for himself, but no political instincts for the party.”
Pain is the norm for White House incumbents when the midterms roll around. In 1994, Bill Clinton suffered a 54-seat setback in the House of Representatives; in 2010, Barack Obama lost 63; in 2018, Trump himself lost 40. He seems unlikely to defy history this time. Trump goes into the elections with the lowest approval rating of any president before the midterms since Harry Truman’s Democrats were crushed 80 years ago.
The coalition that in 2024 powered Trump to the greatest comeback in modern political history has suffered blow after blow: his failure to fully release the Jeffrey Epstein files detailing ties of the elite to the child sex offender; the growth of datacentres in rural communities; an eight-month-old war in Iran that he promised would be over in weeks; a relentless rise in the cost of fuel and food.
The anger over Trump’s broken promises has been compounded by a whiff of corruption, and the perception that he is using the presidency to enrich himself and his family. He accepted a plane from Qatar to use as Air Force One, decorated the Oval Office in gold, demolished the White House East Wing to make way for a $400m ballroom and is planning a triumphal arch in Washington. His personal fortune meanwhile has surged – from $2.3bn in 2024 to $6.5bn, according to Forbes.
‘Much more macro than Maga’
With Republicans clinging to a paper-thin 218–214 margin in the House and 53–47 lead in the Senate, opinion polls indicate a rising “blue wave”. A recent Reuters/Ipsos survey gave Democrats an 11-point lead, 47% to 36%, on the generic congressional ballot, while Trump’s approval rating stood at 32%. Voters will also choose governors in 36 states and three US territories, and decide thousands of state legislative contests.
Tens of millions of early votes have already been cast, with habitual Republican turnout lagging behind Democratic participation in critical battlegrounds. So dire is the environment for Republicans that conservative Super Pacs backed by billionaire Elon Musk, who has poured $366m into saving Republican candidates, are being forced to dump emergency funds into strongholds like Kansas, Iowa and Texas.
Trump won the presidency in 2024 after promising to curb inflation and lower prices; instead, the opposite has happened. Across the country, voters are confronting an affordability crisis exacerbated by two defining choices of Trump’s second term: a sweeping regime of foreign tariffs and the fateful decision to launch airstrikes on Iran in February.
Chris Matthews, a political commentator and former presidential speechwriter and congressional aide, said: “He’s losing on cost of living and affordability. Older people on limited incomes are focusing on what it costs to live each month. It’s much more macro than Maga. No matter what he does for Maga people, the power of macroeconomics is much stronger and people are going to vote against him.”
The economic fallout of the Iran war, which Trump frequently downplays as a “little detour”, has reverberated across global energy markets. Diesel prices have soared, sending shock waves through agriculture and freight transport from the Central valley of California to the grain belts of Iowa and Ohio.
Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and former official in the Clinton White House, points out that voters can directly attribute their economic misery to the president. “There’s a very clear line between his actions and the things people don’t like,” she said.
“It’s going to be the tariffs and it’s going to be the war: both self-inflicted wounds. He didn’t have to raise tariffs; that was his theory of the world, which turned out to be wrong. Bombing nuclear sites in Iran was one thing, but going to all-out war turned out to be a mistake. Voters connect his actions to things they don’t like.”
This frustration is fuelling an energetic mobilisation among Democratic candidates, particularly women running in districts that once seemed out of reach. Jessica Mackler, the president of Emilys List, which is backing 247 female candidates this cycle, notes that voters feel the economic system is actively stacked against them.
“Voters understand that the corruption coming out of Washington is directly linked to why they can’t get ahead, and why they find it so hard to make ends meet,” Mackler said. “Cost of living is a huge driver but voters are desperate for new leadership who have lived their pain and understand it.”
A ‘devastating referendum’ on Trump
For months, Republican strategists urged their candidates in tight suburban races to keep national politics at arm’s length, and focus on local accomplishments, perhaps hoping that Trump might quietly concentrate on his day job in Washington. Instead, the president has embarked on a whirlwind tour across the country, denouncing Democrats as “communists” while touting a strong economy, secure border and historic drop in violent crime.
But Steele, a co-host of the MS Now network’s the Weeknight, argues that core conservative voters feel increasingly betrayed by a president who promised to avoid foreign entanglements and bring down costs. “Donald Trump lied to his tribe … He said he wouldn’t engage us in foreign wars; we’re now turning the corner into a year of a war he started and people are saying: ‘I can’t even afford to put gas in my car.’”
Perhaps no development in the 2026 midterms is more alarming to Republican strategists than the dramatic erosion of support among Latino voters. In 2024, Trump made historic inroads with Latino men, sparking triumphant declarations of a permanent multiethnic, working-class coalition.
Yet no sooner had he taken the oath of office than he unleashed an aggressive, high-visibility deportation campaign featuring heavily armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids in cities and agricultural hubs.
Larry Jacobs, founder and director of the Center for the Study of Politics and Governance at the University of Minnesota, said: “Donald Trump launched his radical deportation strategy and it has powerfully alienated the fastest-growing part of the electorate.
“A year ago, Republicans thought they had established a new Hispanic coalition that would guarantee five new seats in Texas alone. They may lose all of them. Economics is a driving factor, but opposition to Trump’s deportation policies has contributed massively to the magnitude of the defections.”
Henry Olsen, a senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center thinktank in Washington, notes that the Latino shift is visible across public polling and state-level data, saying: “Whether it’s a 15-point shift or a 30-point shift, it’s a big deal. Unless every piece of evidence we have is wrong, Latino voters are having serious buyers’ remorse.”
This dynamic is evident in Texas, where no Democrat has won statewide office since 1994. James Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative and former public school teacher who preaches a gospel of social justice, is taking on Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton in the most expensive Senate race in history.
Paxton, a staunch Trump ally, has been bogged down by years of corruption allegations, personal scandal and securities fraud charges. Despite $300m in outside Republican spending, led by Musk, Talarico has a narrow lead in most polls.
Jacobs views Texas as a bellwether for the post-Trump Republican party. “If Paxton loses, it’s going to send a very powerful signal to future Republican leaders about how they handle immigration,” he said. “It proves that attacking the fastest-growing part of the electorate is political suicide. Texas is a devastating referendum on Donald Trump.”
A test for Democrats
While Democrats appear heavily favoured to pick up the four net seats required to capture the House of Representatives, their path to taking the Senate is a steeper climb. Yet because of Trump’s dismal approval ratings and the economic shock of the Iran war, the Senate battlefield has expanded into states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024.
In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown is mounting a comeback bid against incumbent Republican Jon Husted. Brown, a grizzled populist with deep ties to organised labour, has capitalised on working-class anger over fuel prices and plant closures, as well as local opposition to datacentres. In a peculiar recurring feature of his rallies in the state, Trump has frequently veered off-script to praise Husted’s physique. (“His ass was like a big piece of muscle,” according to the president.)
In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers is up against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a 41-year-old doctor and former Detroit health director bidding to become the first Muslim senator in the US. Republicans have aggressively targeted El-Sayed over past foreign policy statements, while pro-Israel Super Pacs have poured millions of dollars into the state to defeat him. Trump has launched Islamophobic tirades, calling El-Sayed a “jihadist”.
Olsen said: “El-Sayed is the biggest test for progressives. If he wins stateside in an industrial heartland state like Michigan, progressives will argue they have the upper hand heading into 2028.”
However, Kamarck cautions against over-interpreting progressive strength. She insisted: “The progressives are a minuscule portion of the Democratic party. This is an overblown story. The moderates are winning the vast majority of these races across the country.”
In Maine, veteran Republican senator Susan Collins is fighting for her political life against Democrat Troy Jackson, a lumberjack and former president of the state senate. Collins has attempted to distance herself from Trump, appearing on the trail with independent former senator Joe Manchin, but Democrats have relentlessly hammered her votes for conservative supreme court justices and other Trump priorities.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola is mounting a challenge to Republican senator Dan Sullivan. The contest has become embroiled in a legal dispute after the justice department sought to block certification of a possible Peltola victory. Her allies reportedly helped recruit a decoy candidate with the name Dan Sullivan to confuse voters. Peltola’s campaign denies involvement.
‘He’ll do anything’
Election integrity remains a broader national concern. Trump’s repeated, unsubstantiated claims of election fraud have prompted Democrats and voting-rights organisations to prepare legal teams and observers for disputes or federal interference. The administration says federal election monitors will follow the law, and has denied plans to send troops or immigration agents to polling stations.
Tara Setmayer, a co-founder and chief executive of the Seneca Project, a women-led political action committee, said: “I am extremely worried. We have seen what Donald Trump has done when he had guardrails; now he has none. He has power and people who are aligned with him in the attack on our election integrity in positions of power.
“This is a great concern to me because Trump is looking at the sun setting on his presidency and we all know that he is deathly afraid of being out of power. He’ll do anything to stay in power, even if that means creating another constitutional crisis to try to stop Congress from being seated. We cannot suffer from a lack of imagination of what these people are capable of.”
A Democratic victory in either chamber will effectively stall Trump’s domestic legislative agenda, leaving his administration to rely on executive orders. Hakeem Jeffries, who would likely become the first Black speaker of the House, has pledged to immediately unleash subpoena power to investigate administration corruption, foreign policy decisions in Iran, and the personal financial enrichment of the Trump family.
Jacobs said: “It’s going to be a fistfight. I’m not expecting major legislation to pass. I think there will be extensive investigations of Donald Trump and his cabinet, and that’s what we’re going to get for two years.”
Steele believes that a Democratic House will immediately assert control over federal purse strings. “Congress will freeze money on projects like tearing down the East Wing for Trump’s ballroom, and they’ll reassert oversight over the Kennedy Center,” he said, referring to the national arts complex and living memorial to the 35th president. “Trump is effectively a lame duck now. The rest of the country knows his time is coming to an end.”
Indeed, before the last vote is counted, attention will likely turn to the presidential contest in 2028. For Republicans, a crushing midterm loss could accelerate the race to a post-Trump future. JD Vance is currently positioned as the heir apparent to the Maga movement, but figures such as the senator Ted Cruz of Texas and the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, could also be in contention.
Steele commented: “Republicans need to recognise that the future of the party does not rest solely with the Maga base. It rests with winning back the suburban, moderate and Hispanic voters this administration has isolated.”
Under pressure from a restive base, Democrats will also be preparing for a sprawling contest to decide the future direction of their party – and how it can turn the page on the Trump era. The next Democratic presidential candidate is equally uncertain, with outgoing California governor Gavin Newsom, Georgia senator Jon Ossoff, New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and even former vice-president and 2024 nominee Kamala Harris among those regularly mentioned.
Bill Whalen, a research fellow at the Hoover Institution thinktank in Stanford, California, said: “Voters are tired. When you combine high prices, the endless argument and the constant noise of Donald Trump, people want a change from the status quo.”
“On November 3, the voters are going to speak – and Donald Trump is not going to like what they have to say,” he predicted.

articles.title: US's VP JD Vance and Trump are are at loggerheads on Iran war
articles.body:
The positions taken by J.D. Vance in recent weeks—which differ from those of Donald Trump regarding the initiation or continuation of a war with Iran—along with his recent message to Major General Mohsen Rezaei (Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council), may signal an intent by American Republicans to prepare Vance for the 2028 presidential race, regardless of the message's specific content or Iran's response.
 
Facing a weakened base due to Trump’s failed approach toward Iran—and seeing the party on the verge of defeat against the Democrats in congressional elections—Republicans are seeking to groom a figure distinct from Trump for the 2028 presidential election.
 
Republicans believe that Vance—as a vice-presidential candidate who has historically expressed skepticism toward foreign military interventions—could attract a specific segment of the electorate by voicing opposition to a costly and futile war against Iran.
 
To properly assess J.D. Vance’s stance, one must distinguish between his opposition to a prolonged, costly war and an opposition to any form of military action against Iran. Vance’s position is not an objection to the use of American military power to secure national interests; rather, it is an opposition specifically to long, expensive wars.
 
On October 17, 2026, he alluded to a divergence of opinion between himself and Trump regarding a potential war with Iran. In doing so, Vance signaled that he is not merely a continuation of Trump’s warmongering policies, but rather someone who holds independent views on critical issues such as war and foreign policy. During the 2024 election campaign, in a conversation with American comedian and critic Tim Dillon, he stated that a war with Iran would not be in America's interest and would entail an extremely heavy cost.
 
On February 26, 2026, he also told The Washington Post that the United States should avoid becoming mired in a years-long war with no clear end in sight, and should instead favor a diplomatic approach. Nevertheless, Vance did not rule out the possibility of limited military action to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. On one hand, Vance seeks to appeal to the anti-war faction within the Republican Party; on the other, he fears that distancing himself too much from Trump could invite the president's wrath and cost him the support of Trump’s loyal base.
Vance is well aware that if he defends Trump too fervently, he will fail to establish himself as a distinct alternative for the presidency. At the same time, Vance’s opposition to costly wars could be a tactical move by the Republicans to help him forge a political identity independent of Trump.
 
To counter Democratic narratives regarding Trump’s alleged warmongering, the Republican Party might encourage Vance to criticize the prospect of a Trump-led war with Iran—while remaining committed to the "America First" doctrine and opposing the entanglement of the U.S. in protracted conflicts. The Republican Party’s efforts to groom Vance have not gone unnoticed by the media; a report by The Guardian on October 24, 2026, suggests that his prominent role within the party may serve as a dry run for a potential presidential bid in 2028. As the 2028 elections approach, it appears that Republicans will urge Vance to express his opposition to Trump—and to America’s hawkish, interventionist policies—more explicitly and independently.
 
By gradually distancing himself from Trump, Vance would aim to secure the support of Republican donors for a potential electoral bid. The Republicans will likely frame any aggression by Trump against Iran as a unilateral, unauthorized action—one taken without the party’s consent. By positioning Vance as a figure who stands in opposition to Trump, they intend to prepare him for a run in the 2028 presidential election.
Crucially, the defeat of the United States and the Zionist regime—coupled with Iran’s sustained national cohesion and military strength—serves as the primary motivation for Republicans seeking a way out of the current crisis and a means to distance themselves from Trump.
 
According to a Reuters report from October 7, 2026, two-thirds of Republican candidates in critical House and Senate races have either diverged from Trump on certain policy issues or sought to diminish their association with him. In 12 out of the 62 races examined, disagreements regarding the war with Iran emerged as a central issue. The economic strain caused by the conflict—exacerbated by Iran’s strategic management of the Strait of Hormuz—has fueled opposition among some Republicans, who are increasingly concerned about rising fuel prices and the resulting financial burden on households.
 
These developments suggest that America’s failure in the war with Iran is not merely a military setback; it also serves as a litmus test for the future direction of the Republican Party.
 
In essence, the heavy costs of the war for the United States, combined with the failure to achieve stated objectives—a direct result of Iran’s military prowess—are the primary drivers behind the realignment of power within the Republican Party.

articles.title: NATO turns 5G towers into sensors in Baltic battlefield experiment

Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, described the results at Ādaži Military Base near Riga at the close of the Digital Backbone Experimentation, known as DiBaX 2026, which ran from Oct. 19 to 30. He said some tests failed along the way and that the alliance had deliberately accepted that risk.
“We have connected systems that were never designed to communicate with each other, using artificial intelligence to overcome interoperability barriers. It’s the first time that we have, for example, a Maven system that is speaking to a national system, and that has been fixed in hours with Agentic AI,” said Vandier.
NATO bought its own version of Palantir’s AI-enabled Maven Smart System in 2025 to help commanders pull together intelligence and speed up decisions, and has been rolling it out across its headquarters. Vandier did not say which country’s system Maven was connected to. Agentic AI refers to software that can carry out multistep tasks on its own, in this case working out how two systems exchange data.
The counter-drone test crossed a national border. A drone took off in Lithuania, flew into Latvia and was engaged there by a counter-drone system, Vandier said. It was one of several trials under NATO’s Layered Counter-UAS Initiative, which looks at how sensors and weapons from different countries and companies can work together as one layered defense against drones.
“Even if it didn’t work this morning, it has been done this week. So we had a drone taking off from Lithuania, arriving here and being engaged by a counter system,” said Vandier.
DiBaX itself tested three ways to keep NATO forces connected. In the first, organizers set up a private slice of a host country’s commercial 5G network, reserved and secured for military use, so arriving NATO forces could have command and data links from their first day before their own infrastructure arrived. The second tested automatic switching between communication paths when one is jammed, including radio across different frequencies, satellite links such as 5G direct-to-device, and troposcatter, which bounces radio signals off the lower atmosphere to reach beyond the horizon. The third used ordinary 5G cell towers as passive sensors to detect objects moving through their coverage, particularly in cities with dense tower networks. Vandier said a team of medics in the field also sent patient biodata over the network to doctors in the United States.
The scenarios were built around grey-zone incidents below the threshold of NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause, such as drone incursions and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea. A third track, Next Generation Targeting, tested AI-enabled decision support to shorten the time between collecting information and acting on it, and Vandier said the targeting process ran noticeably faster by the end of the week than at the start.
“For us, as a NATO member of the Alliance Eastern Flank here in Latvia, we cannot afford to treat technological innovation and adaptation as a distant objective for us,” said Lt. Gen. Kaspars Pudāns, commander of the Latvian National Armed Forces.
Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, the United States, Canada, Finland and other allies took part, along with NATO bodies including the DIANA innovation accelerator and the NATO Communications and Information Agency. More than 60 technology companies joined, among them Ericsson, Nokia, Thales and Portuguese drone maker TEKEVER, with Latvian telecom company LMT acting as technical integrator. This was the fifth year in a row the experiment has been held in Latvia.
The event closed with NATO FUSE on Oct. 29 and 30, which included live field demonstrations. NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, visited Latvia on Oct. 30 and met President Edgars Rinkēvičs. European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis used the event to announce two pilot European Drone Technology Hubs, one in Latvia and one in the Netherlands, to open in 2027 and speed up development and testing of drone and counter-drone technology in cooperation with NATO.
“The next challenge, and it’s the most difficult, is adoption,” said Vandier.

articles.title: Pro-EU Polish PM brings ‘Russian bots’ into court showdown
articles.body:
Pro-EU Polish PM brings ‘Russian bots’ into court showdown
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has accused his political opponents of receiving support from an “army of Russian bots”amid an escalating constitutional crisis in Warsaw. The pro-EU leader offered no proof for his claim, which came after a government-backed judge moved to oust two key officials supported by his rival, right-wing President Karol Nawrocki, from the Constitutional Tribunal, triggering public outrage.
Unrest erupted on Friday when Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge elected by Tusk’s governing majority, ordered the suspension of Constitutional Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski and his deputy Bartlomiej Sochanski, both linked to the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. The tribunal’s existing leadership rejected the suspensions, declaring that all those participating in the attempted takeover “are committing the crime of a coup d’état.”
The development triggered street protests around the court building and a heavy police deployment. Nawrocki, who canceled a planned trip to Senegal, personally pushed his way into the tribunal to confront Korwin-Piotrowska and her allies, telling them that “you are not judges of the Constitutional Tribunal.”
In a televised address on Saturday evening, Tusk scrambled to defend his actions, accusing his rivals of “seeking to destroy democracy and the rule of law.” The Polish PM, a strong supporter of EU integration who served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019, has long criticized PiS judicial reforms – which he said undermined judges’ independence – as well as Nawrocki’s refusal to administer the oath to five Constitutional Tribunal judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
“Is it greed, stupidity or treason?” Tusk asked, claiming that the opposition was receiving support from “pro-Russian forces worldwide.”
“In this conflict, they’re using an army of Russian bots online. In fact, they’ve even received public compliments from the Kremlin’s chief ideologue,” the prime minister claimed, without providing further proof or elaborating.
Moscow has repeatedly said it does not interfere in other countries’ domestic affairs. While Russian officials have yet to respond to Tusk’s allegation, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov in July denied that Russia was responsible for cyberattacks on Polish energy infrastructure.
Responding to Tusk’s address, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, called the prime minister a “pathological liar” and accused him of setting Poland ablaze while pretending to extinguish the fire. “It’s hard to find a single word, expression, or sentence that would be true, that would reflect the actual or legal reality,” he added.
Tusk’s accusation comes after several Western media outlets, anti-Russia hawks, and Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky propagated the claim that Kiev’s drone strikes, which damaged several data centers operated by Russian technology giant Yandex, crippled alleged Russian bot networks supporting Western right-wing movements, including Germany’s AfD and US President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement.
However, several independent investigations by cybersecurity and research firms quickly debunked the narrative. Experts in particular pointed out that one viral graph supposedly showing a collapse in AfD-related activity was found to contain fabricated or unverifiable figures.
Commenting on the chaos, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev described it as a “constitutional coup.” He suggested that “Brussels’ protégé Tusk” was persecuting PiS conservatives over the latter’s hostility toward Ukrainian Nazi collaborators. Medvedev concluded by sarcastically invoking an old schoolyard joke, saying, “And these are the people who scold my brother and me for picking our noses.”

articles.title: Attack boats stayed in harbour all summer, report warns
articles.body:
Britain’s attack submarine fleet spent the summer tied up in harbour while Russian activity around British waters increased, and the availability of escorts for the ballistic missile boats that carry the nuclear deterrent is among the consequences raised, according to a briefing paper published by the 878 Institute.
The paper, the first in a planned series on the condition of the Royal Navy, opens by saying: “The Royal Navy is gripped by a critical but needless decline in strategic capacity, as demonstrated by a steep reduction in both mass and readiness.
“This comes at a time of intensifying maritime competition and growing threats to British national interests. These threats are most acute in and around British waters, as Russia’s submarines, warships and even its shadow-fleet carrying illicit Russian oil across the globe, are all increasing their operations off Britain’s coasts.”
It records that the Royal Navy spent twenty-one days in July alone monitoring Russian ships, that operations to track Russian activity rose twenty-five per cent on the previous year, and that Russian warships made repeated voyages through the Dover Strait and the North Sea. Ministers have confirmed that Moscow uses commercial proxies to threaten undersea infrastructure, and the paper cites analysis uncovering five hundred incidents of Russian civilian vessels loitering above cables.
Concerns about the frigate and destroyer fleets are set out alongside the navy’s transition to automation through the hybrid navy concept, before the paper turns to its main subject. It says: “However, it is in the submarine fleet that we see an especially stark vulnerability and where, due to its purposes, creates unique threats to Britain’s security.”
On the Astute class, which numbers five in service with two more being readied, the paper states: “Despite maintaining a fleet of five vessels, it was reported that not a single Astute-class submarine was operationally deployed through summer 2026, and that all five remained laid-up in British harbours. Only HMS Agamemnon (one of the two planned additions to the five in service) is at sea conducting trials.
“This is deeply concerning, given both the rise in Russian sub-surface activity around British waters, but perhaps more worrying because of the lack of available escorts for Britain’s nuclear deterrent.” That finding draws on reporting by Navy Lookout, and the Ministry of Defence does not comment on submarine operations.
Turning to the four Vanguard boats, the paper acknowledges that deployment cycles are not discussed publicly and then sets out what it describes as widely understood. It says: “Due to the nature of their deterrent, HM Government rightly does not comment on their deployment cycles or current state. However, it is widely understood that the fleet has been in a poor state for some years.”
Designed for patrols of three to four months, the boats have run planned patrols of under a hundred days well past that mark. The paper says: “Most SSN- and SSBN-operating navies view 100-day patrols as the sensible maximum; at least the last ten deterrent patrols all exceeded five months in duration, up until April this year, with the last coming in at over 200 days, apparently becoming the new normal.”
On the four Dreadnought boats due in the early 2030s, the paper argues that work on their successor cannot wait, since each is designed for thirty years of service and the build alone takes twenty. The Ministry of Defence accepted the Strategic Defence Review’s recommendation to begin early definition and requirement-setting during this parliamentary term, a pledge affirmed in July, and the paper says: “However, this pledge was only affirmed in July 2026, and there have been no major announcements since; with only two full Parliamentary years left before the next General Election must be called, the Government needs to properly commit to Dreadnought’s successor at the earliest opportunity.”
The sharpest warnings concern SSN-AUKUS, where steel cutting on the first British boat is scheduled at Barrow-in-Furness in 2027. The paper says: “Given the likely concurrent Astute and Dreadnought programmes, the sole UK submarine construction site in Barrow-in-Furness risks facing acute labour shortfalls as soon as SSN-AUKUS begins. In the meantime the site has added only about 500 workers against a required 2,500 to run the parallel Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS build lines.
“The projected build-timeframes for SSN-AUKUS are also deeply concerning. Astute-class boats averaged 128 months to build; SSN-AUKUS are projected to take only 18 months each. This feels unrealistic, and risks cost overruns, delays, supply-chain over-stretch, and potentially an even bigger ‘submarine gap’.”
Describing the programme as Pillar One of AUKUS and saying it must not fail, the paper adds: “However, without guarantees of resource from HM Government that are currently absent, and instead a vague pledge of total vessels built, a lack of political leadership and gaps in the defence-industrial base, Britain risks being the weak link in the partnership.”
Four recommendations follow, covering a firm commitment to twelve SSN-AUKUS boats at the spring Spending Review in 2027, increased resources for the Astute class to clear maintenance backlogs and dockyard constraints, a standing requirement for two of the five Astutes to be deployable and operational at all times, and the commissioning of the Dreadnought successor definition phase by the close of 2027.
The 878 Institute published a broader paper on British deterrence gaps in August, which UKDJ reported at the time, covering land, space and naval capability with a foreword by General the Lord Dannatt. The Defence Committee reported this month that Britain has allowed its under-ice submarine capability to lapse and that the department has accepted an anti-submarine warfare gap in northern waters, and the Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise.

articles.title: Iran to receive Russian Su-35 fighter jets after US-Iran war ends, IRGC spokesman says - report
articles.body:
Iran will reportedly receive Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets after the US-Iran war ends, Revolutionary Guards spokesman General Mohammad Akraminia told Iranian media on Sunday.
Akraminia claimed that before the war began at the end of February, the IRGC was in the final stages of procuring the fighter jets. He told the Persian-language outlet Tabnak that the Su-35s were meant to arrive before the war.
Akramina did not elaborate as to why they were not delivered before the fighting began.
“We had already completed the necessary preliminary work, including the procurement process and the signing of contracts. The necessary work concerning pilot training and instruction had also been completed, and there were no longer any problems in that regard,” he said.
“In fact, these aircraft were supposed to arrive before the war. God willing, we will certainly receive them after the war and upgrade our air fleet.”
Iran claims it plans to strengthen air defenses after war with US
Akraminia added that the IRGC plans to roll out more advanced aircraft, including the Su-35.
“We have also made progress domestically. Of course, purchasing equipment from abroad will bring us closer to advanced technologies, which we can then use as a foundation for further development,” he added.
While he did not specifically name Russia in the interview, it is the only established manufacturer of Su-35s. The fighter jet is Russian-designed and produced by Sukhoi, part of Russia's United Aircraft Corporation.
However, Russia allows other countries, including Iran, to operate the fighter jets.
Akraminia added that Iran is working to develop ground-based and airborne radar systems, as well as satellites to strengthen the country’s air defenses.
“When you operate an advanced aircraft such as the Su-35, you must also have ground-based systems, airborne systems, and satellite capabilities supporting it. Only then can the aircraft reach its full operational potential,” he added.
Akraminia noted that the US sanctions against Iran have made it difficult to rebuild the country’s military.
“Sometimes sanctions affect trade, goods, oil, and similar areas. But they also affect defense and military technologies,” he said.
“The Americans have absolutely refused to allow these new technologies to enter our country. They have imposed very severe sanctions.
“Everything we have achieved, all the capabilities you mentioned, has been developed domestically through the efforts of our own specialists and young people working in the country's defense industries, universities, and knowledge-based companies.”
He then claimed that during both wars with the US, Iran “did not use a single foreign-produced weapon.”

articles.body:

Kyiv • UNN

articles.title: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as drones damage Russian facility
articles.body:
By Max Hunder and Alessandra Prentice
Nov 1 (Reuters) - Russian strikes left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, while Russian authorities reported major damage to an industrial site following Ukrainian drone attacks on Nizhny Novgorod region.
Even as a six-day local ceasefire held on its final day around the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky, there was no letup in fighting elsewhere along the front line and both sides kept up long-range air attacks.
Zelenskiy said Russia had hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, cutting electricity to hundreds of thousands of households.
“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” he said on Telegram.
He said Ukraine, meanwhile, had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacture of Russian missiles.
Moscow did not comment on the reported attack in Rostov. In Nizhny Novgorod region, however, Governor Gleb Nikitin said a large-scale overnight Ukrainian drone attack caused “significant damage” to an industrial facility.
He did not identify the site that was hit. The region is home to the NORSI oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest.
Overall, Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had downed 235 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight. Ukraine’s air force said it had shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched by Russia since Saturday evening.
In its morning update, the air force said dozens of Russian drones were still in the air as of Sunday morning. Six separate drone alerts had been issued in Kyiv since midnight.
FUEL SUPPLIES
Nizhny Novgorod’s regional government also did not identify the facility that was struck, but it said it was taking steps to ensure gas stations were supplied with fuel, urging motorists to “buy fuel only as needed and avoid panic buying,” Interfax reported.
The warning suggests the damaged facility was linked to the region’s oil-refining or fuel-supply infrastructure. Kyiv did not immediately claim responsibility for the Nizhny Novgorod attack.
On Friday, Russia said Ukraine had resumed strikes on its oil refineries and accused Kyiv of ignoring a request from US President Donald Trump to stop such attacks, which Trump has blamed for raising the cost of diesel before US midterm elections next week.
Ukraine says it supports a full ceasefire on energy targets, including its own battered power grid, but that Moscow is unwilling to agree to this.
In an interview with state TV channel Vesti on Sunday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the energy sector, did not mention the Nizhny Novgorod strike, but said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were adding to global fuel market imbalances and affecting prices.
(Writing by Alessandra Prentice, Editing by Alison Williams and Ros Russell)

articles.title: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading
articles.body:
Donald Trump’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.
The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.
But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.
The new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.
The paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.
Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order. He described the strategy as building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.
By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.
China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging its overwhelming dominance over the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year, it stunned the Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.
It has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains many other restrictions. While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hit other countries for a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency has estimated that if China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.
Where does the supply chain war go from here? The Trump administration is pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.
China, on the other hand, has announced a range of high-tech export restrictions, covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.
One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.
China will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.
This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?
The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.

articles.title: Are the Houthis attacking Mecca and Medina? Saudi claims ignite battle over Islam's holiest cities
articles.body:
Houthi forces have been attacking Saudi Arabia relentlessly in recent months, launching missiles and drones toward targets including the capital Riyadh and the areas of Al-Kharj, Jeddah, Yanbu, Khamis Mushait and Najran. But when it comes to alleged attacks on Mecca and Medina, Islam's two holiest cities, the facts are far less clear. In recent weeks, Saudi authorities have repeatedly reported air raid alerts in both cities, while the Houthis have vehemently denied targeting either of them. For Muslims, Sunni and Shiite alike, the religious significance of the two cities is profound, as are the implications of attacking them.
Within the broader war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, another battle is now unfolding over which side is violating the sanctity of Islam's holiest sites and behaving like an "enemy of Islam."
On Friday morning, the Saudi-led coalition reported intercepting a drone that it said had been launched by the Houthis toward Mecca. Hours later, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree dismissed the allegation as fabricated. "Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and no one in the world believes these lies and fabrications," he said. Later that day, the coalition announced that it had intercepted another drone in the Medina area, prompting another Houthi denial.
Mecca is Islam's holiest city, regarded as the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad and home to the Grand Mosque, or Masjid al-Haram, the most sacred mosque in Islam. Within it stands the Kaaba, the ancient structure toward which Muslims around the world face during their daily prayers and the focal point of the annual Hajj pilgrimage. Medina, Islam's second-holiest city, is where Muhammad migrated from Mecca in an event known as the Hijra. It is also home to the Prophet's Mosque, where he is buried.
The Houthis regularly emphasize their connection to Islam and the Prophet Muhammad. In August, they held celebrations marking the Prophet's birthday in areas under their control. From the group's perspective, Saudi accusations that it is attacking Mecca and Medina amount to allegations that it is threatening Islam's most sacred places. The Houthis insist that Riyadh is exploiting the cities' religious significance for political purposes, while accusing the Saudi authorities themselves of violating their sanctity.
Claims and denials
The war of competing narratives has continued for weeks. The current round of escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began in July, while Saudi allegations of launches toward Mecca first emerged on September 15, when authorities reported alerts in several areas of the kingdom, including the holy city. The Houthi-affiliated Saba news agency quoted a military source categorically rejecting the accusation. "We strongly deny the existence of any threat from Yemen against the holy city of Mecca or any other sacred sites," the source said. "Promoting these reports is intended to tarnish our image and win sympathy from the Islamic world, a familiar tactic of the Saudi enemy."
Mohammed al-Farah, a member of the Houthi political bureau, also rejected the accusations. "The talk of an attack on Mecca from Yemen is a lie," he said. "Saudi Arabia is facing a real crisis. It is begging the international community and trying to mobilize Muslims using a false pretext to divert attention from its failure. The solution is clear: Stop the aggression, lift the blockade, leave Yemen alone and compensate Yemenis for the years of war and destruction."
The Saudi-led coalition subsequently issued a statement indicating that the alert in Mecca had been triggered by a Houthi drone launched toward the city and intercepted outside its boundaries. "This hostile attempt marks the second time Mecca has been attacked, following an initial attempt to launch a ballistic missile on July 27, 2017," the coalition said. It described the alleged attack as "a black stain on the history of the Houthis" and an attempt to provoke the religious feelings of millions of Muslims, stressing that "the security of the Two Holy Mosques is a red line."
On September 17, Houthi leader Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi rejected the Saudi accusation, saying the alleged attack was an invention that itself violated the sanctity of Mecca, a city sacred to all Muslims, particularly Yemenis. The following day, Houthi supporters demonstrated in areas under the group's control against Saudi Arabia and what they called "the lie about attacking Mecca." The denials continued into October. In a statement on October 16, Saree said: "The lies spread by the Saudi regime about targeting holy Mecca are fooling no one. They are the ones desecrating the holy city through immorality and debauchery. Yemen poses no threat to the holy sites. Our operations are directed against the regime's oil facilities and military bases, which are far from the holy places."
The Houthi political bureau also denied targeting Mecca, describing the accusation as "the biggest lie of our time." It said Mecca and all Islamic holy sites hold a sacred place in the hearts of Muslim peoples, particularly Yemenis, while accusing the Saudi authorities of exploiting the cities' religious significance for warfare. The statement also alleged that Saudi Arabia was desecrating Mecca by "hosting Zionist Jews," as the Houthis put it, and organizing parties characterized by debauchery and moral corruption. "The Saudi regime remembers the sanctity of Mecca only when it needs to exploit the holy sites to serve its positions," it said. Yemeni cartoonist and Houthi supporter Kamal Sharaf joined the campaign with a cartoon and video intended to demonstrate that the Houthis were attacking Aramco, the Saudi oil company, rather than the Kaaba.
‘An unforgivable act’: Turkey and Pakistan back Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia's partners in the "Mecca Defense Alliance," Turkey and Pakistan, backed Riyadh in the dispute. Pakistan's Foreign Ministry issued an official statement condemning the alleged Houthi attack on Mecca, while Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed outrage in a post on X on October 16. "The people of Pakistan feel deep sorrow and concern over this act," he wrote. "Words cannot describe the depth of the pain and grief we feel over this unforgivable act. We salute the vigilance, courage and professionalism of the Saudi forces for their swift action."
"Pakistan stands with Saudi Arabia in defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity, and in ensuring the security and sanctity of the Two Holy Mosques, a duty that every Pakistani carries deep in their heart," Sharif added. Turkey also issued official condemnations following the reports of an attempted attack on Mecca.
The allegations continued over the following weeks. On October 21, the Houthi military spokesman responded to a Saudi-led coalition announcement that drones had been intercepted, including in the Medina area. "The armed forces carried out no military operations deep inside Saudi Arabia today," Saree said. "The Saudi enemy's claim that drones were intercepted over Medina is a lie and a smear against our honorable and courageous people and armed forces."
On October 24, Saudi Civil Defense reported debris falling in several locations following the interception of two ballistic missiles allegedly launched by the Houthis toward the Mecca and Medina regions. According to the Saudi account, fragments fell in Wadi al-Marmas in Mecca, the Al-Nuzha neighborhood in the Jeddah area, Wadi Jalil in the Taif area and the Rabigh district. The Houthis again denied targeting the holy cities, maintaining that their military operations were directed against oil facilities and military bases. In recent weeks, Houthi officials have also repeatedly warned that Saudi airspace is "unsafe," while explicitly excluding the skies over Mecca and Medina from those threats.
On Friday, Houthi government spokesman Omar al-Buhaiti brought Israel into the dispute, alleging that Saudi Arabia and its "Zionist partner" were plotting to attack Islamic holy sites and blame Yemen. "The Saudi enemy's repeated claim that Yemen has attempted to target holy sites reveals malicious intentions already harbored by the Saudi enemy and its Zionist partner," he said. "We hold the Saudi regime fully responsible for any harm, attack or plot targeting the holy sites in Mecca and Medina." He warned that any attack on the Two Holy Mosques by what he called the Saudi enemy would have "devastating consequences" for Riyadh. The accusations against Israel were made without supporting evidence.
Where does the truth lie? ‘The Saudis have an interest’
For now, Saudi Arabia continues to accuse the Houthis, and the Houthis continue to issue categorical denials. But conclusive evidence that Mecca and Medina themselves have been targeted remains lacking. That raises a fundamental question: Are the Houthis really aiming at the two cities, and would they have any reason to attack places that hold such profound religious significance for them as well?
Dr. Yoel Guzansky, a former Israeli National Security Council official and senior researcher who heads the Gulf program at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told ynet that the issue is exceptionally sensitive. He questioned whether the Houthis had actually fired toward the two cities. "It is completely contrary to the Houthis' interests, because doing so could unite the entire Islamic world in opposition to them," he said.
"The Saudis have an interest in showing that the Houthis are attacking Islam's holy sites, Mecca and Medina," Guzansky explained. "That could help them mobilize legitimacy and international support, especially from Pakistan, Turkey and other countries whose assistance Saudi Arabia wants. It could be presented as, 'Here we are, coming to defend Islam's holy sites because Saudi Arabia is in trouble.'"
But he warned that repeatedly invoking the holy cities could also backfire on Riyadh. "The more the Saudis use this, the more dangerous it could become for them. It could create an image of weakness: 'Are they incapable of protecting Mecca and Medina?'"
According to Guzansky, there have been no confirmed strikes on either city. "There were warnings issued to the population, but there were no impacts in those areas, which raises further questions because there have been impacts elsewhere," he said. "The Saudis are taking their struggle with the Houthis into the religious arena as well. That's why I think they may be cautiously bringing Mecca and Medina into the picture. They want to portray the Houthis as infidels and present their actions as being directed against religion."

articles.title: Most Ukrainian brigades are short of troops. One that filled its ranks is helping push Russia back in Operation Vivaldi.
articles.body:
- Ukrainian brigades tend to suffer from low manning and equipment shortages
- One key brigade bucked the trend
- The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade says its main units are nearly fully manned, with tanks and infantry fighting vehicles to match
In four months of deft maneuver, the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps cleared Russian troops from 277 sq km of northern Donetsk Oblast, inflicting—according to the corps—8,000 casualties on the Russian 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies and chasing the armies back across a key terrain feature, the Zherebets River.
There are many reasons for the success of the 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi—which the corps declared finished on 19 October, though elements reportedly keep pushing across the Zherebets to the river's eastern bank.
But one reason is becoming clearer. Bucking a worrying trend, the 3rd Army Corps under its former commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi actually managed to nearly fill out at least one of its five line brigades. The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade's main units—three infantry and tank battalions, which make up around half the overall brigade—have filled between 95% and 100% of their allotted billets, the brigade says.
That means the brigade rolls into battle with as many as 1,500 infantry and vehicle crew. (A battalion typically has around 500 personnel.)
Ukraine may already be pushing Operation Vivaldi across the Zherebets River. It’s a risky gamble
That's highly unusual. Almost all of the roughly 150 ground combat brigades in the Ukrainian armed forces have too few infantry. “Ukraine faces manpower shortage and still does not have a single brigade that is fully manned,” analyst Giorgi Revishvili wrote in June. Some brigades are effectively battalions given their stubbornly low manning.
The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade—commanded by Maj. Volodymyr Fokin—may be one exception to that truism. And if you believe the brigade's own claims, the unit not only has nearly all of its allotted infantry, it also has an abundance of heavy equipment including American-made M2 Bradley infantry fighting vehicles and German-made Leopard tanks. (It's unclear whether they're Leopard 1s or heavier Leopard 2s.) The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade's line battalions should possess around 90 armored vehicles between them.
"3rd Army Corps is built different," observer Moklasen quipped. The corps grew out of the 3rd Assault Brigade, whose soldiers described it as a new army modeled on the freedom-loving Cossacks rather than on the regulations.
Turnaround
The brigade wasn't always so fit. Indeed, as recently as a year ago it was just 17% manned and lacked heavy equipment, the brigade says, making it more typical of the younger Ukrainian brigades including the notoriously "poor" 29th Heavy Mechanized Brigade.
The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade stood up in 2022 as a lightly equipped territorial defense brigade, transferred to the army in 2024 as a mechanized brigade and thereafter underwent reorganization to the new vehicle-centric heavy mechanized structure.
But it took Fokin's strong leadership to actually fill out that structure, the brigade stated. Fokin and his staff "started changing things instead of looking for excuses," according to the brigade's official Telegram account.
"Within just one year, the unit has risen to the top ranks in terms of enemy attrition, mine-laying, artillery operations, air defense, unmanned ground systems, and reconnaissance. Among heavy mechanized brigades, it has held the top spot for three consecutive months."
“We were told brigade couldn’t be saved”: Ukraine’s 125th grew its manning 430% and won back 1,500 absent soldiers in one year
Success bred success. Increasingly confident in the 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade's leadership, some 1,500 troops who had gone absent without leave returned and rejoined the fight, according to the brigade. That helped drive a 430% increase in unit manning, by the brigade's count, until its main units were essentially fully manned.
"The unit no longer fights with unarmed personnel," the 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade reported. "Today, the brigade is active and conducting successful offensive operations. Its arsenal ranges from unmanned systems, unmanned ground vehicles and electronic warfare assets to armored personnel carriers, armored combat vehicles and artillery. It also boasts high-quality medical support, robust rear-echelon logistics, and a cadre of professional commanders."
Brigade troopers and their vehicles and drones underwent a baptism of fire as part of Operation Vivaldi. Robots led the way, but armored vehicles and infantry followed. The 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade and the other assault and mechanized brigades under the 3rd Army Corps banner advanced steadily, exploiting gaps in the overextended 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies and pushing back the bigger Russian formations.
"Operating as part of the corps, our units are once again liberating Ukrainian territory, safeguarding their personnel and continuing to evolve," the 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade stated. Its success, the brigade says, began with strong leadership that inspired confidence in its rank-and-file soldiers—and motivated them to stay and fight.
Armored assaults aren’t dead. Robots got the credit, but it was Ukrainian infantry in armored trucks that reversed a year of Russian gains near Lyman

articles.title: Iranian negotiators in Doha to continue talks to end the US-Iran war, official says
articles.body:
Nov 1 (Reuters) - Iranian negotiators were in Doha on Sunday for a third consecutive day of talks with Qatari mediators aimed at pushing for a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran, an official briefed on the discussions told Reuters.
The talks come amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after the November 3 US midterm elections. President Donald Trump has said the United States will not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action afterwards.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the purpose of the “ongoing and progressing” talks was to continue consultations with the Qatari mediators, adding Tehran is prepared for “both defence and diplomacy”.
Speaking to state media, Araqchi said discussions on a “two-day proposal” were continuing, but that no final conclusion had been reached.
Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera quoted Araqchi as saying in an interview on Saturday that Iranian and Qatari negotiators had developed a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days of a potential agreement with Washington.
Iran has repeatedly said it would respond to any new attacks by striking US and Israeli targets in neighbouring countries, as the eight-month-old war continues to disrupt global oil supplies and spill over across the Middle East.
“We are doing our best in this process, and we hope that there is rationality on the other side so that they prioritise diplomacy over other paths,” Araqchi said of the talks with Qatari officials.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday ordered the armed forces to be prepared for any attack, while the military later announced steps to strengthen its readiness.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump has not decided whether to launch new strikes against Iran, but would prefer to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Friday for discussions with Iranian officials before moving the talks to Doha on Saturday, an official had told Reuters. The talks were being coordinated in regular contacts with Washington, the official added.
(Reporting by Andrew Mills and Elwely Elwelly; Writing by Nayera Abdallah, Editing by Joe Bavier and Ros Russell)

articles.title: Hezbollah unlikely to attack Israel in case of US-Iran war unless regime under threat - report
articles.body:
Hezbollah is not likely to join in if the United States and Iran renew military operations against each other unless Iran’s leadership faces an existential threat, according to a Saturday report from United Arab Emirates state-owned news outlet, The National.
Hezbollah would, according to a senior Lebanese official, join the fight despite its weakened military capacity if the Iranian regime's survival was found to be at stake.
The official said that an explicit red line was crossed in the previous bout, when the Khamenei was killed in a joint US-Israeli strike on February 28.
“We knew earlier this year, when the war in the region first broke out, that Hezbollah would join the fighting if [late Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali] Khamenei were killed,” said the anonymous official. “We even informed the Americans about it.”
KAN news reported last month that Hezbollah terror operatives have maintained their presence in southern Lebanon's pilot zones, gathering intelligence and recuperating their fighting ability.
Hezbollah rearming with Iranian funds
Hezbollah has spent at least three months preparing for a resumption of hostilities with Israel, after receiving an infusion of cash from Iran, according to Lebanese security personnel briefed on its activities.
The terror organization remains committed to attacking Israel and has used a lull in hostilities since June to rearm, with a focus on procuring explosives and producing drones that can be flown into the security zone, two Lebanese security sources told Reuters.
One of the sources, and another close to Hezbollah, said the group had received tens of millions of dollars from Iran to help boost its military capabilities. That is in addition to around $200 million that the terror group previously received from Tehran, which Reuters reported earlier this month.
The group has been restoring command-and-control structures that broke down in key battles, according to one of those sources and three other security officials familiar with the group's operations.
In response to questions from Reuters, Hezbollah's media office rejected the suggestion that its command-and-control systems had broken down.
A US State Department spokesman said Washington would keep strangling Hezbollah's finances through sanctions and other measures. A US Treasury spokesperson said Iran was running out of money and ways to move money.
Trump pulling for Lebanese peace, Israeli withdrawal
US President Donald Trump pledged to secure a full Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon if Beirut agrees to join the Abraham Accords, a senior Gulf diplomatic source told the Lebanese newspaper Ad-Diyar.
The claim was published in an article by Lebanese journalist Nour Naameh amid ongoing diplomatic efforts and concerns in Lebanon over the potential consequences of another military confrontation between the US and Iran.
According to the report, the source described the American promises as official commitments. However, the newspaper provided no documents supporting the claims, did not identify the diplomat or the country he represents, and offered no confirmation from the White House.
The report also did not specify when the commitments were made, who they were communicated to, or whether a timetable had been set for their implementation.
Senior Israeli officials responded to the report by insisting that Israel would not withdraw its forces before Hezbollah was disarmed.
Anna Barsky and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Rubio Doubts Ukraine Peace Deal Before Spring 2027
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio does not believe Russian President Vladimir Putin will agree to any negotiated settlement regarding Ukraine before the spring of 2027, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty correspondent Alex Raufoglu reported, citing three senior European officials.
According to European diplomats briefed on transatlantic discussions, Rubio also characterized near-term Ukrainian accession to NATO as unrealistic as a security guarantee mechanism, expressing conviction that Moscow would never consent to Kyiv’s membership in the alliance.

Speaking at the Group of 20 (G20) foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, the top US diplomat adopted a sober tone regarding the prospects of an imminent diplomatic breakthrough, pushing back against assumptions that an accord is close at hand.
“I don’t know if negotiated peace is achievable in Ukraine. That’s what we’re trying to find out,” Rubio stated during a press briefing. “I don’t think anyone here is claiming that we are on the verge of a negotiated settlement.”
Rubio explained that the Trump administration’s immediate diplomatic efforts are focused on probing the belligerents’ positions to establish whether common ground exists, rather than prematurely declaring the conflict near its conclusion.
Miami G20 summit invitations and Putin skepticism
Rubio expressed skepticism that Putin will travel to the US to attend the G20 leaders’ summit scheduled for Dec. 14-15 in Miami, Florida, despite an official invitation extended to the Russian leader by the White House.

However, both Rubio and US President Donald Trump signaled that President Volodymyr Zelensky could be formally invited to participate in the Miami summit alongside world leaders.
Speaking to journalists during Halloween celebrations at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, Trump was asked whether he plans to invite Zelensky to the summit given that Putin has already received an invitation.
“Yes, no problem,” Trump replied to reporters, confirming his willingness to include the Ukrainian head of state in the gathering.
Rubio noted that leader-level attendance remains an executive presidential prerogative, while indicating openness to the idea if it advances diplomatic progress.
“This is a leader-level meeting. The decision on that has to be made by the president,” Rubio said at a press conference. “I wouldn’t rule out that possibility. Especially if something positive could happen as a result of his participation, but today I have no announcements to make on that front.”
The Kremlin previously stated that Putin’s attendance at the Miami G20 summit depends directly on the outcomes of an anticipated trilateral meeting involving Trump, Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, scheduled for Nov. 18-19.
Territorial framing and diplomatic mediation
Rubio’s cautious timeline follows remarks delivered on Oct. 22, in which he framed the armed conflict as an impasse fundamentally centered on the Donbas region.
“People keep talking about it’s a war in Ukraine. That war is about Donbas. It’s about one region of the country,” Rubio said during a prior briefing.
“At its core, it’s about 11 percent of one part of that country that Russia wants and cannot take militarily and that Ukraine is unwilling to give up. And they have good reasons why they don’t want to do that – for sovereignty and their own security long term.”
The secretary of state reiterated that neither side can achieve an absolute military victory, insisting that an enduring armistice will require mutual accommodations brokered through direct diplomacy.
“This war is not going to be solved militarily. This war is only going to end diplomatically,” Rubio explained, outlining Washington’s desired role as an honest broker.
“Can you arrive at an outcome in which both sides receive something of benefit but also give concessions and bring this to an end? As hard as it is, it is impossible to do unless both sides are at the table talking, and we’re happy to play the mediating role in that regard.”
President Zelensky previously stated that Ukraine is prepared to freeze combat operations along existing front lines to bring a swift end to active fighting, but emphasized that Kyiv will never legally recognize occupied territories as Russian sovereign soil.
Zelensky noted that Russian forces currently occupy 19.3 percent of Ukraine, dismissing suggestions that Ukraine cede the remainder of the Donbas.

articles.title: A hobby computer, a cheap airframe, and a Russian jet drone: how Zirka’s upgrade scored its kill
articles.body:
An upgraded Ukrainian Zirka interceptor caught and destroyed a Russian jet-powered Geran-5 drone, its developer, the ZRK tech project, said. A crew from Ukraine’s drone forces flew the self-guiding drone, ZRK added. At its summer debut, the cheap interceptor looked too slow for Russia’s jet models.
Russia sends waves of attack drones at Ukrainian cities almost every night. It has spent the year moving more of them onto jet engines. The faster models slip past many of the cheap interceptors Ukraine built for propeller Shaheds. That leaves gaps Ukraine often plugs with expensive missiles, and Washington is holding back the ones Ukraine needs most.
Caught at 3,500 meters
ZRK said the upgraded Zirka chased down the Geran-5 at about 400 km/h, at an altitude of 3,500 meters. The developer published the interception video on 31 October.
The crew “Retro” of the Darknode battalion flew the mission, ZRK said. The battalion belongs to the 412th Nemesis brigade of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces. ZRK has not disclosed the upgraded drone’s specifications.
From too slow to catching a jet
When Zirka debuted in late June, its makers listed a top speed above 340 km/h. They also gave a 6 km ceiling and a 30 km radius. At up to $2,000 a unit, they called it the cheapest interceptor in its class with automatic guidance. That speed fell short of the bursts Russia’s jet-powered Shahed variants can reach.
Zirka still found a way against jets. In late July, it downed a jet-powered Geran-4, its maker said in a press release, Militarnyi reported. Instead of chasing the faster drone from behind, Zirka met it head-on or from the side, Ukrainian tech outlet ITC explained.
Oleksii Babenko, director of investor Vyriy Industries, later said Zirka could down jet Shaheds on its own. He also said it once hit a target about 3,000 km from its operator, controlled via Starlink.
A hobby computer does the aiming
Zirka carries a Raspberry Pi 5, a credit-card-sized single-board computer, Militarnyi said. It runs a machine-vision model trained to pick out the features of Shahed-type drones. The system detects a target up to 1 km away. Once the operator confirms it, the system tracks it and steers the interceptor in.
The pilot only has to adjust the closing speed, Militarnyi added. Machine vision makes Zirka up to 60% more effective against maneuvering targets than manual piloting, NOCTIS claims, according to ITC. ZRK’s new video shows the software flagging the Geran-5, then switching to automatic terminal guidance, so the upgraded version likely keeps the same system.
Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet Shaheds: a jet drone named Bars, built to strike Russia and now turned around to hunt them
That is the capability Ukraine’s presidential adviser on defense technology Serhii Beskrestnov has pressed for. Speed alone will not catch jet drones, he argued. Interceptors need machine vision to lock on and guide themselves in.
The battalion behind the brief
Ukrainian company NOCTIS built Zirka to a technical brief drawn up with the Darknode battalion, ITC said. The battalion, one of Ukraine’s top anti-Shahed units, has downed more than 1,500 Russian drones, according to ITC. Vyriy Industries holds a 30% stake in NOCTIS, Babenko said.
Cheap answers to cheap drones
Ukraine’s government wants exactly this kind of trade. “We need asymmetric effect,” Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said, as Kyiv funds its own missiles and radars. The goal is to stop spending costly interceptors on Russia’s cheap drones.
Until cheap tools catch up, Ukraine improvises with what it has. One regiment has paired a Soviet Kub launcher with a Buk radar to hunt jet drones. It has also rewired launchers to fire American RIM-7 missiles.
Russia keeps speeding up
Ukraine shoots down 50–60% of Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds, against 85–92% of propeller ones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in October. Russia builds about 3,000 jet drones a month, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) estimated.
HUR puts the Geran-5’s cruise speed at 450–600 km/h, and Beskrestnov said it has hit 1,000 km/h in maneuvers. He added that Ukraine’s jet interceptors still struggle with guidance, automatic target lock, and mass production.
Zirka is not alone. The 1020th anti-aircraft regiment caught a Geran-5 at 425 km/h in September. Wild Hornets says its new STING-family interceptor has destroyed about ten Geran-4s.
