articles.title: Ukraine flies the first drone rescues of wounded troops
articles.body:
Ukraine has carried out the world’s first medical evacuations by heavy uncrewed aircraft, lifting wounded soldiers out of positions that could not be reached from the ground, and is developing evacuation drones as a dedicated capability of its own, according to the Ukrainian defence ministry.
Brave1, the defence innovation cluster working with the Ministry of Defence, set the requirement in 2024 after working with the military to define what such an aircraft would have to do. The criteria given to the defence technology market were that the aircraft must reliably carry 130 kilograms over a distance of at least fifteen kilometres and must carry an integrated communication system with at least three alternative types to survive in an electronic warfare environment, with lidar, optical stabilisation and navigation that works without satellites listed as options.
The first of those evacuations took place in October, when an infantryman of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade was lifted out of a position the enemy had blocked. A Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 hexacopter built by a Brave1 participant flew the mission, an aircraft weighing 98 kilograms with a payload capacity of 130 kilograms, and it covered more than fifteen kilometres on the outbound leg.
Preparation ran to months and drew on the experience of the uncrewed ground vehicle company of the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade. Equipment had been dropped to the soldier in advance and he had to secure himself to the aircraft’s winch without help, while adjacent units launched bomber drones to pull enemy interceptors away from the rescue aircraft.
A second system, Stargate, was built specifically for evacuation at the request of assault troops. It deploys in ten minutes, carries 150 kilograms at speeds up to 105 kilometres an hour and holds a medical module with a stretcher, and its software can plot a route and return to a safe area without help if navigation is completely jammed.
Assault troops of the CODE 9.2 regiment used it twice in a single week to bring out severely wounded soldiers from the grey zone five kilometres from the Russian border, where terrain, water obstacles and first person view drones ruled out any ground rescue. The aircraft flew nearly thirty kilometres each way and came back with the casualties aboard while under electronic attack, relying on artificial intelligence alone for navigation, with heavy strike drones suppressing enemy positions to cover the run.
Conventional casualty evacuation has become close to impossible along much of the front because the density of drone coverage turns any vehicle movement into a target, and uncrewed ground vehicles took over much of the work at the cost of speed. Survival after serious trauma depends heavily on reaching surgical care quickly, and a crawling robot moving along a mined route can take many hours to cover ground a helicopter would cross in minutes.
Ukraine’s Defence Procurement Agency has contracted three times as many uncrewed systems of all types this year as it did last year.

articles.title: Iran: Any new war with US could be ‘longer than previous conflict’
articles.body:
Vehicles drive past a banner showing the late Hezbollah leaders Hassan Nasrallah, right, and Hashem Safieddine, left, and the group's current leader, Sheikh Naim Qassem, in Palestine Square in Tehran, Iran, Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. (AP Photo)
Iran warned on Nov. 1 that any new war with the United States could last longer than the previous conflict and that U.S. President Donald Trump would not be the one to determine its duration.
“A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion,” said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
He was referring to the most intense phase of the fighting in the war that began on Feb. 28 with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, killing the Islamic republic’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Iran responded by launching missiles and drones across the region, while the militant groups it backs also entered the fray in Lebanon and Yemen.
Iran’s Defense Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi on Nov. 1 warned of a “proportionate, decisive, and impactful response” to any attack on the country, according to state TV.
“Those who pose threats will not dictate the scope, timing, or consequences of Iran’s defensive response,” he added.
Also on Nov. 1, Hossein Mohebbi, the spokesperson of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, echoed the remarks made by the country’s new supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei in a written message the day before.
“In a conflict with America, there are no geographical limitations; a vast theatre has been defined for inflicting damage upon the enemy,” Mohebbi said, according to state TV.
Trump said on Oct. 31 that the United States has knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets.
“We’ve knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” Trump said.

articles.title: Bulgarians vote in presidential runoff amid security tensions in the Black Sea
articles.body:
Bulgarians vote in presidential runoff amid security tensions in the Black Sea
Bulgarians voted Sunday in a presidential runoff between two candidates with opposing views on the Ukraine war and relations with Russia as tensions mount in the Black Sea. Incumbent President Iliana Iotova, who favours dialogue with Moscow, faces off against Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition.
Bulgarians voted Sunday in a presidential runoff between two candidates with contrasting visions on the war in Ukraine, following a series of drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
The race pits President Iliana Iotova, who favours dialogue with Moscow and opposes military aid to Ukraine, against Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition, in the race for the largely ceremonial post.
Read moreBulgaria searches for missing crew as drones hit two Black Sea ships
Iotova won 35 percent of the vote in the first round last week, with Gyurov on 32 percent – a much narrower gap than the 20-point lead for Iotova predicted by opinion polls.
The first round recorded turnout of 23 percent, and election officials were expecting higher participation in the runoff.
Political analyst Teodor Slavev told AFP that voters were giving their verdict on "Iotova's unconvincing response regarding Russian threats in the Black Sea".
Several vessels were struck in the Black Sea off Bulgaria in October, leaving 21 people missing, in suspected spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war.
Read moreNATO to address drone attacks in the Black Sea after seven missing off Romania
While centre-left Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said the attacks appeared to serve Russian interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, his government insists there is so far no evidence directly linking them to Moscow.
'Lesser evil'
At a polling station in Sofia, 64-year-old teacher Krassimira Kostova said she voted despite dissatisfaction with both candidates.
"I don't like either of the two candidates, but I don't like the return of communism we've been seeing in recent years either. That's why I came to vote," she said.
Petar Doitchinov, a 67-year-old retired engineer, said he had skipped the first round because he expected a runoff. He said he voted for "the lesser evil", as neither candidate matched his "vision of democracy".
In rainy, windy weather across much of the country, turnout stood at 6.1 percent at 11:00am local time (0900 GMT), compared with 5.8 percent at the same time in the first round, according to the Bulgarian electoral commission.
Polls opened at 7:00am and will close at 8:00pm, with exit polls shortly after that expected to give an indication of the winner.
'Strong Bulgaria'
After voting in Sofia, Iotova, 62, said she wanted "Bulgaria to be strong in a strong Europe" and remaining "sovereign in its decisions".
A longtime ally of Radev, she supports Bulgaria's EU and NATO membership while arguing that peace in Ukraine can be achieved only through negotiations.
Gyurov, 50, said after voting in Blagoevgrad that he had voted for a "secure, stable and European Bulgaria".
In a television debate before the runoff, Gyurov criticised Iotova for not explicitly blaming Russia for the Black Sea attacks.
"Russia must stop its aggression so that the next steps can be taken," said Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank.
Iotova maintained that "peace can come only through negotiations".
Read more'It is clear that sooner or later we will have European casualties', Romanian MEP
Radev has also argued that a ceasefire and peace talks offer the best chance of preventing further attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
He has presented Iotova as a pair of "safe hands".
A former journalist and member of the European Parliament, Iotova was elected vice-president alongside Radev in 2016 and 2021.
She took over as president this year when Radev stepped down to run in parliamentary elections.
If successful in the runoff, she would become the first woman president in the country of 6.4 million people.
Historically close to Russia, Bulgaria remains deeply divided over its relationship with Moscow.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: On Kramatorsk’s Peace Square, a Russian airstrike takes down the building that outlasted Russia’s 2014 occupation
articles.body:
A Russian airstrike destroyed the city executive committee building on Peace Square in central Kramatorsk late on 31 October, the head of the city's military administration, Oleksandr Honcharenko, said. The building outlasted Russia's occupation of the city in 2014, the fighting, and its liberation. Overnight, Russia sent hundreds of drones across Ukraine, wounding people from Volyn to Sumy.
Russia's offensive in Donetsk Oblast grinds toward the last large cities Ukraine holds there. Kramatorsk serves as the oblast's provisional administrative center and sits about 15 km from Russian-held ground. Moscow already counts the city as its own: it included Kramatorsk in a district for Russia's parliamentary elections. Strikes on its center hit the institutions that keep the city Ukrainian.
"The foundation of Ukrainian Kramatorsk"
Honcharenko called it "the central building of Ukrainian statehood in Kramatorsk." He wrote that it held the city's history and its plans.
"One can destroy a building, burn out our land, and steal memories. But they will not destroy our right to a future," Honcharenko wrote.
Russian forces struck Kramatorsk 10 times over 31 October, four times with guided aerial bombs and four times with FPV drones, Donetsk Oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. Six people were wounded, and 11 apartment blocks, an administrative building, and three cars were damaged. In neighboring Sloviansk, Russian strikes killed one person and wounded two.
Hundreds of drones overnight
From 18:00 on 31 October, Russia launched 433 attack drones, 64 of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force said. Air defenses downed or jammed 371 by 07:30, while more than 40 were still in the air. Drones hit 16 locations.
In Volyn Oblast, drones hit Kamin-Kashyrskyi district and wounded one person, the regional administration said. A house caught fire in Rivne Oblast's Ostroh district, and four people were hurt, Ukraine's emergency service reported. In Kyiv Oblast, a morning attack wounded a man in Bila Tserkva district and left another in acute stress, the oblast administration said. A drone hit the Reshetylivka community in Poltava Oblast, and a child was hurt, according to preliminary information.
According to preliminary information, Russian strikes injured six people in Sumy Oblast, and in the Hlukhiv community a drone struck again where rescuers were fighting a fire, the emergency service said, though none of the rescuers were hurt. Strikes on energy sites left more than 650 settlements in Zhytomyr Oblast without power, its administration said. The attack carried on into Sunday, when Russian forces hit an industrial plant in Dnipro and started a fire, the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast administration said.
Over the past day
Russian attacks wounded 17 people in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on 31 October, including three children, the oblast administration reported. Ten of them were hurt in Pavlohrad. Seven people were wounded in Kharkiv Oblast, including a 16-year-old girl in Zolochiv, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian forces hit 55 settlements 699 times, wounding six people, regional head Ivan Fedorov said.
Kramatorsk has come under rising Russian fire this fall. On 8 October, a Russian bomb hit two passenger buses there, and Russia later cloned Euromaidan Press's website to blame Ukraine for it. Days earlier, Russian FPV drones hit three ambulances in the city and killed a woman in her apartment block.

articles.title: Trump threatens to strike 'one or two targets' still left in Iran
articles.body:
The U.S. had destroyed much of Iran’s military but still needed to "take care of" one or two targets, President Donald Trump said Saturday, as Tehran warned of retaliation if attacked.
Trump said negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the United States and Israel in February, were "going fine, but you know they're not very reliable."
He added that the U.S. was not in a hurry to take offensive action because it had already decimated Iran's military and nuclear program.
"We've knocked out their nuclear program. We still have to take care of one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes," Trump told reporters at his Florida residence.
"You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain and you have to take care of that. We can do that all very quickly," he added, referring to a suspected underground nuclear complex.
The Iranian government denied any nuclear work was carried out there.
Earlier Saturday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump had not made a decision about fresh strikes on Iran and that the United States would be open to a diplomatic solution.
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei Saturday warned the United States and Israel against launching a new offensive, following threats they could resume strikes after crucial elections in both countries.
Trump had previously warned an attack could come after the U.S. midterms this week, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke of a "historic, one-time opportunity" to topple the Iranian government.
The elections in both countries could determine the direction of the conflict. Israel voted in a general election Tuesday but had yet to form a new government.
"Any level or type of threat requires an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response," Khamenei told top military commanders in a statement.
He also ordered commanders to update Iran's target list to include "all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy."
This was the first reported meeting between Khamenei and top military commanders.
The supreme leader had not been seen publicly since before he took the helm in March, after the killing of his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in U.S.-Israeli strikes.
Rubio warned that "we can achieve military objectives if we seek to do so," adding that Trump had not made a decision on any fresh strikes.
Since the recent outbreak of the war, Tehran had restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries around one-fifth of global oil consumption.
Iran had previously warned it would also consider severing undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz.
A ship traversing the strait struck a mine and caught fire, Iranian state television reported Saturday.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Friday three oil tankers were halted after encountering unspecified "incidents" or hitting mines.
The blockade had caused a spike in global energy prices, making the war unpopular among the U.S. public ahead of the upcoming polls.
Gains for the opposition Democrats could somewhat restrict Trump's ability to enact policy.
Voting in Israel had left Netanyahu's political camp with the most seats in parliament but short of a majority, leaving the makeup of the next administration unclear.
Fresh diplomatic efforts were underway to avert any resumption of fighting.
Qatari mediators landed in Tehran Friday, and U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance sent a letter to Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.
"'I had not yet responded. Their tone had completely changed," Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said in a video broadcast on Iranian television, describing it as "a good sign" without elaborating.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were no plans for meetings with U.S. officials.
"Iran's conditions were clear, and consultations regarding them were ongoing among mediators," he said in an interview with Al Jazeera.
Rezaei insisted Iran would continue to blockade the Strait of Hormuz until its conditions, including releasing frozen assets, were met.
Qatar and Pakistan had been mediating between the warring parties, but the talks had yet to produce a lasting agreement.
Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia said any resumption of hostilities would only expand the scope of the war.
"The flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area," he said on social media.
Araghchi posted on X that there would no longer be any "red lines."

Iran has previously warned that it would also consider severing undersea cables in the Strait of Hormuz.
A ship traversing the strait struck a mine and caught fire, Iranian state television reported on Oct 31.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Oct 30 that three oil tankers had been halted after encountering unspecified “incidents” or hitting mines.
The blockade has caused a spike in global energy prices, making the war unpopular among the US public ahead of the upcoming polls.
Gains for the opposition Democrats could restrict, to an extent, Trump’s ability to enact policy.
Voting in Israel has left Netanyahu’s political camp with the most seats in Parliament but short of a majority, leaving the make-up of the next administration unclear.
‘Flames of war’
Fresh diplomatic efforts are under way to avert any resumption of fighting.
Qatari mediators landed in Tehran on Oct 30, and US Vice-President J.D. Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.
“I read the letter,” said Rezaei, in a video broadcast on Iranian television.
“I haven’t yet responded. Their tone has completely changed,” he added, describing that as “a good sign”, without going into more detail.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were currently no plans for meetings with US officials.
“Iran’s conditions are clear and consultations regarding them are ongoing among mediators,” he said in an interview with Al Jazeera, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Rezaei insisted Iran would continue to blockade the Strait of Hormuz until its conditions, including releasing frozen assets, were met.
Qatar and Pakistan have been mediating between the warring parties, but the talks have yet to produce a lasting agreement.
Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said any resumption of hostilities would only expand the scope of the war.
“The flames of war will undoubtedly engulf a much wider geographical area,” he said on social media.
Araghchi warned on X that there would no longer be any “red lines”. AFP

articles.title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,590,270 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
articles.body:
Russia has lost 1,590,270 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 31.
The number includes 2,100 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,451 tanks, 25,622 armored combat vehicles, 168,739 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,755 artillery systems, 2,249 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,730 air defense systems, 452 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,054 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
On Oct. 29, the General Staff reported that October 2026 was the deadliest month for Russian combat losses since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

articles.title: Bulgarians head to the polls in tense presidential runoff
articles.body:
The vote puts together two candidates with sharply contrasting views on how Bulgaria should engage with Russia and the war in Ukraine moving forward.
Bulgarians are voting on Sunday in a tense presidential runoff between incumbent President Iliana Iotova and pro-Western rival Andrey Gyurov.
Iotova won the most votes, around 35%, in the first round of voting, giving her a lead of 43,000 over Gyurov - a surprise result as earlier opinion polls had suggested a more comfortable victory.
Polling stations opened at 7 am local time on Sunday and will close at 8 pm.
The vote puts together two candidates with sharply contrasting views on how Bulgaria should engage with Russia and the war in Ukraine.
Iotova, who is backed by the ruling Progressive Bulgaria party, the Bulgarian Socialist Party and the nationalist VMRO, has pushed for dialogue with Moscow and opposes continuing military aid to Ukraine.
Gyurov is supported by the opposition, Democratic Bulgaria and We Continue the Change, and argues that the Kremlin must end its war before coming to the negotiating table.
In a televised debate on Thursday evening, Iotova said "peace can only be achieved through negotiations."
"If we pour even more money into Ukraine and deliver new, more sophisticated weapons, this will only lead to further destruction and many deaths on both sides," she added.
In contrast, Gyurov argued that "Russia must put an end to its aggression so that the next steps can be taken."
"Let us name the country from which the threats originate," he said.
Bulgaria, an EU and NATO member, has historically had close ties with Russia, and the country is deeply divided over how it should move forward with this relationship.
The vote comes amid a series of attacks on vessels in the Black Sea off Bulgaria, which has further intensified conversations around the topic of relations with Russia.
Prime Minister Rumen Radev maintains that a ceasefire in Ukraine and peace talks are the only guarantees that the Black Sea will once again be a safe route for commercial ships.
While Radev has said the attacks appeared to serve Russian interests and has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incidents, the government says there is so far no evidence directly linking them to Moscow.
Political analyst Teodor Slavev told the AFP news agency that the presidential election would see voters give their verdict on "Iotova's unconvincing response regarding Russian threats in the Black Sea."

articles.title: UK flies Protector drone on first home operation against Russian frigate
articles.body:
- An RAF Protector RG1 flew its first operational sorties in UK airspace, providing more than 10 hours of surveillance over the English Channel.
- The aircraft supported HMS Dauntless and HMS Tyne as they tracked the Russian frigate Neustrashimy between Oct. 1 and Oct. 14.
An RAF Protector RG1 remotely piloted aircraft has flown its first operational missions in UK airspace, giving the Royal Navy more than 10 hours of surveillance over the English Channel while warships tracked the Russian frigate Neustrashimy, the UK Ministry of Defence said.
The unarmed Protector flew alongside military and civilian air traffic while the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless (D33) and offshore patrol vessel HMS Tyne (P281) monitored Neustrashimy and accompanying merchant ships through the Channel between Oct. 1 and Oct. 14. The ministry did not say how many sorties the aircraft flew, which sensors it used or how much of the frigate’s transit it covered.
“Protector’s first operational sorties in UK airspace demonstrate the significant value this capability brings to UK Defence. Working alongside Royal Navy vessels, it provided persistent intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance coverage, highlighting its ability to operate seamlessly across military and civilian airspace in support of maritime security, NATO commitments and wider UK tasking,” said Wing Commander Sam Haley, officer commanding XIII Squadron.
Protector is the RAF’s version of General Atomics’ MQ-9B SkyGuardian, flown from RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire by 31 and XIII squadrons. The UK Military Aviation Authority issued it a military type certificate on April 29, 2025, clearing it to fly without geographic restrictions in UK airspace, and it entered service in June 2025 as the first remotely piloted aircraft authorized to do so. The MQ-9A Reaper it replaced never flew in UK airspace during its RAF career. The first of 16 Protectors arrived at RAF Waddington in 2023.
The RAF lists the aircraft’s endurance at more than 30 hours and its ceiling at up to 40,000 feet (12,200 m), with full-motion video, infrared imagery, synthetic aperture radar and ground target tracking among its sensors. In June 2026, a Protector flew from Waddington to RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus through European civil airspace, covering more than 2,000 nautical miles in about 13.5 hours.
The Channel mission was one of several Royal Navy operations against Russian ships between late September and mid-October. Merlin helicopters from Royal Naval Air Station Culdrose deployed to Glasgow Prestwick Airport under Operation Iceblast, a test of how quickly the Merlin force can operate away from its home base. From Sept. 29 to Oct. 8, they tracked the Vishnya-class intelligence-gathering ship Viktor Leonov near the Outer Hebrides, where NATO’s Exercise Strike Warrior was underway with more than 2,000 personnel from six nations.
From Oct. 11 to Oct. 14, HMS Tyne and a Wildcat helicopter from 815 Naval Air Squadron followed the Ropucha-class landing ship Aleksandr Shabalin, the cargo ship MV Energy-2 and the tug Proton through the Channel as they headed for the Baltic.
“HMS Dauntless monitored the movements of RFN Neustrashimy during her transit through the English Channel, contributing to the wider maritime picture and supporting UK maritime security,” said Commander Neil Skinner, commanding officer of HMS Dauntless.
Royal Navy activity monitoring Russian movements rose 25% in the first seven months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, the ministry said. Most of that work falls to patrol ships, frigates and helicopters; in January, HMS Mersey, HMS Severn and a Wildcat shadowed a Russian corvette and tanker through the same waters in a two-day operation coordinated with NATO allies.
“For the first time, Protector has joined Royal Navy warships and helicopters monitoring activity around our shores, demonstrating how we are constantly innovating to monitor and deter threats and irresponsible provocation,” said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting.
The ministry tied the operations to £298 billion (about $399 billion) in planned defense spending over the next four years and a commitment to reach 3% of GDP on defense in 2030. It also pointed to £330 million (about $442 million) over four years to protect undersea infrastructure and to Atlantic Bastion, a Royal Navy effort combining warships, patrol aircraft and autonomous systems against Russian submarines in the North Atlantic.

articles.title: Bulgarians vote in highly polarized presidential runoff overshadowed by Ukraine war
articles.body:
Bulgaria votes in closely contested presidential runoff
November 1, 2026
Bulgarians on Sunday began voting in a highly contested presidential runoff following a tight race between the two main contenders last weekend.
The November 1 runoff pits two competing visions of Bulgaria against each other. Moscow-friendly incumbent Iliana Yotova opposes military aid to Ukraine, while former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov is backed by the pro-Western opposition.
In last Sunday's first round, which saw voter turnout fall to a historic low, Yotova won with 34.76% of the vote, less than three percentage points ahead of Gyurov with 31.95%.
Although Bulgaria's presidency has largely ceremonial duties, the president can appoint interim governments during political crises, serve as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, and veto legislation.
Ukraine war divides Bulgaria
The war in Ukraine has become a central issue in the election, with voters heading to the polls amid growing security concerns in the Black Sea, which borders Bulgaria, following a rise in drone attacks targeting commercial vessels.
Yotova has presented herself as a "president of peace" who favors dialogue with Moscow.
In a TV debate before the runoff, Gyurov accused Yotova of avoiding direct criticism of Russia over the Black Sea attacks.
"Russia must stop its aggression so that the next steps can be taken. Let us name the country from which the threats are coming," he said.
In response, Yotova argued that "peace can come only through negotiations," and maintained that continued aid for Ukraine "leads only to more destruction and the deaths of many people on both sides."
Yotova vs Gyurov: Between Russia and the West
If elected, Yotova is expected to pursue a similar approach to Prime Minister Rumen Radev — keeping Bulgaria on its European path while seeking closer ties with Russia and advocating the lifting of sanctions.
Her opponent Gyurov previously served as deputy governor of Bulgaria's central bank and as caretaker prime minister, leading the country in early 2026.
He has repeatedly voiced strong support for Ukraine and signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership.
After the first round of voting, Gyurov said that Bulgaria faced a choice "between two personalities, two directions, and two ways of exercising presidential powers."

articles.title: Binance says 90% of losses from $6.3bn hack covered as FBI says North Korea behind attack
articles.body:
The cryptocurrency exchange Binance has started to allow its customers to withdraw their funds from the platform, as it recovers from a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack.
The exchange was hit by the theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach, but on Sunday announced that it had began a phased reopening after 2pm Singapore time.
The first phase will allow people who hold the ethereum, USDT and USDC tokens on the ethereum blockchain to withdraw their funds, as well as some others held on the BNB Smart Chain blockchain.
The platform said it had replenished 90% of the amount stolen. The remaining 10% of tokens were less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday.
Richard Teng, Binance’s co-chief executive, said separately that the company was “committed to covering the remaining 10%” and that users would not bear the financial impact of the hack.
It came as the FBI on Saturday confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
“The Federal Bureau of Investigation is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6bn in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29,” the law enforcement agency said in a statement.
The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors” were “using to launder these stolen assets”.
Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.
Binance said it had set aside about $6.34bn of company funds to cover the losses. “Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said.
The money spent rebuying tokens came from using part of its $1bn Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company’s own corporate treasury, it said on X.
The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.
Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.
The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea – which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes – to find illicit means to capture revenue.

articles.title: U.S. Deploys Avenger Air Defense Systems to Protect Trump’s Florida Residence

In addition to the Avenger systems, the military deployed mobile Counter-UAS Fly-Away Kits designed to detect and track drones. These kits include passive and active detection and tracking equipment, including electro-optical and infrared cameras.
The kits may also include electronic warfare systems designed to jam drones.
The deployment comes amid heightened security concerns over threats against Donald Trump, including previous assassination attempts against the U.S. President and threats from Iran.
Meanwhile, the U.S. military and the Secret Service have not disclosed the specific reason for deploying additional air defense systems.
According to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), more than 160 incidents involving aircraft and drones violating flight restrictions have been recorded since the airspace restrictions over Palm Beach were introduced in October 2025.

articles.title: The tactics of fighting in gas pipelines: why it matters in the Russian-Ukrainian war
articles.body:
The tactics of fighting in gas pipelines: why it matters in the Russian-Ukrainian war
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian and Russian troops move through gas pipelines, avoiding drones and launching surprise attacks on the enemy’s rear.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces have adopted the Russians’ tactic of fighting in underground tunnels. Military personnel from both warring countries are covering considerable distances through gas pipelines, trying to avoid the threat of drone strikes and catch the enemy by surprise. This is reported in an article by The New York Times, UNN reports.
Details
According to Maria Varenikova, a correspondent for The New York Times, while heading toward the entrance to the tunnel network, she narrowly escaped being hit by a Russian drone. She, the publication’s photographer, and the Ukrainian soldiers accompanying them had to jump out of the pickup truck on the move and hide from the Russian UAV along the road.
At the same time, journalist Simon Shuster notes in a publication on The Atlantic’s website that the new tactical methods are important for the course of the war. He discussed the issue with Ihor Obolenskyi, commander of the 2nd “Khartia” Corps of the National Guard of Ukraine.
The brigadier general said that initially, the Defense Forces tried to find the points where the Russians emerged onto the surface and destroy them. But they continued to appear several kilometers behind Ukrainian positions and attack.
The “Khartia” commander then turned to the state energy company with a request to provide maps of the pipeline network. The documents revealed the scale of the danger: it was a labyrinth of at least 57 steel pipes running beneath the combat zone, most of them one to two meters in diameter.
Previously, these pipes were used to pump Russian gas through Ukraine to European countries. But this stopped in 2025.
That same year, the Russians carried out “Operation Pipe”: between one hundred and several hundred soldiers crawled several kilometers along a section of the Urengoy–Pomary–Uzhhorod main gas pipeline and emerged behind Ukrainian troops in the Kursk region.
According to Obolenskyi, in October, after approximately six months of underground fighting, “Khartia” regained control of approximately 14 kilometers of pipelines in northeastern Ukraine as part of an operation codenamed “Veles.”

articles.title: Sybiha: Oleshky Success Proves War Can Be Stopped Everywhere
articles.body:
The verified success of the humanitarian operation in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky demonstrates that active hostilities can be halted and can serve as a vital confidence-building measure to advance a broader, permanent peace, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Writing on X, Sybiha confirmed that evacuated civilians had safely crossed the state frontier into Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, emphasizing that the operation represents hundreds of innocent lives preserved following months of severe deprivation.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Ukrainian citizens evacuated from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region. This is about saved lives,” the foreign minister stated.
“After months of hunger and isolation under Russian occupation, they are finally safe. Those who chose to stay must have unhindered humanitarian access.”
Addressing the broader strategic implications of the localized armistice, the foreign minister stressed that the ability of both belligerents to honor a localized silence regime establishes a concrete operational precedent for ending the war.
“Ukraine acted in good faith and kept its word. As I said in Helsinki, results in Oleshky can serve as a confidence-building measure and pave the way for further steps in the peace process,” Sybiha emphasized.
“If hostilities can be stopped in one place, they can be stopped everywhere, and permanently. Ukraine is ready. We expect the same from Russia.”
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 31, 2026
Gratitude to Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV, and allied partners
Sybiha expressed official gratitude to the international mediators and religious figures who helped broker the localized armistice and alleviate the humanitarian crisis in the Dnipro left-bank enclave.
Sybiha commended US First Lady Melania Trump for her direct diplomatic mediation, which facilitated the synchronization of the localized ceasefire between Ukrainian and Russian negotiating teams.
“We thank the American side and First Lady Melania Trump for their mediation,” Sybiha wrote.
“For months, Ukraine raised the alarm about Oleshky, including at the UN Security Council. We urged partners, international organizations and religious leaders to act. Today, lives have been saved.”
The foreign minister extended formal appreciation to Pope Leo XIV, who had previously conducted high-level appeals – including personal communications with Russian President Vladimir Putin – urging humanitarian corridors for trapped non-combatants.
Sybiha also thanked international partner governments, foreign ministers, and Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets alongside his operational field team for executing the multi-stage mission under hazardous frontline conditions.
The foreign minister reiterated that for the estimated 1,700 civilians who chose to remain in the occupied town, the international community must ensure continuous, unhindered humanitarian access and aid deliveries as winter approaches.
Ukrainian citizens evacuated from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region. This is about saved lives.
After months of hunger and isolation under Russian occupation, they are finally safe. Those who chose to stay must have unhindered humanitarian access.… pic.twitter.com/djDxn19pns
— Andrii Sybiha 🇺🇦 (@andrii_sybiha) October 31, 2026
Sybiha’s remarks follow the arrival of the evacuation convoys in Chernihiv region late on Saturday, Oct. 31, concluding an intricate multi-stage transit corridor that began inside occupied Kherson region.
Under the negotiated framework, a humanitarian convoy of 25 buses and specialized ambulances entered Oleshky following de-mining operations around the municipal hospital.
Trapped civilians – prioritizing the elderly, individuals with disabilities, and families with domestic animals – transited overland through Russian-occupied Crimea to the Russian Black Sea port of Anapa.
From Anapa, four charter flights airlifted the evacuees to Gomel in Belarus, where the final aircraft touched down on Saturday afternoon before the group boarded cross-border coaches into northern Ukraine.
At the Chernihiv reception point, Ukrainian authorities, medical detachments, psychologists, and volunteer organizations mobilized emergency warming shelters, hot food distribution, and specialized animal care depots for pets brought by the evacuees.
The humanitarian mission was executed under a strict, localized 87-hour silence regime that took effect at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time on Tuesday, Oct. 27, and was scheduled to remain in force until 10:59 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Throughout the designated ceasefire window, Ukrainian and Russian armed forces adhered to commitments suspending drone interdictions, tactical aviation, artillery bombardments, and ground maneuvers across the Oleshky perimeter, recording zero kinetic violations.
The compliance underscored statements delivered on Saturday by Melania Trump, who characterized the Oleshky mission as grounds for hope for a sustainable peace and proof that humanity can rise above war.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also thanked the US First Lady, noting that American mediation enabled life-saving deliveries and civilian evacuations.

Ukraine and NATO to deepen cooperation on innovative technologies
The Ministry of Defense reported this, according to Ukrinform.
The Defense Ministry noted that this is the first agreement of its kind between DIANA and a NATO partner country. It lays the groundwork for closer cooperation between the innovation ecosystems of Ukraine and the Alliance.
“Ukraine has gained unique experience in rapidly developing, testing, and improving technologies in modern warfare. For its part, DIANA gives Ukraine access to NATO’s defense expertise and infrastructure, helping promising technologies move from idea to practical application. This will allow Ukrainian developers to gain a deeper understanding of the Alliance’s standards, open up new avenues for testing their own solutions, and help remove obstacles to scaling them up,” the ministry said.
The signing of the memorandum will provide additional funding for joint Ukraine-NATO projects, the Defense Ministry emphasized.
In addition, the memorandum will contribute to:
- building a comprehensive defense innovation system that combines the cataloging, testing, and adoption of technological solutions with deeper cooperation with NATO and other international partners;
- continuing to build and develop a catalog of innovative defense technologies that covers, in particular, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), electronic warfare (EW) systems, radars, and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs).
The catalog is to contain coordinated information on existing and promising solutions, their level of readiness, test results and potential applications, and will be used to identify priorities for technology development, procurement and scaling.
Other benefits include:
- deeper engagement with NATO institutions, including the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC) and DIANA, ensuring that Ukrainian combat experience and the needs of the Defense Forces of Ukraine are taken into account when setting technological priorities, preparing and announcing innovation competitions, supporting projects, and testing solutions, including in Ukraine;
- synchronization of the innovative technology catalogs of Ukraine and NATO member states;
- exchange of information to strengthen situational awareness, identify common needs, and plan joint competitions, testing, and technology adoption.
The ministry said that the consistent implementation of these tasks would strengthen Ukraine’s ability to influence the development of NATO’s innovation priorities and secure partner support in line with the needs of the Defense Forces.
The synchronization of catalogs and joint identification of technological priorities will lay the groundwork for systematic situational awareness, long-term planning and forecasting of the development of defense technologies.
The Defense Ministry also recalled that it is working on implementing the NATO Status of Forces Agreement (NATO SOFA). The document defines the legal status of the armed forces of States Parties while they are in the territory of another State Party. It regulates entry and exit, criminal and disciplinary jurisdiction, compensation for damage, and customs and tax regulation.
As Ukrinform reported, Jacqueline Borsboom, NATO Support and Procurement Agency's Director of Support to Operations, said that NATO will allow Ukraine to procure weapons, ammunition and military equipment through its centralized procurement agency, which will help Kyiv obtain the weapons it needs faster and at lower cost.

articles.title: A Gulf non-aggression pact could be the path forward
articles.body:
A Gulf non-aggression pact could be the path forward
Oman is in a unique position to mediate talks on a security arrangement that could stabilise the region.
Proposing a non-aggression pact amid regional hostilities may seem premature. Yet agreements to stop war matter most when distrust is the deepest. The key question is whether regional governments can agree on rules that make their disagreements less destructive.
In a recent lecture at Cambridge University in the UK, Oman’s Foreign Minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, called for a non-aggression pact among all eight Gulf littoral states: the six members of the Gulf Cooperation Council along with Iraq and Iran. He described it as the essential prerequisite for an inclusive regional security architecture.
Could such a pact work? As Albusaidi conceded, it would be hard to achieve. But as another major escalation looms between Iran and the United States, the region urgently needs a diplomatic path forward.
Indeed, the ongoing conflict has proved so hard to resolve because the region’s security arrangements have remained underdeveloped, relying for too long on external powers. The way forward then can be an inclusive agreement.
Reviving the promise of 1976
The Omani proposal is anchored in a historic precedent. In November 1976, the foreign ministers of all eight Gulf littoral states met in Muscat to pursue collective security after Britain’s withdrawal from the region.
It remains the only time all eight have sat at one table. The Iranian Revolution, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran–Iraq war then pushed the region towards defensive arrangements that later hardened into exclusion.
For decades, Iran, in particular, was seen as a threat to the rest of the region. Yet, given that the country holds roughly half the Gulf coastline, any security architecture without it is structurally unsound.
It was not until 2019 that the idea of a regional security arrangement was revived. In May of that year, then Iranian Foreign Minister Javad Zarif proposed a regional non-aggression pact with Gulf neighbours during a visit to Baghdad, which Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov endorsed.
That September, Iranian President Hassan Rouhani launched the Hormuz Peace Endeavour (HOPE) at the UN General Assembly, envisaging a non-aggression pact among Hormuz states. Gulf reactions were largely dismissive, citing Iranian support for armed groups threatening regional stability.
The US-Israeli war on Iran has revived the idea on the Arab side. In May, the Financial Times reported that Saudi Arabia was discussing a non-aggression framework with Iran, reportedly modelled on the Helsinki process between the US and Russia during the Cold War.
This month, Qatar’s defence minister called for GCC–Iran dialogue, joined by Turkiye and Pakistan, towards a non-aggression agreement.
Oman’s proposal comes as the latest iteration of this regional shift. Muscat is in a unique position to mediate given its history of acting as a mediator and its recent record of hosting US-Iran talks in 2025 and February 2026. It has access that few others have.
Concluding a pact that works
The strongest objection against a Gulf pact with Iran is simple: Why trust a state whose conduct has threatened the region’s security? Gulf concerns about Iranian actions are not misunderstandings. Oman itself formally protested to Iran after drone attacks targeting Musandam and Al Wusta in July.
Reassurance is therefore insufficient. Inclusion must mean obligation. Membership in a regional pact would have to bind Iran as much as any other signatory, providing a means to constrain threatening behaviour and address legitimate grievances.
A pact must rest on observable conduct, reciprocal restraint and consequences for violations. At minimum, it would need commitments against the threat or use of force, interference in internal affairs, attacks on civilian infrastructure and support for armed groups conducting cross-border attacks, alongside protection of navigation.
To reach a workable agreement, negotiations can adopt a gradual approach. Consultations among the eight countries could first identify minimum shared interests: territorial security, functioning ports, reliable energy exports, civilian protection and uninterrupted trade. Oman can facilitate, but each state would represent itself; Muscat’s channel to Tehran confers no mandate to negotiate for its neighbours.
Initial talks should yield limited, reciprocal measures: military hotlines, rules for maritime encounters, notification of exercises and rapid communication after attacks. An understanding about protecting energy facilities, desalination plants and commercial shipping would offer an early test of compliance.
Hormuz is the obvious starting point, though progress could be hard. Oman-Iran talks have already outlined a temporary navigation arrangement. However, as Albusaidi conceded, it cannot be implemented unless Washington and Tehran compromise, including by reversing wartime actions that halted maritime traffic. Any wider framework must respect international navigation rights.
Armed groups would be the hardest issue to resolve. Governments should undertake neither to direct nor materially support cross-border attacks by such actors, and demonstrate compliance through verifiable steps. Where control is contested, the pact would need procedures for establishing evidence and requiring corrective action.
Compliance with initial measures could open cooperation on maritime safety, environmental protection and emergency response. Serious violations should trigger investigation, urgent consultation and agreed diplomatic consequences, while the right of self-defence would remain intact.
A regional pact would not settle every conflict touching the Gulf. The United States and Israel, both parties to this year’s war on Iran, would remain outside it and Yemen’s war involves actors whose agendas a Gulf arrangement could not easily bind. But a framework need not end every war to be worth having. It need only make it harder for any of them to become a war among its signatories.
The pact’s credibility will depend on whether it changes conduct. Fewer or no attacks, functioning crisis channels and demonstrable respect for sovereignty will matter more than signatures.
Present hostilities make the task difficult, but they also expose the cost of postponing it. The first achievement would be modest but consequential: establishing that disagreement entitles no state to endanger another’s security.

articles.title: Zelensky, Erdogan Discuss Peace Talks and Black Sea Security
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan met in Istanbul on Saturday, Oct. 31, to discuss the resumption of tripartite diplomatic negotiations to end the war, measures to restore safe navigation across the Black Sea, and prospects for hosting future peace talks in Turkey.
The bilateral discussions focused on integrating Turkey and European partners into prospective negotiations between Ukraine, the US, and Russia planned for the first half of November.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Speaking following their consultations, Zelensky confirmed that Kyiv is actively preparing for the three-way format while exploring avenues to expand allied participation and consider Turkey as a host venue.
“We are currently preparing for a trilateral format – Ukraine, the United States, Russia – in the first half of November,” Zelensky stated.
“We discussed… the prospects of such a format and other opportunities, in particular the possibilities of involving Turkey, involving Europe, involving all partners, and the possibilities of meeting here, in Turkey.”
Erdogan reaffirmed Ankara’s readiness to facilitate a diplomatic settlement, welcoming the renewed momentum surrounding international mediation efforts.
“During our negotiations today, we discussed in detail recent active efforts aimed at ensuring peace in Ukraine and the security situation in the Black Sea,” Erdogan said.
Russian Energy Strikes Cut Power to 280,000 Across Ukraine
“We note with great satisfaction that the initiative to end the war through diplomatic means has once again gained momentum.”
The Turkish president emphasized that establishing a binding agreement on the safety of navigation in the Black Sea could serve as a vital catalyst for achieving a comprehensive and lasting peace in Ukraine.
Condemnation of attacks on merchant shipping
The Istanbul summit occurred amid acute instability across western Black Sea maritime corridors following repeated kinetic drone strikes on commercial cargo ships navigating near Romanian and Bulgarian territorial waters.
Erdogan issued an explicit condemnation of strikes targeting commercial vessels, urging all belligerents to avoid further escalation across the maritime theater.
“It is obvious that attacks on civilian vessels and actions that further escalate tensions in the Black Sea will benefit no one,” Erdogan said.
“Under no circumstances can we accept these attacks – regardless of who carries them out and what motives are used to justify them. We call on all parties to act responsibly and behave accordingly.”
Zelensky highlighted the protracted degradation of regional security resulting from Russian maritime aggression since the illegal annexation of Crimea.
“Russia, through its aggression since 2014, has step by step made the situation in the Black Sea difficult and worse,” Zelensky stated.
“Turkey consistently supports our sovereignty, territorial integrity, and our steps that can protect safe navigation in the Black Sea and restore normal living conditions in the Black Sea region.”
The leaders also reviewed the uninterrupted operation of Ukrainian agricultural export corridors and bilateral economic cooperation.
Diplomatic alignment ahead of prospective November talks
Zelensky’s visit follows an Oct. 28 telephone conversation between Erdogan and US President Donald Trump, during which the Turkish leader affirmed that Ankara stands ready to help revive formal diplomatic talks between Ukraine and Russia.
The meeting also comes as international mediators explore venues for prospective working-level trilateral talks between Kyiv, Washington, and Moscow, with Abu Dhabi, Switzerland, and Turkey cited as potential host locations.
Zelensky previously stated that Kyiv hoped discussions could convene between Nov. 6 and Nov. 10, while Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov indicated that Moscow would be prepared to resume tripartite talks after its Nov. 4 National Unity Day holiday.

articles.title: Foreign media on Kazakhstan: Nuclear power, landmark Türkiye visit and major construction plans
articles.body:
Foreign media on Kazakhstan: Nuclear power, landmark Türkiye visit and major construction plans
As President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev calls for faster construction of nuclear power plants, receives a ceremonial welcome from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and proposes declaring 2027 “the Year of Large-scale Construction” to develop public infrastructure nationwide, Qazinform News Agency presents its weekly review of Kazakhstan coverage in foreign media.
Euronews: Kazakhstan's Tokayev calls for faster construction of nuclear power plants
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for a national uranium reserve and faster construction of two nuclear power plants in his annual state-of-the-nation address, Euronews reports.
“I believe it is possible, and perhaps even necessary, to begin construction of the Balkhash NPP as early as next year,” he said, also urging an agreement to advance the Moyynkum project.
Tokayev described an electricity surplus as essential for digitalization and artificial intelligence, while criticizing costly winter electricity imports followed by cheap summer exports.
He also urged Kazakhstan to capitalize on growing demand for overland transport.
“Kazakhstan must seize this historic opportunity to truly become a leading logistics hub for Eurasia,” he said.
The Aral-Caspian Highway is expected to shorten the Trans-Caspian route by 1,000 kilometres, while the Bakty-Ayagoz railway will add a third crossing with China.
Tokayev designated next year as the Year of Nationwide Construction, prioritizing public infrastructure.
Milliyet: President Erdoğan welcomed President Tokayev of Kazakhstan with an official ceremony
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan welcomed Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev with an official ceremony at the Presidential Complex in Ankara before bilateral and delegation-level talks, Milliyet reports.
The ceremony included both countries’ national anthems and a 21-gun salute. Tokayev greeted the guard of honor with “Hello, soldiers.”
According to Türkiye’s Directorate of Communications, the leaders discussed bilateral relations and regional and global issues.
Erdoğan said the two countries would strengthen their enhanced strategic partnership through further cooperation in trade, investment, energy, transport and the defense industry.
He also pledged close coordination with Kazakhstan during Türkiye’s chairmanship of the Organization of Turkic States.
Erdoğan invited Tokayev to attend the COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Antalya and was scheduled to host an official dinner in his honor.
Anadolu Agency: Türkiye, Kazakhstan to deepen defense industry cooperation
According to Anadolu Agency, Türkiye will deepen defense industry cooperation with Kazakhstan through joint production and mutually beneficial partnerships, Turkish defense industry chief Haluk Gorgun said on Wednesday.
His remarks followed talks in Ankara, where President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.
Gorgun described Türkiye as a reliable, long-term partner offering competitive defense products and policies supporting joint production.
"We will diversify and deepen our areas of cooperation with friendly and brotherly Kazakhstan within the framework of a win-win approach," he said.
He added that combining the two countries’ expertise would contribute to the security and prosperity of the Turkic world.
Hürriyet: Turkic world leaders gather in Ankara for landmark summit
Ankara is hosting the 13th Organization of Turkic States summit on October 29-30 as Türkiye celebrates the republic’s 103rd anniversary, Hürriyet reports.
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev was the first leader to arrive, receiving a ceremonial welcome from President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan before bilateral talks.
Held under the theme “Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Action,” the summit will address trade, energy, defense and transport, particularly the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor linking Asia and Europe.
Türkiye will assume the organization’s rotating chairmanship from Azerbaijan. Leaders are expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration, appoint a new secretary-general and agree on measures to strengthen cooperation.
Commonspace.eu: Kazakhstan set for major construction program after Tokayev’s speech
According to Commonspace.eu, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed declaring 2027 “the Year of Large-scale Construction”, calling for new and renovated public infrastructure nationwide.
Priorities include roads, airports, railway stations, housing and healthcare facilities, alongside rehabilitation centers for children with special needs.
Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said the “People’s Construction” programme would drive infrastructure development and economic reforms.
“This large-scale project will provide significant momentum for employment growth and improving citizens’ well-being,” he said.
Healthcare Minister Akmaral Alnazarova outlined plans for nearly 70 healthcare facilities, including perinatal centers, children’s hospitals and rehabilitation branches. The projects would add or modernize 9,200 hospital beds.
Euronews: Gold market and central banks: Russia and Kazakhstan sell as Poland and China buy
Kazakhstan plans to reduce gold’s share of its reserves from around 78% to 75% by year-end, after ranking among the world’s biggest buyers in the first eight months of 2026, Euronews reports.
“Kazakhstan has been buying gold for a long time, so it will now be selling at a significant profit,” says Adam Stroniawski, managing director of Polish precious metals dealer Mennica Skarbowa.
He believes the limited reduction and gradual sales will have little impact on global prices. Russia has also reduced its holdings, while Poland continues buying.
AP: As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them
Kazakhstan is seeking access to both American and Chinese AI ecosystems as rivalry between the two powers puts pressure on countries to choose sides, AP reports.
AI Minister Zhaslan Madiyev joined the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative in June, and then travelled to Shanghai three weeks later as Kazakhstan became a founding member of China’s World AI Cooperation Organization.
Kazakhstan hopes to attract investment, enter global AI supply chains and influence standards.

Russia’s War Losses in Ukraine Exceed 2 Million, Independent Estimate Finds
Russia’s mounting battlefield losses are reaching a staggering scale, with new estimates revealing how heavily Moscow has paid for its prolonged war against Ukraine.
Russia may have suffered between 1.4 million and 2.1 million military casualties, including as many as 770,000 soldiers killed, since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

According to The Economist on October 30, an updated statistical assessment estimates Russian military deaths at between 374,000 and 770,000, with the remaining casualties consisting of wounded personnel.
The figures represent a substantial increase from the publication’s previous estimates. In July 2025, The Economist assessed Russia’s total casualties at 900,000 to 1.3 million, including 190,000 to 350,000 deaths. By May 2026, those estimates had risen to 1.1–1.5 million casualties and 280,000–518,000 deaths.
The Economist’s calculations combine Western intelligence assessments, defense ministry data, independent research, and battlefield tracking. Russia does not publish comprehensive official casualty figures, making independent verification difficult.
Despite these losses, Moscow continues its military operations. The Economist also reported that Ukrainian forces had recaptured approximately 73 square kilometers of territory over the previous three months.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 31 that Russian forces had suffered another 1,670 personnel losses over the previous 24 hours, bringing Ukraine’s cumulative estimate to approximately 1,588,170 since February 2022.

articles.title: India trying to bring Russia, Ukraine & Europe to the table on 3 fronts: Jaishankar
articles.body:
India's External affairs minister S Jaishankar has discussed the protection of civilian shipping with Russia, Ukraine, and European nations
External affairs minister S Jaishankar on Sunday said India has held discussions with Russia, Ukraine and European countries on protecting civilian shipping, restoring grain exports through the Black Sea and preventing attacks on energy infrastructure amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war.According to news agency ANI, Speaking on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar said India was engaging with the parties on three key aspects of the conflict, including the safety of civilian vessels and seafarers, the restoration of grain shipments from Russia and Ukraine, and preventing attacks on energy infrastructure. He said India was trying to bring the concerned parties together to address these issues."One, not to attack civilian shipping and seafarers," he said, outlining the first of the three areas discussed with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.
On the second issue, Jaishankar stressed the need to restore grain shipments from both Russia and Ukraine, warning that exports through the Black Sea had declined sharply amid the conflict."The second, to find a way by which the grain exports from both Russia and Ukraine, these are two major exporters of grain for the global markets, can be restored, because that flow has cut down very sharply in the Black Sea," he said.
Jaishankar further highlighted the complexities involved in ensuring the safety of energy infrastructure, saying different parties had different interpretations of what should be covered under such an understanding."And the third is with regard to energy. Non-attack on energy is probably the most complicated piece because it means different things to the different players. There is energy infrastructure itself. To some, it would mean a refinery; to some, it would mean grids. There would be issues relating to ships carrying fuel," he said.He added that India is attempting to bring the concerned parties together to find common ground on these issues, particularly on the protection of energy infrastructure and fuel shipments.
The concerns raised by Jaishankar extend beyond the immediate conflict, given the Black Sea's importance to global trade. Any disruption to commercial shipping can affect the movement of essential commodities, raise freight and insurance costs and put pressure on international supply chains.Similarly, attacks on refineries, electricity grids and fuel-carrying vessels can disrupt energy supplies and push up global prices. Together, the safety of maritime routes, grain exports and energy infrastructure remains critical to maintaining stability in global food and energy markets.
Aryan Singh is a journalist with The Times of India, covering breaking news, defence and global conflicts. An alumnus of the IIMC, he tracks the people, weapons and geopolitics behind the headlines, with a focus on India’s national security, military affairs and conflicts shaping the world.

articles.title: 'Life simply returned' – Oleshky ceasefire gives Kherson short respite amid years of Russian terror
articles.body:
'Life simply returned' – Oleshky ceasefire gives Kherson short respite amid years of Russian terror
A woman poses for photographs next to Kherson Gateway Stela, next to a road covered by anti-drone nets, during a temporary ceasefire in the southern Kherson region, at the entrance to the city of Kherson, southern Ukraine, on Oct. 31, 2026. (Roman Pilipey / AFP via Getty Images)
Editor's note: Ukrainian journalist Daria Litovchenko contributed to reporting on the ground in Kherson, while Francis Farrell compiled the material from Kyiv.
In all of Ukraine, perhaps no city has suffered as much, for as long, during Russia's full-scale war as Kherson.
From the initial eight months of brutal Russian occupation in 2022 — with all of the associated torture, looting and deportation — to Russia's man-made flood caused by the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam, to the systematic "human safari" attacks targeting civilians by Russian drones that have gone on since 2024, Kherson has lived from horror to horror without a break until now.
Over the last few days, this city at the delta of Ukraine's Dnipro River enjoyed something that has become an almost unknown sensation: quiet.
On Oct. 27, along the section of front line following the river through Kherson Oblast, Russian and Ukrainian forces began observing a ceasefire of a scale and length unprecedented in four and a half years of the full-scale war.
Every morning that the ceasefire continued, the daily updates of Kherson Oblast Governor Oleksandr Prokudin — normally filled with reports of attacks and casualties in Kherson and other riverbank communities — read "attacks and casualties were not recorded."
The ceasefire, agreed upon as part of a U.S.-mediated humanitarian mission to the beleaguered Russian-occupied city of Oleshky across the river, also gave the residents of Kherson the opportunity to walk the streets of their city without the fear of death from Russian glide bombs, artillery and, especially, drones.
read also
Despite the gloomy autumn weather, the temporary peace brought locals out onto the streets in numbers unseen since Kherson was liberated from Russian occupation in November 2022.
"People can just feel calm and walk around, ride a bike, not run from one place to another," said Iryna Leonova to the Kyiv Independent outside a supermarket.
"It's not that life has changed in the last few days, it simply returned."
Normally, the danger all around Kherson is particularly felt in the so-called "red zone," the neighborhoods and settlements closest to the river, where civilization has almost completely disappeared due to the round-the-clock threat of Russian drones.
Now, these areas are once again accessible, although not completely safe, as landmines dropped over years by Russian forces across the river continue to present a threat, as the tragic death of Marines press officer Volodymyr Obertas showed on Oct. 28.
Usually a resident of the city's Ostriv neighborhood, Inna Sapai has long moved to a safer part of Kherson, further away from the river.
In the last days, she has not only been able to run errands that would have otherwise carried with them too much danger, but she also checked on her home in Ostriv.
"It's strange to feel this sense of movement in the city. Not just the people or the cars, but this intangible feeling in the air," Sapai said to the Kyiv Independent.
"Before, any fleeting moment of quiet just weighed down on you, but now, the silence really lifts your mood."
Since the ceasefire, thousands of Kherson locals have returned to their hometown from outside the city.
Some have come to inspect their homes and collect personal belongings, others just for the short-lived feeling of returning to a hometown that has long become unfit for life.
Markets once almost abandoned have come back to life, while city workers have used the opportunity to repair critical infrastructure that was inaccessible until now due to the drone threat.
But everywhere, local resident Natalia said, who declined to give her last name, the bittersweet feeling of how temporary the quiet will be hangs.
"I feel very mixed emotions, there is not really any joy per se, because even though you see how many people have come to the city — yesterday I was stuck in traffic for the first time in years — but there is an understanding that in just a few days everyone will leave again," she said.
"There have been a lot of tears, as people come home to see how their homes have been damaged or ruined completely. But home is home, and Kherson is a place of power for all of us."
According to Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, the ceasefire will continue until 11 p.m. on Nov. 1, upon which the daily strikes across the river are expected to begin again.
Despite the major international effort to make it happen, the Oleshky ceasefire also displayed to the world how quickly the fighting can end in Ukraine if Russia makes the decision to stop.
But with the resumption of hostilities, residents now anticipate that the worst of Russia's campaign to rid the city of life could still be ahead of them.
"I feel sad knowing that soon this will all end, and a great fear of the unknown, that we don't know what will come next," said Natalia.
"People are worried, and I am too, at the fact that it can only get worse."

articles.title: Hellenic Navy Receives Second French-Built FDI Frigate
articles.body:
The Hellenic Navy has received the second of four FDI HN-class frigates ordered by Greece – HS Nearchos (F602) – built by French shipbuilder Naval Group.
Naval News reported on this, citing Greece’s Ministry of National Defense.
The handover ceremony took place on October 30, 2026, at Naval Group’s shipyard in Lorient, France. Nikos Dendias, Greek Minister of National Defense, and Catherine Vautrin, French Minister of the Armed Forces, attended the ceremony.
HS Nearchos is the second frigate of this class to be delivered to the Hellenic Navy, following the lead ship, HS Kimon, which was handed over in December 2025. Nearchos is also the first Greek FDI frigate delivered in the Standard 2 configuration, which provides enhanced combat capabilities.
In particular, this configuration includes two additional SYLVER A50 vertical launching system modules, four SYLENA Mk1 decoy-launching systems, and a 21-cell RAM launcher for short-range surface-to-air missiles, providing the ship with additional air-defense capabilities.
Today, Naval Group delivered HS Nearchos, the second FDI frigate for the Hellenic Navy, in presence of @NikosDendias , Minister of National Defence of the Hellenic Republic, and @CaVautrin, Minister of the Armed Forces. https://t.co/ZdfQ1E4rlD
— Naval Group (@navalgroup) October 30, 2026
The Greek frigates are scheduled to receive further upgrades to the Standard 2+ and Standard 2++ configurations. In particular, the third ship of the class, HS Formion, is expected to be the first delivered in the Standard 2+ configuration, in April 2027. HS Nearchos is scheduled to be upgraded to the Standard 2++ configuration by April 2029.

Radar surveillance systems operated by Romania's Ministry of National Defence detected two unmanned aerial vehicles that had entered the country's airspace without authorisation on the evening of 31 October.
